title: fused_moe: remove incorrect topk adjustment in get_2stage_cfgs for EP
body:
## Summary

  Removes `topk -= int(is_ep)` from `get_2stage_cfgs` in `aiter/fused_moe.py`.

  ## Root Cause

  When `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_FUSED_MOE_SHARED_EXPERT=1` is set together with EP (`expert_mask is not None`), the removed line incorrectly reduces
  `topk` by 1 before building the config lookup key. This strips the Fused Shared Expert column from the key, causing a wrong tuned-config to be
  selected (or a cache miss falling back to untuned defaults).

  The adjustment was originally intended to strip the fake always-masked expert slot that EP callers append to `topk_ids`. That convention no longer
   applies uniformly — fused shared expert uses the last expert slot as a real expert, so subtracting 1 is invalid in that path.

  ## Change

  Removes 4 lines from `get_2stage_cfgs` — the comment block and the `topk -= int(is_ep)` mutation.

  ## Test Plan
  - Reproduce with EP + `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_FUSED_MOE_SHARED_EXPERT=1` and confirm correct config is selected
  - Run `op_tests/test_moe_2stage.py` to verify no regression on standard EP path

  Fixes #5595

title: [Config] configs: GLM-5.3 fused shared MoE rows for gfx950
body:
## Why

GLM-5.3 shared-expert fusion changes the routed fused-MoE dispatch from `E=288, topk=8` to `E=289, topk=9`. The ninth expert is always selected with weight 1.0, so one AITER launch performs the routed and shared gate/up GEMM, `SiLU(gate) * up`, down GEMM, and routed-weight accumulation.

The two TP-local signatures are:

- TP4: model/intermediate `(4096,512)`, `E=289`, `topk=9`
- TP8: model/intermediate `(4096,256)`, `E=289`, `topk=9`

The existing model-config set does not cover either signature. Without exact rows, both use fallback kernels.

## What this adds

Sixteen gfx950/cu256 rows are added in a dedicated GLM-5.3 fused-shared table:

- TP4: `M={4,8,1024,2048,4096,8192,16384}`
- TP8: `M={8,32,128,256,512,2048,4096,8192,16384}`

The matching untuned table records the complete 15-shape power-of-two ladder for both TP4 and TP8 (30 source rows).

Both signatures were tuned with the standard fused-MoE tuner over the compatible one-stage ASM block-FP8 family. Only rows improving AITER's production operator by at least 3% were retained. The remaining buckets are intentionally absent and keep fallback dispatch.

## Validation

- All 16 retained rows have `err1=0.0%`, `run_1stage=1`, `kernelName2` empty, and `us2=0`.
- Production-operator execution passed for every retained row: 7 TP4 and 9 TP8, all status `OK`.
- TP4 retained rows improve production-operator latency by 10.98-48.12%.
- TP8 retained rows improve production-operator latency by 4.61-45.11%.
- Direct fused-versus-separate tensor comparison passed at TP4 and TP8 from M=1 through M=16384: all outputs finite, minimum cosine 0.999822, maximum mean absolute error 7.45e-6.
- `test_csv_validation.py` and `test_config_shape_collision.py`: 32 passed, 37 subtests passed.
- Every new dispatch key occurs exactly once across the complete current-main fused-MoE config set.
- No open AITER PR contains any new dispatch key.

Hardware: MI355X (`gfx950`, 256 CUs).  
Image: `rocm/sgl-dev:v0.5.20-rocm724-mi35x-20260921`.  
Tuning branch base: upstream `ROCm/aiter` `main` at commit `7d2f6a51a6364e0aad4d2e81dda5cc28c82bfdd9`.

## Submission Checklist

- [x] Looked over the ROCm contributing guidelines.
- [x] Targeting the repository default branch (`main`).
- [x] Included successful config-validation and production-operator results.
- [x] Commit includes the required DCO sign-off.
- [ ] CI green for the updated head.

title: [Config] Tune a8w8 bpreshuffle for Kimi-K3's KDA gate at tp4
body:
## What

Adds the 62 missing `N=3072, K=128` rows to `a8w8_bpreshuffle_tuned_gemm_kimik3.csv`, plus the matching shapes in the untuned CSV.

## Why

Kimi-K3's KDA gate projection `f_b_proj` is `[M, 128] x [128, 128 * heads/tp]`. K is the KDA head dim, 128 at any tp; N is `num_local_heads * 128`, so the 96 KDA heads give **N=1536 at tp8** and **N=3072 at tp4**. Only 1536 was tuned, so tp4 misses the table on every token.

A miss here is not a slower kernel. `gemm_a8w8_bpreshuffle` falls through to `gemm_a8w8_bpreshuffle_ck`, whose `rowwise_heuristic_dispatch` has branches only for `K >= 512` and `K >= 192 && K % 64 == 0`. K=128 hits:

```
TORCH_CHECK(false, "Unsupported K for heuristic dispatch: 128. Supported K greater than 192 and K % 64 == 0.")
```

so the process raises on its first token. Tuning confirms there is no CK kernel for this shape at all: every `ck` candidate reported `This GEMM is not supported!`, and every winner is cktile or flydsl.

## How

Same M grid the `N=1536` rows carry (64-step between 1024 and 4096), so padded-M lookups behave the same at both widths.

```
python3 csrc/ck_gemm_a8w8_bpreshuffle/gemm_a8w8_bpreshuffle_tune.py \
  -i aiter/configs/model_configs/a8w8_bpreshuffle_untuned_gemm_kimik3.csv \
  -o aiter/configs/model_configs/a8w8_bpreshuffle_tuned_gemm_kimik3.csv \
  --mp 8 --errRatio 0.01
```

62 shapes, zero failures. 5 pick cktile at small M, 57 flydsl above -- the same split `N=1536` has.

The rows are inserted in the file's existing `(N, M, K)` order rather than letting the tuner re-sort the whole file, so the diff is 62 additions and no deletions.

## Verification

gfx950 / 256 CU, via `gemm_a8w8_bpreshuffle` directly:

| shape | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| tp8 `M=1..16384 N=1536 K=128` | OK | OK |
| tp4 `M=1..16384 N=3072 K=128` | **FAIL** `Unsupported K for heuristic dispatch: 128` | **OK** |

End-to-end: Kimi-K3 at `--pipeline-parallel-size 2 --tensor-parallel-size 4` on MI355X x8 now serves with no framework-side GEMM override, GSM8K 5-shot over the full 1319 questions at **0.9598 flexible-extract / 0.9606 strict-match**, inside the range `recipes/Kimi-K3.md` records for this model (0.9591-0.9659 / 0.9591-0.9666).

title: Fp8 mqa logits gfx950 dsa tune
body:
> **Status: do not submit.** Re-measured on current upstream `main` (`4927f8f5c`, 2026-09-23), the tile change makes the DSA indexer **5.8% slower**. Upstream already fixed the same problem in #5216 and #5603, and fixed it better. This file records the measurement so nobody reopens this.

## What this PR was going to do

On gfx950, give the DSA indexer shape of `fp8_mqa_logits` (32 heads × head size 128) its own tile: 128-wide KV tiles, `waves_per_eu=2`, `num_warps=2`. It also moved the `BLOCK_M=2` threshold from `seq_len > 4096` down to `>= 1024`.

The reason: sglang splits each prefill's indexer call into chunks of roughly 1–2k rows, to keep the fp32 logits under 2 GiB. The old `seq_len > 4096` threshold almost never fired, so every chunk ran `BLOCK_M=1` and re-read the whole cached context once per row.

## Why it no longer applies

Upstream changed this code twice after our base (merge-base 2026-08-29):

- **#5216** (09-09): general optimization of the gfx950 kernel.
- **#5603** (09-16): adds split-k. `BLOCK_M=2` is now also chosen when there are enough workgroups (`cdiv(seq_len, 2) * num_kv_splits >= 1024`), no longer only when `seq_len > 4096`. That is the same gate problem we fixed.

gfx950 also always takes the buffer path now, so the LLVM crash that our `use_buffer_store` guard was avoiding cannot happen.

## Measurements

MI355X, one GPU, Triton 3.7. 39 `(rows × context)` chunk shapes taken from a GLM-5.2 AgentX replay, weighted by each shape's share of GEMM work. Script: `bench_upstream.py`, raw data: `bench_*.json`.

| aiter version | total time | vs upstream `main` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| our base (09-21 snapshot) | 81.4 ms | 1.59x |
| our base + this PR | 65.6 ms | 1.32x |
| **upstream `main`** | **49.1 ms** | **1.00x** |
| upstream `main` + this PR's tile | 51.7 ms | 1.06x (slower) |

- On our old base this PR was worth −16.5%. That matches the earlier −23% measured with a different weighting.
- Upstream `main` alone is 25% faster than our patched version.
- Adding our tile on top of upstream makes 96% of the work slower. The worst shape is 1.22x, the best 0.93x. The output is bit-identical to upstream on all 39 shapes, so the tile only costs speed, not correctness.

Correctness was not re-run beyond the bit-exact check above: `op_tests/triton_tests/attention/test_fp8_mqa_logits.py` and GSM8k were skipped because the PR is not going out.

## What to do instead

Bump sglang's aiter to upstream `main`. On this benchmark that gives a 1.59x faster indexer GEMM, far more than this PR delivered. Upstream's output is not bit-identical to our old base because the kernel was rewritten, so the bump needs an accuracy check (GSM8k with GLM-5.2) and an AgentX TTT / Interactivity rerun.

Files in this directory:

- `PR.orig.md`: the previous draft of this file.
- `tile_on_upstream.diff`: this PR's tile ported onto upstream, as measured above.
- `aiter_base/`, `aiter_upstream/`, `aiter_old_base/`, `aiter_old_opt/`: the git worktrees that were benchmarked.

title: [Triton/Gluon] [Bugfix] [Perf] Support page size 8 in paged MQA logits on both layouts, and fix large KV offsets
body:
## Problem

On `main` the non-preshuffle ("plain") Gluon paged MQA logits kernel has no block-paging path at all: it indexes `kv_indices` with the *token* position, which is only correct when `KVBlockSize == 1`. A KV cache paged at more than one token per page therefore reads the wrong pages — and nothing rejects it, because `deepgemm_fp8_paged_mqa_logits` only asserts `KVBlockSize == 1` on gfx1250. On gfx942/gfx950 a paged cache is silently mis-scored rather than refused. The preshuffle path cannot stand in for it either: it requires `KVBlockSize % 16 == 0`, because the shuffled KV feeds the 16-token MFMA B operand directly and a page of 8 is half a tile.

That leaves **page size 8** — what DeepSeek V4.1 decode uses for the indexer KV cache — unreachable on `main` on either layout.

Separately, both paths form KV and FP32-scale addresses through 32-bit strides, so a cache past the 2 GiB buffer-descriptor range wraps; and the preshuffle logits store is not bounded by `max_model_len`, so a short final chunk spills into the next output row.

These are all silent-wrong-answer bugs: the indexer logits feed a top-k, so a corrupted tail turns into wrong sparse-KV indices rather than a crash.

## What this changes

### Plain path

- **Block paging in the plain kernel.** Derive the page index as `token // KVBlockSize` and the in-page offset as `token % KVBlockSize`, instead of treating the token position as a page index. The backward-shifted first tile can carry negative positions, so those lanes are clamped to token 0 of page 0 before the offset is formed, including for the scale.
- **64-bit KV addressing on the plain path.** `stride_k_seq` and `stride_scale_seq` become `i64`, and the K and scale reads become global loads, so a cache beyond 2 GiB still addresses correctly. The plain path builds per-token addresses from the page table, so the 32-bit stride product was the overflow site.
- **Preshuffle large offsets and tail store.** Widen the page index to 64 bit before scaling by the stride, and bound the logits store by `max_model_len` so a short final chunk cannot reach into the next row.

### Preshuffle path

Page 8 on the plain path works but is the slow layout. No new load structure is needed to reach the fast one: the per-lane page index already varies at `KVBlockSize` granularity, and a page shorter than `ChunkK // 2` already takes the "page index per lane" branch, so the two pages behind one tile are already addressable. What was hardcoded is the shuffle group.

- **`ShuffleRows = min(KVBlockSize, 16)`** in both `_gluon_deepgemm_fp8_paged_mqa_logits_preshuffle` and its `_varctx` twin, replacing the literal 16 in the B-operand offset. One tile is then assembled from two pages.
- **The wrapper admits 8**, and only 8, below the tile size. The addressing generalises to any page that divides 16, and pages 1, 2 and 4 do run correctly — max abs error 0.0043 to 0.0058 against FP32, the same band as page 16, and faster than plain at the same page size (on a one-off probe, page 1: 271.0 us vs 398.1 us; page 4: 189.2 us vs 287.7 us). They stay rejected because no caller asks for them and the sweep does not cover them. gfx1250 preshuffle reshapes by a literal `KVBlockSize // 16` for its TDM block load, so pages below 16 stay rejected there outright.
- **The row-group stride** goes from a literal `16 * 128` to `ShuffleRows * HiddenDim` to stay consistent with the above. This is not what makes page 8 work — a page that short holds one group, so the term is zero either way — and at `HiddenDim` 128 the two expressions are equal. No configuration a caller can reach today changes; every caller runs `HiddenDim` 128.
- **The bench gets the host side of this.** `--kv_preshuffle` used to fall back to plain whenever the page was not a multiple of 16, quietly reporting the wrong path, and it shuffled at a fixed 16 rows. It now honours the flag, derives the layout from the page size, and reports `kv_tokens` so a run can be turned into bandwidth. Defaults do not move: 16 preshuffled, 1 plain.

**Caller-visible:** a page of 8 must be shuffled in groups of its own length, `shuffle_weight(kv, layout=(8, 16))`, rather than the default `(16, 16)`. Getting this wrong is not silent — `shuffle_weight` asserts `shape[-2] % 16 == 0` on the default layout.

## Performance

Measured with the bench in this PR on gfx950, heads 32 / head-dim 128, three shapes x two layouts x page 8/16, three rounds per point with the arms rotated inside a round, medians below. Round-to-round spread is under 1.9 us everywhere. The rows below carry a 286 MB working set, past the 256 MB MALL, so their TB/s is DRAM-bound; the other two shapes fit in MALL and their TB/s is not an HBM figure.

batch 16, next_n 1, 1M context:

| page | path | latency | effective BW |
|---:|---|---:|---:|
| 8 | plain | 431.384 us | 5.125 TB/s |
| 16 | plain | 410.064 us | 5.382 TB/s |
| 8 | **preshuffle** | **379.863 us** | **5.820 TB/s** |
| 16 | preshuffle | 359.784 us | 6.134 TB/s |

Halving the page costs 5.58% here, and 3.01% to 5.20% across the five other shape and layout pairs. Both layouts move together, so what is paid for is the page and not the shuffle: one tile's contiguous run drops from 256 B to 128 B, and the page table doubles in width. The page table is 0.18% of the byte model, which leaves the contiguity.

That cost does not change what a page-8 caller should do, because page 16 is not one of its options. Against the only alternative it has — page-8 plain — preshuffle is **11.9% faster**, and it also beats page-16 plain by 7.4%. The speedup preshuffle already had is essentially kept at the smaller page: 1.096x to 1.692x over plain at page 16, 1.088x to 1.664x at page 8 across the three shapes.

## Testing

`op_tests/test_pa_mqa_logits_offset.py`, 105 cases, all passing on gfx950 (MI35x):

- `test_paged_mqa_logits_non_preshuffle` — block sizes 1 / **8** / 16 / 64 / 128 x ChunkK 64 / 256 x compact / padded page tables x the decode and MTP shapes. Compact tables expose token-indexed out-of-bounds reads; padded tables keep those reads in allocated memory and expose wrong scores instead. Output rows are sentinel-guarded on both sides so a store that walks off a row is caught.
- `test_paged_mqa_logits_preshuffle` — new, and the sweep the preshuffle path never had; previously only the large-KV-offset cases reached it, all at the default ChunkK. Pages **8** / 16 / 32 / 64 / 128 / 256 x ChunkK 128 / 256 x compact / padded tables x the decode and MTP shapes. The page sizes pick out how the B tile gets assembled: 8 is half a tile and draws from two pages, 16 is exactly one, 32 through 128 are several row groups inside one page, and 256 exceeds `ChunkK // 2` and so takes the one-page-per-stage branch. ChunkK 128 and 256 are the two the callers ask for — the bench runs preshuffle at 128, the indexer at 256.
- `test_paged_mqa_logits_large_kv_offsets` — plain and preshuffle, including a `preshuffle-B8` row, with the referenced pages placed around the 2 / 4 / 8 GiB boundaries, so the offset arithmetic is exercised without allocating a multi-GiB reference.
- `test_paged_mqa_logits_wide_output_no_tail_drop` — the dense `[rows, 1<<20]` layout whose row 512 store lands exactly on 2**31 bytes.

Everything is compared against an FP32 reference built from the same FP8 inputs. Before the preshuffle commit, the 8 page-8 rows of the new sweep fail — rejected by the wrapper before they reach the device — and the other 40 pass unchanged.

The bench was run in all three configurations it can take — `--kv_preshuffle` (page 16), `--kv_preshuffle --blocksize 8`, and plain (page 1) — with `logits_diff` at 0.00046 to 0.00047 in each.

## Relationship to #5614

#5614 carries the plain-path fixes plus a batch of decode-grid and persistent-CTA perf work, and its review surface has grown accordingly. This PR is page size 8 on both layouts, plus the addressing bugs in the way of it, split out so it reaches `main` without waiting on that perf review. The decode-grid and persistent-CTA commits stay in #5614.

The preshuffle half arrived here through #5768, which was merged into this branch rather than reviewed separately.

title: [Triton/Gluon] [CI] [Kernel] Gluon paged-decode attention with sigmoid output gate and group-128 FP8 epilogue (gfx950)
body:
# [Kernel] Gluon paged-decode attention with sigmoid output gate and group-128 FP8 epilogue (gfx950)

## Summary

Adds `paged_attention_output_gate_group_fp8_quant`, a Gluon paged-decode
attention op for gfx950 whose epilogue applies a sigmoid output gate and
optionally emits group-128 FP8 alongside the BF16 result.

It replaces **three launches with two** at the Qwen3-Next full-attention
boundary — paged decode attention, then `out * sigmoid(gate)`, then the
per-group activation quant the next GEMM consumes — by folding the gate and the
quant into the split-K merge the attention already performs.

## Motivation

**aiter has no op that fits this shape.** Checked at HEAD:

| existing op | KV layout | why it does not fit |
|---|---|---|
| `pa_decode`, `pa_decode_gluon` | block-table, `kv_block_size ∈ {16,64,1024}` | the target runs `page_size = 1` with a CSR index list; and neither has an epilogue seam — the store is a bare `tl.store` in eight kernel bodies |
| `pa_decode_sparse` | CSR, `page_size = 1` ✓ | **MLA-style: K and V are the same tensor.** Measured, not assumed — feeding a `[pages, 2D]` pool and testing three candidate references, only `K = V = kv[:, :D]` matches (mean rel 0.0019; reading `V = kv[:, D:]` is off by 1.48). It cannot express distinct K and V caches. |

So there is currently **no separate-K/V CSR paged-decode op in aiter at all**,
with or without an epilogue. That gap is worth filling independently of the gate.

**Both halves of the epilogue already exist here, unfused.**
`fusions/fused_sigmoid_mul.py` is exactly `out * sigmoid(gate)`;
`_triton_kernels/quant/fused_fp8_quant.py::_fp8_quant_op` is the same
`max(abs)/FP8_MAX` group formula with a `1e-10` floor. This op folds both into a
merge that is already reading the partials, so they cost no extra pass over
`[tokens, H*256]`.

**Emitting `(fp8, scales)` is an established argument in this repo.**
`fusions/attn_res.py:352 attn_res_gate(..., out_quant_dtype=None)` makes it in
its own docstring — *"an `(fp8, scale)` pair a GEMM can consume directly instead
of a BF16 tensor that each consumer quantizes for itself."* This op follows that
convention, and the FP8 output is opt-in via `quant_dtype=None`.

## Changes

| file | content |
|---|---|
| `_gluon_kernels/gfx950/attention/paged_attention_output_gate.py` | long-context body: split-K attention producing `(numerator, denominator, maximum)` partials, plus the merge carrying the gate + group-FP8 epilogue |
| `_gluon_kernels/gfx950/attention/paged_attention_output_gate_short_context.py` | short-context body |
| `attention/paged_attention_output_gate.py` | wrapper, body selection, `paged_attention_output_gate_supported() -> (bool, reason)` |
| `op_tests/triton_tests/attention/test_paged_attention_output_gate.py` | fp32 reference, `torch.testing.assert_close`, `pytest.skip` off-gfx950 |
| `op_tests/op_benchmarks/triton/bench_paged_attention_output_gate.py` | `run_benchmark(args)`, CSV + PNG |

No tuned config JSON: no `pa_*` op in the tree ships one, and
`configs/CLAUDE.md` forbids reusing the GEMM `M_LEQ_x`/`M_GEQ_x` scheme for
attention.

### API

```python
paged_attention_output_gate_group_fp8_quant(
    query,            # [T, H, 256] bf16
    key_cache,        # [pages, 1, 256] fp8_e4m3
    value_cache,      # [pages, 1, 256] fp8_e4m3
    kv_indptr,        # [T+1] int32, true prefix sum
    kv_indices,       # [total] int32, per-token slots (page_size = 1)
    gate,             # [T, H*256] bf16
    *,
    scale: float,
    max_context: int | None = None,         # body selector; never clamps
    k_scale=None, v_scale=None,             # per-tensor
    quant_dtype: torch.dtype | None = None, # None -> skip the FP8 epilogue
) -> tuple[Tensor, Tensor | None, Tensor | None]
#    (bf16 [T, H*256], fp8 [T, H*256], fp32 scales [T, H*2])
```

**Two bodies, one range check.** `max_context <= 32768` selects the
short-context body, above it the long-context one; they differ in the split-K
decomposition, which is what the two regimes want differently. `max_context` is
a body selector only — it never clamps, the live length always comes from
`kv_indptr`.

**Neither body is specialised to batch.** `BATCH` is not a kernel constant in
the long body (the row comes from `gl.program_id(0)`), so one binary serves any
batch size at any context length.

That matters for coverage: a CUDA graph capture asks for decode
batches of 1, 2, 4, 8, **12**, 16, **24**, 32, **40**, **48**, **56**, 64, and
dispatch happens once at capture — a miss is baked into the captured graph
permanently rather than retried per step. The test parametrizes over exactly
those sizes.

## Performance

MI355X (gfx950), ROCm 7.0, Triton 3.8, torch 2.9.0a0. Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B shapes:
`H=4`, `head_dim=256`, `page_size=1`, fp8_e4m3 KV.

**Method.** A CUDA graph holding one kernel costs ~9.3 µs to replay on this host
regardless of the kernel, so every measurement captures 50 invocations per graph
(live floor 1.70 µs). This matters for the comparison and not just the absolute
numbers: `triton.testing.do_bench` has no graph mode in this Triton, and the
distortion is **not** common-mode — the fused op is two launches and the stock
composition is four — so `do_bench` reads this as 1.31× where graph capture reads
2.12×. The shipped benchmark graph-captures by default; `--do-bench` restores the
conventional path.

**Configuration: vs. the three launches this op replaces** — `paged_attention_ragged`
(what SGLang's aiter backend calls today) + a sigmoid-gate multiply + a group-128
activation quant. Microseconds per decode step for one attention layer,
`H=4`, `head_dim=256`, `page_size=1`, fp8_e4m3 KV.

34 (context, batch) cells, 3 rounds each with measurement order shuffled and the
fixture seed varied per round; live floor 1.70 us and no cell within 2x of it.
Representative batches shown.

| context | batch | Before (us) | After (us) | Improvement |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 536 | 1 | 16.81 | **5.15** | **3.26x** |
| 1 536 | 8 | 17.22 | **5.04** | **3.41x** |
| 1 536 | 32 | 17.78 | **7.05** | **2.52x** |
| 1 536 | 64 | 23.89 | **10.59** | **2.26x** |
| 8 192 | 1 | 17.50 | **5.92** | **2.96x** |
| 8 192 | 8 | 18.74 | **8.09** | **2.32x** |
| 8 192 | 32 | 39.28 | **22.89** | **1.72x** |
| 8 192 | 64 | 63.57 | **41.18** | **1.54x** |
| 32 768 | 1 | 19.74 | **8.60** | **2.29x** |
| 32 768 | 8 | 41.22 | **24.13** | **1.71x** |
| 32 768 | 32 | 119.28 | **95.81** | **1.24x** |
| 32 768 | 64 | 237.59 | **172.01** | **1.38x** |
| 65 536 | 1 | 23.69 | **12.49** | **1.90x** |
| 65 536 | 8 | 68.49 | **45.78** | **1.50x** |
| 65 536 | 32 | 222.82 | **167.56** | **1.33x** |
| 65 536 | 64 | 483.62 | **336.17** | **1.44x** |
| 131 072 | 1 | 37.42 | **19.23** | **1.95x** |
| 131 072 | 8 | 139.00 | **90.00** | **1.54x** |
| 131 072 | 32 | 480.82 | **333.73** | **1.44x** |

**Geomean 1.97x over all 34 cells; range 1.24-3.41x.**

### Bandwidth utilisation and roofline

The roofline shows why the long-context ratio settles where it does. Traffic is
`bs * context * 256 * 2` bytes and is **identical for both implementations at a
given cell** -- same bytes, same gather. Achieved bandwidth is therefore just
`traffic / time`, i.e. the same fact as runtime re-expressed against the hardware
limit. It is reported because it answers what a raw speedup cannot: **how much
headroom is left.** MI355X HBM3E peak is 8.0 TB/s, and at the largest cells:

| | achieved | % of peak |
|---|---|---|
| this op | 6.52 TB/s | **81%** |
| stock | 4.82 TB/s | 60% |

4.82 / 6.52 = 0.74, which is exactly the long-context ratio in the table above.
At 81% of peak
there is at most 19% more available to any implementation, so the asymptotic win
is gather efficiency, not fusion. Below bs~8 the kernel is latency-bound rather
than bandwidth-bound (9% of peak at bs=1) -- only a few MB to move, and the limit
is occupancy and launch, which is why the fused epilogue matters most there.

## Testing

- [x] Unit test added — fp32 PyTorch reference, `torch.testing.assert_close`,
      over batch ∈ {1,2,4,8,12,16,24,32,40,48,56,64,128}, heads ∈ {4,8,16},
      context ∈ {1,129,1024}, a `max_context` on each side of the crossover so
      both bodies are exercised, with and without `quant_dtype`, plus a
      non-contiguous-gate case, a case proving `max_context` never clamps, a
      both-bodies-agree case, and predicate coverage.
      **488 passed, 9 skipped on gfx950** (the skips are heads 1/2/3, which
        have no short-body path, and say so). Correctness is additionally established outside
- [x] Benchmark added.
- [x] `pytest.skip` on non-gfx950.
- [x] `FILE_TIMES` entry added in `.github/scripts/split_tests.sh` (7.6 s
      measured, registered at 20 for headroom on a loaded runner).

**The epilogue's numerics are contract.** Three BF16 rounding boundaries —
attention→bf16→fp32, sigmoid→bf16→fp32, product→bf16 — before the group absmax.
The test reproduces them exactly; an implementation that keeps the intermediates
in fp32 produces different FP8 codes.

**Two guards the reference implementation lacked**, both now asserted by tests:
the gate is indexed through its row stride rather than assuming
`stride(0) == heads*256`, and the support predicate checks the cache dim stride
the gather relies on.

## Documentation

A Quick Reference row plus a detail section in
  `aiter/ops/triton/gluon/README.md`, matching the format the other two attention
  kernels use. The bandwidth quoted there is the output of the command that row
  cites (`--context 8192 --compare --metric bandwidth`, tokens=64: 6530 GB/s),
  since that column documents the perf of the typical test.

## Dependencies

- [x] No new third-party dependencies.

## Breaking changes

None — new op, no existing signature touched.

## Scope

- **gfx950 only.** Guarded by `arch_info`; `paged_attention_output_gate_supported()`
  returns `(False, reason)` elsewhere so callers fall back rather than crash.
- **No CUDA path affected.**
- `page_size = 1`, `head_dim = 256`, `heads ≤ 16`, per-tensor `k_scale`/`v_scale`,
  fp8 e4m3 KV. All checked by the predicate, all reported with a reason.

## Reproduction

The measurements use a public base image plus one change — Triton upgraded to
3.8. **The upgrade is required, not incidental:** the Gluon launcher passes
`llvm_fn_attrs=`, which does not exist in Triton 3.7, and the first launch fails
without it.

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
ARG BASE=lmsysorg/sglang-rocm:v0.5.19-rocm700-mi35x-20260910
FROM ${BASE}

# Gluon needs llvm_fn_attrs, added in Triton 3.8. The base ships 3.7.
ARG TRITON_VERSION=3.8.0
ARG TRITON_INDEX=https://download.pytorch.org/whl/nightly/rocm7.0
RUN python -m pip install --no-deps --force-reinstall --pre \
      --index-url "${TRITON_INDEX}" \
      "triton==${TRITON_VERSION}"
```

```bash
docker build -t pa-gate:local \
  --build-arg BASE=lmsysorg/sglang-rocm:v0.5.19-rocm700-mi35x-20260910 .

docker run --rm --device=/dev/kfd --device=/dev/dri \
  --security-opt seccomp=unconfined --group-add video --group-add render \
  --ipc=host --shm-size 32G -e ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 \
  -v $PWD:/w -w /w pa-gate:local bash -lc '
    python3 -m pytest op_tests/triton_tests/attention/test_paged_attention_output_gate.py -q
    python3 op_tests/op_benchmarks/triton/bench_paged_attention_output_gate.py \
      --context 8192  --compare
    python3 op_tests/op_benchmarks/triton/bench_paged_attention_output_gate.py \
      --context 65536 --compare
  '
```

Exact versions the numbers above were taken on:

| | |
|---|---|
| base image | `lmsysorg/sglang-rocm:v0.5.19-rocm700-mi35x-20260910` |
| ROCm | 7.0.0 |
| torch | `2.9.0a0+git7bcbafe` |
| triton | **3.8.0** (upgraded from the base's 3.7.0) |
| aiter | `4ad99832` + this PR |
| GPU | 1x MI355X (gfx950) |

**ROCm 7.0 specifically.** The same base is published for 7.2
(`...-rocm724-...`); this op has not been validated there, and on ROCm >= 7.2
SGLang additionally enables FP8 weight preshuffling, which changes surrounding
behaviour.

## Numerical note on the stock baseline

The stock FP8-KV path is **not numerically equivalent** to this op: it diverges
from an fp32 reference by ~14% mean relative error (13.7–14.8% at every measured
cell), where this op agrees to **0.18–0.27%**.

That is a defect in `paged_attention_ragged` — it casts already-normalized
softmax probabilities to e4m3, where at `partition_size = 256` they sit at ~2⁻⁸
and are **subnormal** (`csrc/cpp_itfs/pa/pa_kernels.cuh:586-588`, `:633-647`).

**It is already fixed: https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/5642.**

**The fix is timing-neutral, so every "Before" number in this PR stands as
measured.** Verified directly on the same container before and after: FP8 kernel
time 13.49 → 13.51 µs at bs=1 and 59.68 → 59.50 µs at bs=64, i.e. within noise,
while the error drops 0.142 → 0.027 (5.2×) and the BF16 path is bit-identical.
The defect is a scaling choice with no instruction-count, branch or
data-movement consequence.

The two columns should still be read as *not computing the same thing to the
same accuracy* until #5642 lands.

title: [Triton/Gluon] [gfx950] pa_decode_sparse: bound split-K by wave count and tile budget (up to +22%)
body:
Bounds the split-K count in the gfx950 gluon sparse-decode driver from both sides: the launch stops
overshooting one wave of workgroups, and it stops cutting splits once each workgroup carries enough
KV tiles to pay for itself.

## What changes

`_decode_num_splits_occ` bounds the split count by `cta_cap = 2 * num_sms // base_wg`, which lets
`base_wg * splits` exceed `num_sms`. Capping that alone is not enough, though — past a point, cutting
splits stops removing overhead and starts removing parallelism. So the count is bounded by both:

```python
wave_cap = 1 << max(0, (num_sms // base_wg).bit_length() - 1)
return max(1, min(cta_cap, tiles, max(wave_cap, tiles // 4)))
```

`tiles // 4` is not a new constant — it is the split floor the `base_wg >= num_sms` branch of this
same function already uses. Only the `base_wg < num_sms` branch changes.

## Why both bounds are needed

Every split costs a fixed amount — its own partial write and its own Q re-read, both paid **inside the
attention kernel** — and that cost does not depend on how much KV the split actually covers. So the
tradeoff is per-split fixed cost against parallelism, and where it balances depends on how many KV
tiles a workgroup has to amortise it over. That is set by top-k, which is why one bound cannot do it.

An earlier revision of this PR had only `wave_cap`. Measured over 24 shapes, that is a **net
regression**:

| | wins | losses | worst | best | mean |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `wave_cap` only | 6 | **15** | **-43.1 %** | +22.1 % | **-7.6 %** |
| with the `tiles // 4` floor | **10** | **0** | -1.0 % | +21.9 % | **+4.2 %** |

## Measurements

MI355X / gfx950 (256 CU), DeepSeek-V4.1 decode shape: 16 heads, head_dim 512 (448 NoPE + 64 RoPE),
packed fp8 cache, 128-slot SWA window plus a top-k list per query, 8 GiB KV pool. Median of 100
samples of 4 calls in one HIP graph. Each arm runs its own `_decode_num_splits_occ` — `kv_splits` is
not pinned — so this is what merging actually gives you. Speedup against current `main`:

| queries | top-k 512 | top-k 1024 | top-k 2048 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | +0.4 % | +0.5 % | -0.2 % |
| 36 | **+15.6 %** | **+21.9 %** | **+14.8 %** |
| 48 | **+16.3 %** | +5.7 % | +6.0 % |
| 96 | +5.5 % | +8.1 % | -0.2 % |
| 126 | +5.2 % | -0.1 % | +0.3 % |
| 150 | -1.0 % | -0.5 % | +0.0 % |
| 192 | -0.3 % | -0.2 % | +0.1 % |
| 252 | +0.4 % | +0.2 % | +2.9 % |

Against a per-point sweep of `kv_splits` over {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 14, 16} at every shape, the
guarded rule lands on or within 2.5 % of the measured optimum at every one of the 24 points. The
worst cell is -1.0 %.

## Tests

`test_decode_num_splits_occ_bounds` asserts the four bounds the split count is built from — at most
`tiles`, at most `cta_cap`, at least `tiles // 4`, and within one wave where the tile floor is not
what holds the count up — plus monotonicity in top-k, over 165 shapes.

`num_sms` is patched rather than read from the device, so the body allocates nothing and the bounds
are checked at partitioned CU counts (256 / 128 / 64 / 32) rather than only whatever the runner has.
The `torch.cuda.is_available()` guard matches the in-body form the other tests in this module use.

It discriminates, and the two failing arms fail for different reasons:

```
main                4 failed   cu=32 q=1 topk=8192: 64 workgroups over 32 CUs    <- the wave ceiling
wave cap, no floor  4 failed   cu=32 q=6 topk=2048: 4 splits leaves 8 tiles/WG   <- the floor
this PR             4 passed
```

Note it fails on `main` by design: the wave ceiling is behaviour this PR introduces, so asserting it
makes the contract explicit rather than incidental. The floor assertion is the regression guard, and
it is not masked by the ceiling — the un-floored version trips the floor first.

The H=16 subset of the existing kernel test is **42 passed, 10 skipped**, identical across all three.

## Numerics

Unchanged in kind: the split count only changes how many partials the fp32 combine sums, as it
already does across the existing `cta_cap` and `tiles` bounds. Checked directly — output max
absolute deviation across every split count at every shape is **<= 9.8e-04** against the single-split
result, which is fp8 accumulation order, not a behaviour change.

`op_tests/triton_tests/attention/test_pa_decode_sparse.py`, the H=16 subset: **42 passed, 10 skipped**,
identical on `main`, on the bare cap, and with the floor.

## On the mechanism

An earlier revision explained this as a partly filled second wave costing a full wave of latency. A
`rocprofv3 --kernel-trace` of the launch does not support that, and the description is corrected:

- The saving is **entirely in the attention kernel** (103 % of the delta at 48 queries, 8 -> 4
  splits); `_aiter_sparse_decode_reduce_kernel` is flat to +0.1 us. The partial write happens inside
  the attention kernel before the workgroup exits, which is where the per-split cost actually lands.
- The kernel reports `LDS_Block_Size = 0` — no static LDS — so occupancy is VGPR-limited at 128
  VGPRs, giving 4 workgroups per CU. 384 workgroups is nowhere near a wave boundary, and there is no
  partly filled second wave to pay for.

`wave_cap` is still the right shape for the upper bound; the reasoning for it is amortisation, not
wave quantisation.

## Reproducing

Measured with a standalone benchmark that calls `pa_decode_sparse` directly, independent of any
serving stack, and cross-checked against an sglang-based harness that shares no code with it. Both
agree on where the win and loss zones fall. Happy to attach the benchmark if useful.

One methodology note for anyone re-running: a first measurement process reads 3-11 % fast from cold
start, so arms must be compared back to back within one process rather than across processes.

title: [Triton/Gluon] [Perf] Add persistent CTA scheduling for paged FP8 MQA decode
body:
## Summary

This re-opens the same single commit as #5723. That PR was merged into #5614's branch, then the branch was rolled back to `95e292923` so this change can be reviewed on its own instead of being folded into #5614. Commit content is unchanged.

Add a reusable, GPU-built persistent CTA schedule for paged FP8 MQA decode logits. `deepgemm_fp8_paged_mqa_logits_persistent_schedule` builds a `[CTA, 4]` work table once; passing it as `PersistentSchedule` makes the compute kernel read its tile from that table instead of deriving it from `pid`. Work is balanced across variable-length contexts, so one long sequence no longer strands the rest of the grid.

This PR targets **#5614's branch**, `zhiding512/fix-paged-mqa-block-paging-20260917`, based on `95e292923`.

## Motivation

The regular SplitKV path maps CTAs per (batch, query, head tile, split). With ragged or skewed contexts most CTAs finish early and idle behind the longest sequence. The schedule finds the smallest per-CTA chunk budget whose CTA count still fits the grid, gives empty sequences no slots, and balances chunks within each sequence so its last CTA is not a short straggler.

## Changes

- Add `_deepgemm_fp8_paged_mqa_logits_persistent_schedule` and the `deepgemm_fp8_paged_mqa_logits_persistent_schedule` helper. The table can be rebuilt in place into an existing buffer, and stays valid while `context_lens` is unchanged.
- Add a `PERSISTENT` compile-time branch to both the plain and preshuffle Gluon compute kernels; tiles are read through `_load_persistent_mqa_tile`. The regular path is untouched.
- Specialize the persistent query count; cover MTP causal masks in every stage, output guards, zero contexts and large KV offsets.
- Persistent AOT binaries use a distinct `_persistent` name.

This PR carries the kernel and dispatch changes only. Tests and the benchmark harness are kept out to keep the diff reviewable; the validation they produced is summarized below.

## Performance

gfx950 / 256 CU; H=32, D=128, next_n=1, KVBlockSize=64, ChunkK=256, WavePerEU=2, output bound 131072. Six alternating-order rounds, median; CPU work and output initialization excluded. `schedule` is the table build measured on its own — the kernel column excludes it because the table is reusable across calls that share `context_lens`.

Uniform context 131072, plain layout, helper-default CTA counts:

| Batch | CTAs | baseline μs | persistent kernel μs | schedule μs | kernel change |
| ----: | ---: | ----------: | -------------------: | ----------: | ------------: |
| 1     | 512  | 6.774       | 6.396                | 1.823       | -5.58%        |
| 4     | 512  | 15.942      | 16.140               | 2.428       | +1.24%        |
| 16    | 512  | 46.084      | 45.907               | 2.417       | -0.38%        |
| 64    | 1024 | 232.865     | 227.337              | 2.401       | -2.37%        |
| 128   | 2048 | 398.570     | 395.846              | 1.886       | -0.68%        |

Variable-length contexts, where the schedule actually pays off. `ragged` is `ctx[0]=0`, `ctx[i]=(i+1)*131072//128`; `skewed` is one 131072-token sequence plus 257-token sequences:

| Workload         | Layout     | baseline μs | persistent kernel μs | kernel change |
| ---------------- | ---------- | ----------: | -------------------: | ------------: |
| B16 skewed       | plain      | 31.403      | 8.545                | -72.79%       |
| B16 skewed       | preshuffle | 21.441      | 6.257                | -70.82%       |
| B128 skewed      | plain      | 110.212     | 9.100                | -91.74%       |
| B128 skewed      | preshuffle | 72.325      | 6.655                | -90.80%       |
| B128 ragged      | plain      | 266.589     | 209.158              | -21.54%       |
| B128 ragged      | preshuffle | 270.079     | 228.483              | -15.40%       |
| B64 uniform 4096 | plain      | 10.957      | 11.385               | +3.90%        |
| B64 uniform 4096 | preshuffle | 8.438       | 8.748                | +3.68%        |

Two caveats for callers. Uniform long contexts gain at most about 2%, so the schedule is not worth it there. Rebuilding the table on every call costs a fixed 1.8–2.4 μs that does not scale with the workload, which dominates at small batch — B1 plain goes from 6.396 to 8.219 μs end to end. Build the table once per decode step and reuse it across layers while contexts are unchanged.

Measured on ROCm device 6 with unlocked clocks using a local harness that is not part of this PR; absolute values are not comparable with earlier reports on other devices, but all variants within a row were timed in one process on the same inputs in alternating order.

## Testing

No test files are touched by this PR. The existing suite is unaffected, and the new path was validated with a separate local suite that is not included here.

- [x] **62 passed** — `op_tests/test_pa_mqa_logits_offset.py` on gfx950, unmodified, confirming the regular SplitKV path is unchanged.
- [x] **47 passed** — local persistent suite: schedule reuse after changing contexts inside one CUDA Graph, random physical pages, per-token scales, compact and padded page tables, zero contexts, short tails, `KVBlockSize > ChunkK`, 2/4/8 GiB KV address boundaries, output row offsets across 2 GiB, output guards, and `next_n=65/129` cross-stage MTP.
- [x] AOT load verified for plain and preshuffle with `next_n=3`, including the distinct `_persistent` name.
- [x] Every benchmark variant above was checked against the full FP32 reference before timing: 0 mismatches.
- [x] Black, Ruff and `git diff --check` pass.
- [ ] gfx942 hardware validation (not available in this session).

Happy to bring the persistent tests and the benchmark in as a follow-up PR, or fold them back into this one if reviewers prefer them together.

## Dependencies

Depends on #5614. No new third-party dependencies.

## Breaking Changes

None intended. `PersistentSchedule` defaults to `None` and the regular SplitKV path is unchanged. The persistent entry point requires Triton >= 3.5 and gfx942/gfx950.

title: [HIP] Guard GroupNorm vectorization at channel boundaries
body:
## Summary

- Require the per-channel element count to be divisible by four before enabling GroupNorm vectorization.
- Keep Python workspace sizing consistent with the HIP launch configuration.
- Make GroupNorm correctness failures fatal and report the worst mismatch.
- Add a regression shape where the group span is divisible by four but the channel span is not.

## Motivation

The vectorized output path applies the affine parameters selected for the vector's first element to all four values. Therefore, a vector must never cross a channel boundary.

The previous condition checked whether the complete group span was divisible by four. That could enable vectorization when an individual channel had an incompatible element count.

This is a general correctness fix and is not specific to gfx908.

## Testing

Tested on AMD Instinct MI100 (`gfx908`) with:

- FP16
- BF16
- FP32
- small tensors
- multi-batch odd spatial dimensions
- aligned channel spans
- the odd `32769` channel-span regression case

All 12 dtype/shape combinations passed with zero tolerance violations.

`git diff --check` also passes.

title: [Triton/Gluon] [JIT] [Feature] Add tuned native group32 A8W8 Triton GEMM for gfx950
body:
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash projections use unshuffled E4M3 weights and compact E8M0 group32 scales. This adds a gfx950 Triton backend for those operands to `gemm_a8w8_blockscale`, together with tuned configurations for TP4, TP2 and attention-DP local GEMMs.

### Implementation and dispatch

- Keep activations, weights and scales in their native formats. Support compact 32x32 or per-row 1x32 weight scales, FP32 accumulation, and BF16/FP16/FP32 output.
- Use native microscaling MFMA, packed-K execution for small M, and the existing non-atomic split-K reduction. The public interface accepts an optional native-group32 `split_k` partition count, preserving explicit caller controls while keeping configured backend selection first.
- Query `get_CKGEMM_config` before selecting a fallback. Native E8M0 operands have a separate `AITER_CONFIG_GEMM_A8W8_BLOCKSCALE_GROUP32` CSV family, so an identical M/N/K in the FP32 128x128 table cannot select an incompatible kernel. Unsupported configured backends raise instead of silently falling back.
- Add 450 DSV4.1 model-config rows: 18 geometries and 25 M buckets, all selecting `libtype=triton`. Tile, split-K and packed-variant settings remain in the existing Triton JSON configuration system. Of these rows, 262 reuse exact-shape measured timings; remaining timing fields are empty.
- Extend the shared GEMM loader with optional file-defined `M_BOUNDS`, retaining explicit-argument precedence and legacy bounds. Config copies preserve nested mutation isolation while avoiding per-scalar `deepcopy` overhead.

The new native backend requires gfx950. Existing FP32 128x128 operands retain their CK/CKTile paths. Group32 currently supports the Triton backend; configuring legacy CK/CKTile for its E8M0 operands is rejected.

### Performance

Hardware: AMD gfx950, 256 CUs; PyTorch 2.9.1 ROCm 7.1.1 and Triton 3.8.0 ROCm build. Measurements use BF16 output, CUDA graphs and at least 512 MiB of rotating weights. The baseline is the initial imported native group32 configuration in the first commit of this PR.

The sweep evaluated 49,304 candidates across 234 representative M/N/K cases and validated 603 cases, including interval boundaries. The geometric-mean speedup is **1.179x** (15.18% lower GEMM latency). Of 300 intervals checked, 252 use improved configurations and 48 retain the baseline. The largest sampled slowdown among changed configurations is 0.97%. Measurements affected by other GPU users were discarded and rerun on available cards.

| Projection | N | K | Geometric-mean speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| qkv_a | 1792 | 5120 | 1.366x |
| indexer_q | 4096 | 1280 | 1.211x |
| q_b TP4 | 8192 | 1280 | 1.061x |
| q_b TP2 | 16384 | 1280 | 1.063x |
| q_b attention-DP | 32768 | 1280 | 1.112x |
| o_b TP4 | 5120 | 2048 | 1.188x |
| o_b TP2 | 5120 | 4096 | 1.221x |
| o_b attention-DP | 5120 | 8192 | 1.121x |
| shared_up TP4 | 1152 | 5120 | 1.131x |
| shared_up TP2 | 2304 | 5120 | 1.217x |
| shared_up TP1 | 4608 | 5120 | 1.194x |
| shared_down TP4 | 5120 | 576 | 1.273x |
| shared_down TP2 | 5120 | 1152 | 1.268x |
| shared_down TP1 | 5120 | 2304 | 1.243x |
| Engram | 25600 | 6144 | 1.123x |
| draft_main | 5120 | 15360 | 1.180x |
| draft_kv_fused | 1536 | 5120 | 1.176x |
| draft_kv | 512 | 5120 | 1.146x |

These are standalone GEMM results. End-to-end serving throughput was not measured. Tuning covers M through 4096; larger M retains the original JSON fallback. Model CSV entries through M=16384 choose the backend without claiming newly tuned tiles at those larger sizes.

### Validation

- **136 AITER tests passed** on the rebased branch: native numerical contracts, column/K tails, extreme scale codes, per-row scales, split-K, output buffers, live-input graph replay, dynamic-M fullgraph compile, CSV format isolation, and configured-backend precedence. CK/CKTile dispatch-priority tests use stubs; native numerical and graph tests execute GPU kernels.
- **100 ATOM integration tests passed** with the companion migration to the public AITER interface, covering actual backend-config lookup, blockscale projections, accumulation, GPU quantization, graph replay and dynamic batched fullgraph compilation.
- All **294,912** combinations of the 18 model geometries and integer M=1..16384 resolve through the real shared loader to Triton; unknown geometries still miss the table and reach fallback.
- Six representative cases comparing dispatch before/after the configuration-priority change have bitwise-equal BF16/FP32 outputs, identical GPU kernel sequences, and graph-latency differences below 0.5%.

title: [HIP] Fix grouped topk tie handling for GLM-5.2 accuracy
body: ## Motivation PR [#5632](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/5632) added a register-resident kernel for the single-group Top-K path. However, its output did not exactly match the original `grouped_topk_kernel`: ties at the Top-K cutoff could change the selected expert set, and the selected experts and weights could be emitted in a different order. This changed downstream floating-point accumulation and caused an accuracy regression on GLM-5.2. This PR makes the register-resident kernel match `grouped_topk_kernel` exactly, including selected expert IDs, output order, and weights, while retaining the register-resident fast path. ## Technical details - Retain the register-resident fast path introduced in #5632. - Emit experts in the same score order as the legacy kernel. - When multiple experts have equal scores at the Top-K selection boundary, use the deterministic priority and comparison rules of the legacy kernel, including the register-resident fallback path. - Accumulate the renormalization denominator in the same serial order as the legacy implementation, producing bitwise-equal weights. - Handle NaN/`-Inf` inputs without producing invalid or duplicate expert IDs. There are no API, dispatch-gate, dtype, or supported-shape changes. ## Test plan No new test file is added. Compatibility cases are added to the existing `op_tests/test_moeTopkSoftmax.py`. They cover the GLM-5.2 router shape (`biased`, BF16, `E=256`, `topk=8`, `G=1`) with random inputs, all-equal scores, and a 16-way cutoff tie. title: [Triton/Gluon] FlashKDA in-kernel paged state_cache I/O
body:
## Motivation
 
FlashKDA still spoke a dense ABI: `initial_state[N, H, V, K]` plus a freshly allocated `out`. vLLM Kimi-K3 serving keeps recurrent state in a paged pool `[slots, H, V, K]` with `state_indices` / `has_initial_state`.

Wiring that through AITER meant:
 
1. `gather_initial_states` (or `state_cache[indices]`) into a dense tensor

2. run `chunk_kimi_delta_attn`

3. scatter `final_state` back

4. `out.copy_(kernel_out)`
 
Those copies sit in the serving timer. On MI350, a K3-shaped FlashKDA prefill paid ~40–60 µs for them (4K: 171 → 130 µs, 16K: 499 → 440 µs with the same segment pin). The fused vLLM path already reads and writes the pool in-kernel ([vLLM #54038](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54038)); this PR gives FlashKDA the same cache contract so a later vLLM dispatch ([#56036](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56036)) does not have to gather around AITER.

 
## Technical Details
 
Public kwargs on `chunk_kimi_delta_attn` / `flash_kda_fwd`:
 
- `state_cache`: fp32 V-first `[slots, H, V, K]`. Each slot plane is dense; `stride(0)` may pad.

- `state_indices`: int32 `[N]`

- `has_initial_state`: bool `[N]`; false starts that sequence from zero and does not read a dirty slot

- `out`: required with `state_cache`, same shape as `v` (K2 still loads `v`, so `out` must not alias it)
 
K2 and the scan load/store `slot * stride(0) + head * V * K + …`. The last segment writes the final state back to the same row. Segmented pass A does not bind `state_cache` (keeps the existing K2 binary / autotune; binding it here previously ~2× slowed K2).
 
`@input_guard(skip=("state_cache",))` leaves the pool’s storage and `stride(0)` alone. Other operands are still packed. The skip is an AITER decorator default, not a vLLM flag; the caller just passes `state_cache=` as a keyword.
 
Dense `initial_state` is unchanged and mutually exclusive with `state_cache`. `final_state` is `None` when the cache is used.
 
The default five-kernel path indexes a dense `h0` and is GVA / C=64 / K-first. If `state_cache` is set and FlashKDA is not selected,

`chunk_delta_attn_fwd` raises instead of ignoring the argument.
 
 
## Test Plan
 
```bash

pytest op_tests/triton_tests/chunk_delta_attn/test_flash_kda.py \

  -k 'paged_cache or flash_kda' -q

```
 
Added cases:
 
- `test_paged_cache_matches_dense` — paged vs dense `initial_state`, bit-identical `out` and selected slots; empty slots untouched; unsegmented and segmented

- `test_paged_cache_has_initial_state_false` — false flag matches a zero `initial_state`

- `test_paged_cache_padded_stride_writes_live_pool` — non-contiguous `stride(0)` updates the original storage pointer

- `test_paged_cache_rejected_on_default_pipeline` — non-FlashKDA call with `state_cache` raises
 
Serving-shaped A/B (K3 H=12, D=128, `lower_bound=-5`, varlen `cu_seqlens`)

vs gather and vs vLLM fused prefill on gfx950.
 
## Test Result
 
Paged vs dense FlashKDA: `torch.equal` on output and selected cache rows (rel err 0).
 
Paged FlashKDA vs vLLM fused prefill (same op, not e2e): output rel L2 ~4.8e-3, state ~2.5e-3 at 4K/16K.
 
MI350X, official vLLM ROCm image, serving-style call (µs, smaller is better):

 
| shape | gather FlashKDA | paged FlashKDA | fused |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1×4096, H=12 | 171 | **130** | 125 |
| 1×16384, H=12, `--segment 8` | 499 | **440** | 389 |
| 1×16384, H=12, auto segment | — | **380** | 388 |

 
Default-pipeline reject and padded-stride tests pass.

 
## Submission Checklist
 
- [x] Look over the contributing guidelines at https://github.com/ROCm/TheRock/blob/main/GOVERNANCE.md#pull-requests.

title: [Bugfix][MLA] Size PS prefill partial buffers from the real token budget
body:
## Motivation

Fixes https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/issues/5729.

The MLA PS metadata scheduler returns a pessimistic bound on the max number of partial entries needed to be allocated. This could lead to OOM. The pessimism stems from the fact that it assumed that all requests used the same (maximal) number of query tokens which is not true in inference engines with a fixed query token budget per step.

This PR fixes it to correctly give a much tighter bound by accounting for fixed token budget (c.f. max num batched tokens in vllm) if passed.

## Technical Details

A temporary fix was required on serving engine side: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57923/changes

It's better if we do this in AITER.

title: WORKAROUND - fix a1_scale out-of-bounds read in fmoe_fp8_blockscale_g1u1
body:
`fmoe_fp8_blockscale_g1u1` indexes the activation scale by `sorted_ids // topk`, so it can touch row `sorted_ids.numel() // topk`. `sorted_ids` is padded out to whole blocks per expert, but `per_group_quant_hip` allocates the scale with exactly one row per token, so the kernel reads `(num_experts * block_size - topk) // topk` rows past the end of the buffer.

The values there are read and discarded, so the over-read is usually invisible: the caching allocator normally has slack after the buffer. It becomes a hard memory access fault whenever the scale happens to be allocated at the tail of an allocator segment, since the next page is unmapped.

Pad the scale to the row count the kernel can address and return a view with the original shape, so the read lands on mapped memory without changing any observable value.

Reproduced on gfx950 with DeepSeek-V3.2 (per_1x128, topk=2, num_experts=8, block_size=32), where the kernel reads 1024 bytes past the scale. Padding to fewer rows than `sorted_ids.numel() // topk + 1` still faults 3/3; padding to that bound or beyond passes 3/3. Filling the padded tail with 0.0, 1.0, and 1e30 all produce byte-identical model output, confirming the tail is read but unused.

`op_tests/test_moe_blockscale.py` shows the same 6 pre-existing a8w8 asm checkAllclose failures with and without this change, over identical shapes.

---
AI assistance was used for this PR. All changes reviewed by submitter.

title: [HIP] Mask partial vectors in sampling kernels
body:
## Summary

Fix out-of-bounds vector accesses in the sampling kernels when the vocabulary size is not divisible by the vector width.

The implementation separates the branch-free full-vector path from the final partial-vector path, preserving bulk-path performance while making tail loads and stores bounds-safe.

This covers:

- `greedy_sample`
- `random_sample_outer_exponential`
- `random_sample`
- `mixed_sample_outer_exponential`
- `mixed_sample`
- `exponential`

## Problem

The kernels previously entered a vector load or store whenever the vector's starting offset was less than `N`. For a final partial vector, that could access elements beyond the end of the row.

Depending on allocation layout, those accesses could read the next row, sample an invalid token, or overwrite memory following an exponential-output row.

## Implementation

- Keep complete vector loads and stores on a branch-free bulk path.
- Handle only the final partial vector with scalar-masked helpers.
- Pad invalid input lanes with `-inf`.
- Pad invalid external-exponential lanes with `1.0`.
- Store only valid lanes from the final exponential vector.
- Distribute the greedy tail across lanes instead of serializing it in one lane.
- Preserve one Philox vector draw per owned vector, including a partial vector.
- Leave public APIs, launch geometry, and generator ownership unchanged.

The sampling test also now forces an independent FP32 reference buffer. Previously:

```python
logits = input.to(torch.float)
logits.div_(...)
```

aliased and repeatedly modified the original input when it was already FP32. Using `copy=True` prevents benchmark iterations from corrupting their input.

## Validation

Hardware:

- AMD Instinct MI100
- `gfx908:sramecc+:xnack-`
- PyTorch 2.10.0 with ROCm 7.2

Deterministic tail coverage:

```bash
for dtype in bf16 fp16 fp32; do
  AITER_REBUILD=0 python op_tests/test_sample.py \
    --tail-only \
    -d "$dtype" \
    -n 1 17 4097 16385
done
```

All 12 dtype/size cases passed. Each case exercises greedy sampling, both random paths, both mixed paths, and guarded exponential output.

Reference comparisons were also run for:

- BF16, FP16, and FP32
- `M=1,32`
- aligned `N=32000`
- partial-vector `N=32003`
- greedy, random, and mixed sampling
- internal and external exponential generation

All comparisons passed with exact token equality.

Additional large-vocabulary BF16 coverage passed at `N=151936` and `N=151937`.

The translation unit also compiles directly for gfx908 without private-memory use or register spills.

## Performance

The bulk/tail split was compared against the initial bounds-safe implementation, which performed bounds checks throughout the vector loop. Values below are three-run medians on MI100:

| Path | Shape | Initial safe patch | Bulk/tail implementation | Improvement |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Greedy | M1 × 32000 | 8.612 µs | 7.173 µs | 16.7% |
| Greedy | M32 × 32000 | 8.823 µs | 7.450 µs | 15.6% |
| Greedy | M1 × 151936 | 22.772 µs | 20.468 µs | 10.1% |
| Greedy | M32 × 151936 | 21.687 µs | 20.341 µs | 6.2% |
| Random, external exponential | M32 × 32000 | 39.721 µs | 37.622 µs | 5.3% |
| Random, internal exponential | M32 × 32000 | 41.356 µs | 35.648 µs | 13.8% |
| Random, external exponential | M1 × 151936 | 108.752 µs | 99.754 µs | 8.3% |
| Random, internal exponential | M1 × 151936 | 166.134 µs | 146.698 µs | 11.7% |

Across the measured aligned-shape matrix, the bulk/tail implementation was 5.3%–26.5% faster than the initial bounds-safe version.

This performance comparison is against the first correctness implementation, not a claim of speedup over the previous out-of-bounds upstream path.

## CI impact

No workflow or runner configuration is changed. This does not add a required gfx908 CI job.

title: [Triton/Gluon] [Perf] Support page size 8 in the preshuffle MQA logits kernel
body:
## Problem

DeepSeek V4.1 decode pages the indexer KV cache at 8 tokens per page. #5749 makes that page size *work*, but only on the plain (non-preshuffle) path, which is the slow one. Preshuffle is refused outright:

```python
assert KVBlockSize % 16 == 0, "Preshuffle mode only supports KVBlockSize aligned to 16."
```

The shuffled KV feeds the 16-token MFMA B operand directly, and a page of 8 is half a tile, with the other half in a physically unrelated page.

This is not hypothetical. ATOM's V4.1 index scorer already calls this op with `Preshuffle=True` (`atom/model_ops/deepseek_v41/paged_scoring.py`), and its `candidate_block_size` is 8, so the plain-path fix alone does not reach it.

## What this changes

No new load structure is needed. The per-lane page index already varies at `KVBlockSize` granularity, and a page shorter than `ChunkK // 2` already takes the "page index per lane" branch, so the two pages behind one tile are already addressable. What was hardcoded is the shuffle group: the B-operand offset assumed 16 rows per group.

- **`ShuffleRows = min(KVBlockSize, 16)`** in both `_gluon_deepgemm_fp8_paged_mqa_logits_preshuffle` and its `_varctx` twin, replacing the literal 16 in the B-operand offset. The tile is then assembled from `16 // KVBlockSize` pages.
- **The wrapper accepts a page that divides the tile**, not only one that is a multiple of it. gfx1250 preshuffle reshapes by a literal `KVBlockSize // 16` for its TDM block load, so pages below 16 stay rejected there rather than mis-addressed.
- **The row-group stride** goes from a literal `16 * 128` to `ShuffleRows * HiddenDim` to stay consistent with the above. This is not what makes page 8 work — a page that short holds one group, so the term is zero either way — and at `HiddenDim` 128 the two expressions are equal. No configuration a caller can reach today changes; every caller runs `HiddenDim` 128.
- **The benchmark can now express a page-8 run.** `--blocksize` applied only to the preshuffle path and had to be a multiple of 16, `Preshuffle` was inferred from it rather than taken from the flag, and the host shuffle used the default `(16, 16)` layout. Those are the same assumptions the kernel drops. It also records the scored token count, which a bandwidth figure needs.

**Caller-visible:** a page below 16 must be shuffled in groups of its own length, `shuffle_weight(kv, layout=(KVBlockSize, 16))`, rather than the default `(16, 16)`.

## Performance

gfx950, heads 32 / head-dim 128, via `op_tests/op_benchmarks/triton/bench_deepgemm_attention.py`. Three rounds per point with the arms rotated inside a round, medians below; round-to-round spread is under 1.9 us everywhere. Every point passes the benchmark's own FP32 reference check, and the four arms of a row share a seed, so their context lengths and page tables are identical.

The rows below carry a 286 MB KV working set, past this card's 256 MB MALL, so their TB/s is DRAM-bound.

**batch 16, next_n 1, 1M context**

| page | layout | latency | effective BW |
|---:|---|---:|---:|
| 8 | plain | 431.384 us | 5.125 TB/s |
| 16 | plain | 410.064 us | 5.382 TB/s |
| 8 | **preshuffle** | **379.863 us** | **5.820 TB/s** |
| 16 | preshuffle | 359.784 us | 6.134 TB/s |

**Halving the page is not free: it costs 5.58% here**, and 3.01% to 5.20% across the five other shape and layout pairs measured (batch 32 / next_n 2 / 128K and batch 128 / next_n 1 / 128K, each on both layouts). Plain and preshuffle move together, so what is being paid for is the page and not the shuffle — one tile's contiguous run drops from 256 B to 128 B, and the page table doubles in width. The page table is 0.18% of the byte model, which leaves the contiguity.

That cost does not change what a page-8 caller should do, because page 16 is not one of its options. Against the only alternative it has, page-8 plain, **preshuffle is 11.9% faster**, and it also beats page-16 plain by 7.4%. The preshuffle speedup itself barely changes with the page: 1.140x / 1.692x / 1.096x at page 16 against 1.136x / 1.664x / 1.088x at page 8, over the three shapes.

An earlier revision of this PR claimed page-8 and page-16 preshuffle were level. That came from a single point measured with a throwaway probe whose KV allocation differed from the benchmark's; the numbers above replace it.

## Testing

`op_tests/test_pa_mqa_logits_offset.py`, 105 cases, all passing on gfx950 (MI35x).

The new `test_paged_mqa_logits_preshuffle` gives the preshuffle path the sweep the plain one already had — previously only the large-KV-offset cases reached it, all at the default ChunkK. It covers pages 8 / 16 / 32 / 64 / 128 / 256 x ChunkK 128 / 256 x compact / padded page tables x the decode and MTP shapes, 48 cases, against an FP32 reference built from the same FP8 inputs, with the output rows sentinel-guarded on both sides.

The page sizes pick out the ways the B tile gets assembled: 8 is half a tile and draws from two pages, 16 is exactly one, 32 through 128 are several row groups inside one page, and 256 exceeds `ChunkK // 2` and so takes the one-page-per-stage branch. ChunkK 128 and 256 are the two the callers ask for — the bench runs preshuffle at 128, the indexer at 256.

Against the parent commit the 8 page-8 rows fail, rejected by the wrapper before they reach the device, and the other 40 pass unchanged. `test_paged_mqa_logits_large_kv_offsets` also picks up a `preshuffle-B8` row at the 2 / 4 / 8 GiB boundaries.

## Relationship to #5749

Stacked on #5749, which is the plain-path half of the same page-8 requirement. Only the top two commits belong to this PR; please review it after #5749 lands, or with base set to that branch.

title: [Triton/Gluon] Assert SPLIT_UNMASKED_LOOP is not used with sliding window
[SMI] Add opt-in summary plots and raw-sample timelines
body:
SMI benchmark results currently require manual processing to compare cases, and aggregate logs discard the timing of individual observations. This adds opt-in automatic summary reports and lossless raw-sample capture with a standalone per-case timeline renderer.

- `AITER_SMI_PLOT=1` captures summary records and renders a report at normal process exit. `AITER_SMI_PLOT_DIR` defaults to `./smi_plots`; each process gets a separate run directory. Existing stdout and `AITER_SMI_OUTPUT_PATH` output are preserved.
- `AITER_SMI_TRACE=1` independently saves every collected sample and its timestamp, plus window boundaries and benchmark metadata. `AITER_SMI_TRACE_DIR` defaults to `./smi_traces`. Raw records are written after each monitoring window, outside the polling loop.
- `aiter/smi_plot.py` renders existing logs or directories into all-test, per-test, and per-case summary views. `aiter/smi_trace_plot.py` explicitly renders raw traces into per-case timelines, comparing variants in separate columns with clocks, power, activity, temperature, and VRAM panels.
- Reports include PNG/SVG plots, an HTML index, CSV, and a manifest. Timeline plots preserve every observation at its actual timestamp without smoothing, resampling, or downsampling; missing and firmware `N/A` readings remain gaps. Aggregate-only logs cannot reconstruct timelines.

Matplotlib is optional and the renderers work without a GPU. Automatic summary rendering runs in a CPU-only subprocess after the benchmark. Detailed timeline rendering is an explicit CLI step. Identical inputs/options produce deterministic report content within the same rendering environment. Documentation covers toggles, output paths, regeneration, and sample interpretation in `docs/smi_plotting.md`.

Validation: 30 combined CPU unit tests pass, plus Black, Ruff, and `git diff --check`. Tested inside `distracted_wu` on b9-2 across six GEMM shapes with both preshuffle variants: 12 ten-second monitoring windows produced 2,403 timestamped samples at a median 50.097 ms interval. All timestamps and original sample dictionaries were retained in the CSV, and six case plots were checked against the raw data. The existing summary path generated its 12-record/eight-plot report, and all 19 container compatibility tests passed. The benchmark source was preserved.

Two shapes emitted elementwise tolerance warnings but passed the benchmark's relative-L2 gate; A-preshuffle and split-K checks passed.

title: fix(custom_all_reduce): send the real IPC offset instead of 0
body:
## Problem

`_broadcast_ipc` (`aiter/dist/device_communicators/custom_all_reduce.py:602`) pins the IPC offset to `0`:

```python
self._ipc_handle_fn(data_ptr, handle.data_ptr())
return self._gather_ipc_meta((handle, 0))
```

`hipIpcGetMemHandle` always returns a handle for the **whole allocation** containing the pointer, never for the pointer itself, and the importing rank maps that allocation at its own base. A buffer that is a sub-block of a larger allocation therefore has to carry its `ptr - base` offset. Offset `0` is only correct when the pool pointer happens to *be* an allocation base.

Whether it is depends on the state of PyTorch's caching allocator:

- **Fresh allocator** — the IPC pool is the first large allocation and gets its own segment, so `ptr == base` and offset `0` is accidentally right. This is why single-engine runs are fine.
- **Allocator already holding a cached large segment** — a co-resident second engine on the same node, or simply any earlier allocate-and-free — the pool lands as a sub-block, `ptr != base`, and peers read from the base of that segment instead. **No error is raised; the all-reduce just returns data from whatever else lives there.**

The C++ graph path already does this correctly, and even carries the comment — `get_graph_buffer_ipc_meta` in `csrc/include/custom_all_reduce.cuh:3947`:

```cpp
// note: must share the base address of each allocation, or we get wrong address
if (hipPointerGetAttribute(&base_ptr, HIP_POINTER_ATTRIBUTE_RANGE_START_ADDR, ...))
offsets[i] = ((char*)ptr) - ((char*)base_ptr);
```

Only the Python side, for the named pool buffers (`meta` and `input`), was missing it. The C++ importers already apply `offsets[i]` (`custom_all_reduce.cuh:3911`, `:4001`, `:4025`, `:4124`), so no kernel-side change is needed.

## Fix

Resolve the base with `hipMemGetAddressRange` and send the real offset. New helper `_ipc_base_ptr`; `_broadcast_ipc` exports the handle from the base and gathers `data_ptr - base`. Raw `hipMalloc` / `hipExtMallocWithFlags` buffers are their own base, so this is a no-op for them.

## Relation to `AITER_CUSTOM_AR_RAW_INPUT_POOL`

That env var forces a raw `hipMalloc` input pool, whose pointer is always an allocation base — which is exactly why setting it made the problem disappear. It stays as an escape hatch and is still the right thing under `expandable_segments` (VMM pointers genuinely cannot be exported, #4174), but it should no longer be needed for co-resident engines. That matters in practice: a raw pool is invisible to torch's memory accounting, so an engine that sizes its KV cache from torch's numbers over-estimates free memory and can OOM later.

This is a different bug from #4921 (which was `init_dist_env` reading `_pool["input"].tensor` on a raw pool); they were both reachable in the same co-resident configuration, which is why the env var looked like the cure.

## Not a duplicate

Searched open PRs on this repo for `custom_all_reduce ipc offset` and `RAW_INPUT_POOL` — no open PR touches `_broadcast_ipc` or the IPC offset. #4921 is closed and addressed a different failure in the same file.

## Tests

`op_tests/test_ipc_base_ptr.py` (new, single-GPU) pins the offset arithmetic: sub-blocks of one allocation share a base and report distinct non-zero offsets; a raw `hipMalloc` buffer is its own base.

`op_tests/multigpu_tests/test_init_dist_env.py` gains a `dirty` mode that leaves a large segment in the caching allocator before `init_dist_env`, so the pool comes back as a sub-block — the shape a co-resident second engine produces incidentally. Each rank's pool offset is reported, so a run that never landed on a sub-block is distinguishable from one that did and handled it; the existing allreduce-correctness check is what proves the result.

**Validated on gfx950 (MI350X)** — full before/after table in [this comment](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/5775#issuecomment-5788840837). Summary: three allocator states that put the input pool at a non-zero offset produce **silently wrong** all-reduce results on the unpatched tree and correct results with this patch; states that leave the pool at offset 0 are unaffected either way.

## Note

AI assistance was used to write this change. I have reviewed every changed line.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: [ASM] [CI] Remove committed scratch files and stop two from coming back
body:
Six tracked files that nothing reads and nothing will read again.

CI scratch committed by the bot. update-split-tests.yaml writes split-tests-update-summary.md and then pr-body.md into the workspace and hands them to peter-evans/create-pull-request, which has no add-paths filter and so commits every dirty file it finds. Both landed in the repo root that way in #5131. The workflow regenerates them on every run, so the tracked copies are stale by definition; .gitignore now keeps the bot from re-adding them.

Merge and POC leftovers that ship in the wheel.
hsa/gfx950/pa/pa_bf16_noquant_gqa8_1tg_4w.co.orig and .co.poc_kl_merg arrived with #3211 next to the real .co. Nothing references either by name, and the ASM loaders build .co paths explicitly rather than globbing the directory, so neither is reachable. They are not merely inert: setup.py copies all of hsa/ into aiter_meta and MANIFEST.in grafts it, so 48 KB of scratch binaries go out in every wheel. *.orig is now ignored so the next conflicted merge does not leave another one behind.

One-off files their PRs forgot. probe_noqa_check.py is a single line, x = 1, added in #4403 to confirm the pinned ruff config flagged it. REPO_CLEANUP_PLAN.md is a pull request description from #2167 in March. Its Phase 1 shipped -- the .pt test data is gone from main and the size rules are in .gitignore -- and its Phase 2 history rewrite needs a coordinated force push that has not happened in the six months since. Neither file is referenced anywhere in the tree.
