title: [Triton/Gluon] Add a16w4 MoE tuned dispatch and gfx942 DSv4.1 tables
body:
## Summary

`get_kernel_config_triton` hardcodes `block_k=256`, `block_n=512` and `num_stages=1` for every architecture. Those suit CDNA4's 160 KiB of LDS; CDNA3 has 64 KiB, so the gfx942 prefill tile runs at very low occupancy.

This routes the kernel through the tuned dispatch that `a8w4` already uses and ships a gfx942 table for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at TP4 and TP8.

- `get_moe_dispatch("A16W4", get_arch(), "triton")`, keyed by `bm<block_m>_n<N>_k<K>`
- `configs/gfx942/triton/moe/a16w4/DEFAULT.json`, 8 entries

`get_moe_dispatch` returns `{}` when no file is shipped, so untuned architectures are unaffected. On gfx942 only the 8 listed prefill shapes change; decode (`block_m` 16/32) and unlisted shapes keep the existing defaults.

## Results

MI325X (gfx942), ROCm 7.2.3, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, E=384, topk=6.

| entry | stock | tuned | speedup |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `bm128_n1536_k5120` | 16.484 ms | 4.219 ms | 3.91x |
| `bm128_n5120_k768` | 8.131 ms | 1.924 ms | 4.22x |
| `bm128_n1024_k5120` | 11.275 ms | 2.688 ms | 4.20x |
| `bm128_n5120_k512` | 5.288 ms | 1.463 ms | 3.67x |
| `bm64_n1536_k5120` | 2.155 ms | 1.291 ms | 1.68x |
| `bm64_n5120_k768` | 1.152 ms | 0.660 ms | 1.75x |
| `bm64_n1024_k5120` | 1.477 ms | 0.882 ms | 1.65x |
| `bm64_n5120_k512` | 0.839 ms | 0.503 ms | 1.68x |

End to end via vLLM (`--moe-backend aiter_triton_mxfp4_bf16`, random 65536 in / 512 out, concurrency 8, TP=4, 3 repeats, CV 0.14%):

| metric | stock | tuned | delta |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Output throughput | 97.35 tok/s | 111.88 tok/s | +14.9% |
| TPOT mean | 55.70 ms | 44.80 ms | -19.6% |

## Notes on Tuning

No a16w4 tile tuner exists in-tree, so the entries come from a sweep over all six knobs the kernel forwards to the launch.

Worth knowing when adding shapes:

- `block_k=64` compiles only with `matrix_instr_nonkdim=32`, and it wins at `block_m=128` on most shapes. Sweeping with `nonkdim` fixed hides it entirely.
- `block_n=256` won on every shape; the stock 512 never did.

## Tests

- All 8 entries verified resolving to the measured tiles against a live install; decode and unlisted shapes confirmed returning the existing defaults.
- Tuned vs stock output differs by exactly 0.5 bf16 ULP, caused by `block_k` changing the K-split. `block_n`, `num_stages` and `num_warps` are bit-identical.
- GSM8K 8-shot (200 examples, chat endpoint): 0.905 exact_match (flexible-extract) on both the tuned and stock-tile arms are identical.

## Limits

- Measured on MI325X. gfx942 also covers MI300X, which shares the 64 KiB LDS but not the memory bandwidth; untested there.
- TP4 and TP8 only. TP2 needs ~287 GiB/GPU for this model and cannot load.
- Keys use the **padded** intermediate: the per-rank shard is rounded up to a multiple of 256 before reaching the kernel (TP4 576 -> 768, TP8 288 -> 512), so gemm1 is `n=2*

title: [FlyDSL] Add token-major layout option to GDN prefill h kernel
body:
Summary

Adds an optional token-major layout for the w/u inputs and the v_new output of the FlyDSL gated-delta-rule hidden-state kernel chunk_gated_delta_rule_fwd_h_flydsl_opt. New public param wu_head_major: bool = True on the host wrapper (aiter/ops/flydsl/linear_attention_prefill_kernels.py); when False, w/u are consumed token-major ([B,T,H,D]) and v_new is stored token-major ([B,T,H,V]). Default True preserves the existing head-major behavior exactly. Implemented via a compile-time const_expr branch in the device kernel (aiter/ops/flydsl/kernels/gdr_prefill/chunk_gated_delta_h.py), so the head-major path is unchanged.

Motivation: lets a consumer with native token-major GDN tensors (e.g. SGLang's linear-attention path) reach the kernel without a transpose.

Technical Details

- Head-major path is provably unchanged: emitted ISA is byte-identical between base and this branch (same VGPR/occupancy). Zero regression by construction (compile-time dead-branch elimination).
- Correctness: token-major output is bit-exact against the head-major reference on dense and production varlen shapes, including an unaligned tail.
- wu_head_major=False changes both the v_new store base/stride and the w/u input loads, which move from head-major ([B,H,T,D], token-row stride D) to token-major ([B,T,H,D], token-row stride H*D) — see chunk_gated_delta_h.py:394-400. K/V stays the unit-stride innermost dimension in both layouts, so lane-level coalescing is unchanged; the difference is inter-token-row locality (head-major advances 256 B/row for K=V=128 BF16, token-major advances H·256 B/row).
- Performance is layout- and architecture-dependent, not neutral. On gfx950 (CDNA4, the target arch) token-major is within noise to slightly faster. On gfx942 (CDNA3) token-major measures ~4.3% slower (dense T=1024) and ~6.1% slower (varlen 8×1024) than head-major, from the reduced token-row spatial locality above (a secondary cache/prefetch effect, not a coalescing failure). For a consumer with native token-major tensors, the saved host transpose can still make wu_head_major=False a net win; on gfx942 it is a trade-off to weigh against the transpose cost.

AOT / prebuild

The FlyDSL AOT enumeration (aiter/aot/flydsl/chunk_gdn_h.py) now fans out wu_contig over both values with layout-matched compile dummies, so the token-major specialization is prebuilt into the packaged cache rather than cold-JIT-compiling on the first wu_head_major=False serving-path call. Verified on gfx950: enumeration count doubles (288 → 576 jobs, 288 head-major + 288 token-major), and a fresh-process token-major call under FLYDSL_RUNTIME_RUN_ONLY=1 (which forbids compile-on-miss) hits the prebuilt cache — with an empty-cache negative control raising the expected "no usable AOT cache" error, confirming the hit depends on the prebuilt artifact and not a JIT fallback.

Test Plan

- op_tests/test_flydsl_linear_attention_prefill.py runs a direct token-major == head-major torch.equal exact assertion (on h, layout-normalized v_new, and final_state) on every case in the default sweep.
- Default run also exercises two dedicated review cases: review-unaligned-varlen (varlen T=1000, a non-multiple-of-BT=64 tail) and review-dense-b2 (dense_batch=2, token-major dense base path).
- ISA diff of the head-major path between base and this branch.

Test Result

- Bit-exact match (torch.equal) between token-major and head-major outputs on all tested shapes, including the unaligned-tail and dense_batch>1 cases, on gfx950.
- Identical emitted ISA (VGPR/occupancy) for the head-major path, confirming no regression.

Submission Checklist

- [x] Default behavior (wu_head_major=True) unchanged
- [x] New path validated bit-exact against reference (direct token-major == head-major torch.equal assertion)
- [x] Token-major specialization AOT-prebuilt (no cold-JIT serving stall)
- [x] Performance characterized per architecture (gfx950 neutral/faster; gfx942 ~4–6% slower

body: Here, we replace all instances of the stale `rocm/vllm-dev:nightly` with the official vLLM nightly image `vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:nightly`. The `rocm/vllm-dev:nightly` tag will be deleted soon, so any attempt to pull it from Dockerhub moving forward would fail.

title: [CI] Triton tests selection script
body:
PR CI ran the whole op-type folder for any kernel edit. Select the paired
test for each edited kernel instead, plus every test whose imports reach
that module, so fused coverage is computed rather than maintained by hand.
A GEMM kernel edit now runs 3 tests instead of 25; a kernel with no paired
test falls back to its op-type folder, and shared machinery (utils/,
package __init__, CI infra) still falls open to the full suite.

Configs are read at run time rather than imported, so the import graph
cannot say which variants consume them: a config change runs its whole op
folder plus any test outside it that imports the module the family is
named after. Tuning attention/mha therefore also runs test_mha_with_pe
and test_mha_with_sink.

title: [HIP] [OPUS] [JIT] [GFX950]OPUS PA MQA Logits MXFP4
body:
## Motivation

Adds an OPUS (HIP) MXFP4 paged MQA-logits kernel for DeepSeek-V4-style sparse-attention
indexers on gfx950, as an alternative to the existing FlyDSL fp4 path.
Two things motivate it beyond raw speed:
- **The per-row window is an input, not a rule.** A CSA/compressed KV cache scores row `n`
  over `floor((pos + 1) / ratio)` rows, which no `ctx - (next_n - 1 - n)` derivation can
  express. Both entry points take `local_ends` per query row, so any window rule works.
- **No device-side schedule.** The grid is a function of static shapes, so callers need no
  persistent `cta_info` buffer and no per-forward schedule kernel to be CUDA-graph safe.

## Technical Details

Two entry points in `aiter.ops.opus.pa_mqa_logits_opus`, both schedule-free, cudagraph-safe,
`gfx950` only:
- `..._prefill` — 1D grid, one CTA per row, window `[local_starts[r], local_ends[r])`.
- `..._decode` — 3D grid `(batch, next_n_max, split_kv)`, packed row `cu_seq_q[b] + n` over
  `[0, local_ends[row])`.

`compute_prefill_windows` builds tail-causal windows device-side for either. `block_k` picks
one of two compiled variants (256 → 4 waves/CTA, 64 → 1 wave, default 64); `H=64`, `D=128`,
`PAGE=64` are compile-time.

`q [T,H,D/2]`, `weights [T,H]` bf16 and `kv_cache [num_blocks,4,PAGE,16]` are natural /
standard-paged, `kv_cache` byte-identical to FlyDSL's. Only `q_scale [T,2,32,4]` and
`kv_scale [num_blocks,2,32,4]` carry a 32x32-MFMA E8M0 permutation.

Decode pads `grid.x` to a whole number of XCDs so a batch's MTP rows — `gridDim.x` apart in
workgroup id — share one XCD's L2; the padding CTAs return immediately.
VGPR 223 / 224, occupancy 2, LDS 0, no spill.

## Test Plan

gfx950, both compiled variants (`block_k` 64 and 256), random data.

```bash
python3 op_tests/test_pa_mqa_logits_opus.py
```

Performance at the shapes ATOM's DeepSeek-V4 indexer runs (CSA ratio 4), OPUS at
`block_k=64` against FlyDSL at its shipping `block_k=256`:

- prefill, `total_q=16384` — fresh (`bs 2/4/8`) and chunked into a long sequence
  (`bs 1/2/4`, 25000 committed compressed rows). Geometry follows the reported prefill
  regression, so the two are directly comparable.
- decode, 48 shapes — `product(max_ctx {1024, 8192}, next_n {1,4,8}, batch {1..128})`.

Both sides share one set of `q` / `kv_cache` / `weights`, each gets the scale layout it
reads, and each is timed by one `run_perftest(iters=50, warmup=10)` — torch-profiler GPU
kernel time, identical for both. FlyDSL is handed the precomputed `cta_info` ATOM gives it,
so neither side builds a schedule inside the timed region. Agreement is checked after
timing, masked to the window.

## Test Result
Correctness — all pass. `err` is `checkAllclose`'s mismatch fraction, so 0 is exact
agreement within `rtol=2e-5`:
| suite | cases | err | vs flydsl | oob -inf | window written |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | :--- | :--- |
| `test_pa_mqa_logits_opus.py`, `block_k=64` | 12 | 0 | 0 | all True | all True |
| `test_pa_mqa_logits_opus.py`, `block_k=256` | 12 | 0 | 0 | all True | all True |

`vs flydsl` is `nan` and omitted from the count on the four decode cases — FlyDSL's decode op
has a different ABI and is compared in the perf harness instead — and on the two
unaligned-start cases, for the reason in the Test Plan.

Resources, clean build:

| | VGPR | occupancy | LDS | spill |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| prefill | 223 | 2 | 0 | none |
| decode | 224 | 2 | 0 | none |

Performance — faster on every shape measured, agreement 8.6e-08 .. 1.3e-07:

| | shapes | OPUS faster by |
|---|---|---|
| prefill, chunked (25000 compressed rows) | 3/3 | +7.9 .. +8.4% |
| prefill, fresh | 3/3 | +17.0 .. +34.5% |
| decode, 48-shape sweep | 48/48 | +30.3% mean; +36.4% over the 5 above 9 us |

Two caveats worth carrying with the numbers. Decode's small end is a scheduling artifact:
43 of the 48 shapes fall under 9 us once compression shortens the windows, and down there
the margin is mostly FlyDSL's 512-CTA floor under ATOM's `FP4_MQA_PARALLEL_UNIT_NUM`. The
throughput end is the largest shape — 1024 rows over ~2000 compressed columns, 15.15 vs
26.32 us, 2164 vs 1245 TFLOPS. And prefill's fresh column is partly the `block_k` choice,
which was already known; the new result is chunked prefill, where the reported long-context
deficit (−8.1 .. −9.7%) is now +7.9 .. +8.4%, i.e. ~3108 against ~2855 TFLOPS.

Each figure is the third of three passes; passes agree to ~1 point on prefill and to a 1.0%
median per-shape drift on decode.
## Performance
### Prefill
- **fresh** -- the sequence starts empty, row n sees `(n+1)//4`. Windows 0 -> qlen/4.
- **chunked** -- the sequence ends this forward with K **compressed** rows committed and

title: [Triton/Gluon] [FlyDSL] feat(flydsl): Add HSTU Backward kernel
body:
## Motivation

The purpose of this work is to implement the backward counterpart to the FlyDSL HSTU forward kernel.

Jira ID : SILOTIGER-616

## Technical Details

Depends on the FlyDSL HSTU forward kernel in [#4441](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/4441). This PR adds the backward pass for the same attention block defined in [HSTU (arxiv 2402.17152v2)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.17152v2).

The backward does **not** stash activations from the forward — it recomputes `S = alpha * Q K^T` and the SiLU derivative from `(Q, K)`, then produces `(dQ, dK, dV)` via two lock-free FlyDSL kernels:

1. **Fused KV-owned kernel** (`hstu_attention_bwd.py`) — owns a KV tile, streams query tiles, and computes **dV** and **dK** from a single `S` recompute.
2. **Q-owned kernel** (`hstu_attention_bwd_dq.py`) — mirrors the forward layout; each program owns a query tile and streams KV tiles to compute **dQ**.

Shared indexing/layout helpers live in `hstu_attention_common.py`. The public API is `flydsl_hstu_attention_bwd` in `hstu_attention_kernels.py`, wired into `FlydslHstuAttention` for end-to-end autograd.

**Feature parity with the forward kernel:**
- Jagged (variable-length) batching via `seq_offsets`
- Causal masking plus the same optional variants: `num_targets`, sliding window (`max_attn_len`), and contextual prefix (`contextual_seq_len`)
- `attn_dim != hidden_dim` (asymmetric head dims)
- `{f16, bf16}` inputs, fp32 accumulation, fast-math SiLU (same conventions as forward: `alpha`-in-score, `1/N` on `dS`)

**Tuning & dispatch:**
- Per-kernel tuned configs in `hstu_attention_bwd_tuned.csv`

## Test Plan

- **Correctness (pytest)** — `op_tests/flydsl_tests/test_flydsl_hstu_attention_bwd.py`

- **Perf / op-test gate** — `op_tests/test_flydsl_hstu_attention_bwd.py`

- **Benchmark harness** — extended `op_tests/op_benchmarks/triton/bench_hstu_attn.py` with `--provider flydsl --mode bwd` (and optional `--sort_by_length`).

## Test Result

- All unit tests in `op_tests/flydsl_tests/test_flydsl_hstu_attention_bwd.py` pass on gfx942 and gfx950.

title: [FlyDSL] fp8 unified attention for gfx950
body:
## Motivation

Qwen3-VL MLPerf inference on MI355X/gfx950 needs native FP8×FP8 MFMA unified
attention on a paged KV cache. aiter's Triton `unified_attention` upcasts the FP8
KV cache before the QK GEMM, forfeiting the FP8 MFMA peak; the CK kernel that does
the FP8 intersection was never merged. This ports the
kernel to FlyDSL so the FP8 path is native and in-tree.

## Technical Details

- Native FP8×FP8 MFMA unified attention (QK and PV) for gfx950, ported to FlyDSL
  v0.3.0 (`aiter/ops/flydsl/kernels/flash_attn_{fp8_gfx950,dualwave_common}.py`).
  Lifts the three FP8 rejections the production call hits: **varlen** (packed
  ragged Q), **paged KV** (block_size 64), and **split-K** (multi-partial combine).
  The fp8 paged/varlen/split-K/sinks machinery is aiter-owned, not
  upstream-tracked; main loop is 8-cluster restructured (softmax-VALU bound).
- **Shuffled 5D KV-cache support** (`SHUFFLED_KV_CACHE_1`, the vLLM-v1 production
  layout): vectorized K/V loaders, coalesced V staging, a 5D descriptor-geometry
  override. Auto-selected from tensor rank (`k.dim() == 5`); no new caller flag.
- **GQA-packed M**: factors M as query-positions × GQA-group (mirroring Triton) so
  one kernel serves prefill and decode.
- **Decode-specialized kernel** (`aiter/ops/flydsl/kernels/flash_attn_fp8_decode_gfx950.py`,
  new): a `BLOCK_M=16` GQA-group `mfma_16x16x32_f8` body sized to the live M-rows
  of GQA-16:1 `query_len=1` decode (the shared 2d body fills only 1 of 16 M-rows
  there). Multi-wave cooperative workgroup with on-chip LSE combine, async
  `buffer_load...lds` KV staging + register V-prefetch, fill-aware inter-workgroup
  split-KV (grid.z) with a global-memory LSE-combine kernel, and per-page
  `BufferDesc` rebasing so the 2 GB / 65536-block production pool stays inside
  int32 buffer offsets. Serves the decode region behind a centralized
  decode-dispatch gate; a narrow mid-batch/deep-context band
  (9 ≤ num_seqs ≤ 48 and max_seqlen_k ≥ 8192) is conservatively ceded to Triton.
- **Adaptive dispatch, no caller flag**: split-K auto-fires for underfilled regimes
  (decode-only, ragged decode, low-chunk mixed; cap 16, overridable via
  `AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN_MAX_KV_SPLITS`, verified to 128). Mixed prefill/decode
  batches are partitioned and each half routed to its optimal tier when the decode
  context is deep enough (gate + decline-memo so the partition check isn't re-paid
  per decoder layer); underfilled shallow-mixed batches cede to Triton
  (return `None`); full batches stay single-pass.
- Shape widening: non-causal, fp16 output, and attention sinks.
- Wired into the public `unified_attention()` entry point via a return-`None`
  opt-in adapter (`aiter/ops/flydsl/unified_attention_kernels.py`). Known
  constraint (gated): the block-table LDS stager caps KV at 131072 tokens
  (2048 pages × 64).

## Test Plan

gfx950, `~/.flydsl/cache` cleared. Under `op_tests/flydsl_tests/`:

```
python3 -m pytest op_tests/flydsl_tests/test_vendored_fp8_attention.py -rs
python3 -m pytest op_tests/flydsl_tests/test_fp8_paged.py -rs
python3 -m pytest op_tests/flydsl_tests/test_fp8_splitk.py -rs
python3 -m pytest op_tests/flydsl_tests/test_packed_splitk_{decode,mixed}.py -rs
python3 -m pytest op_tests/flydsl_tests/test_flydsl_unified_attention.py -rs  # consolidated prefill/decode/mixed
python3 -m pytest op_tests/flydsl_tests/test_unified_attention_routing.py -rs  # end-to-end via public entry point
```

## Test Result

Correctness — worst absolute error 0.055, cosine ≥ 0.9996 across all regimes:

| Test | Coverage | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `test_vendored_fp8_attention` | dense bit-identical to upstream + ragged varlen | pass |
| `test_fp8_paged` | paged, paged×varlen, page-order permutation | pass |
| `test_fp8_splitk` | split-K 1/2/4/8, paged×split-K | pass |
| `test_packed_splitk_{decode,mixed}` | packed-M × split-K, decode-only + low-chunk mixed | pass |
| `test_flydsl_unified_attention` | consolidated prefill/decode/mixed × bf16/f16, 5D shuffled, 2 GB pool, split-K ragged | pass (20/20) |
| `test_unified_attention_routing` | end-to-end, prefill/chunked/decode/mixed + routing gates | pass |

Decode-specialized kernel — correctness across all split counts and the full
production pool: 209/209 production-pool cases (48 at the full 2 GB / 65536-block
pool), stage matrix 24/24, 44/44 pytest, prefill bit-identical to upstream.

Performance vs aiter `main`'s Triton `unified_attention` on the production 5D
shuffled fp8 KV-cache (`SHUFFLED_KV_CACHE_1`, the vLLM-v1 layout — the only
production-truth baseline; a linear-cache comparison overstates the win):

| Regime | Ratio | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Pure prefill, weighted total (trace-v1) | +9.1% (Triton 7372ms -> FlyDSL 6699ms) | dominant M=32768 (~77% of prefill time) 1.06x; 25k-30k band ~0.98-1.0x |
| Pure prefill, small / KV-bound shapes | 1.87-2.26x | |
| Mixed batch, deep decode (ctx>=16384), dispatch split fires | 1.06-1.10x | |
| Mixed batch, shallow/underfilled | ceded to Triton | fallback confirmed served via the entry point |
| Decode, specialized kernel, GQA-16:1 fp8 shuffled paged | beats Triton on 6/8 of the batch×context grid | ~79-81% of the `pa` asm bandwidth ceiling at b=64; the 2 sub-parity cells (b=16/32, ctx=16384) are the ceded band, served by Triton |
| **Total attention (trace-weighted)** | **~+12%** (approximate) | |

## Submission Checklist

- [ ] Look over the contributing guidelines at https://github.com/ROCm/ROCm/blob/develop/CONTRIBUTING.md#pull-requests.
- [x] Ran the `flydsl-kernel-code-cleanup` skill over the changed kernels before human review.

title: Opt qk_norm_rope_group_quant in gfx1250
body:
## Motivation

<!-- Explain the purpose of this PR and the goals it aims to achieve. -->

## Technical Details

1. Carry the Q e8m0 run in the payload store. Hand the run to the lane whose payload slot already covers it, gathered through 32B of per-wave LDS. The pickup goes through __builtin_memcpy — a typed load lets alias analysis reorder it against the uint16_t publishes (one wrong byte in 29,360,128 at G=32). MERGE_Q_SCALE is a template parameter, not a runtime flag: selecting at runtime cost the small shapes ~6% with the branch never taken.

2. Write the whole Q row in one store. Widening to all 32 lanes costs 10% more bytes and wins more back — the price here is partial sectors, not bytes.

3. Defer the Q TDM refill by one head. The refill races the ds_read of the slot it overwrites (latent on main); tensorcnt does not order the TDM engine against this wave's DS reads. Deferring puts the math's own s_wait_dscnt in between, so the race closes for free — an explicit drain cost +2.1%. Needs Q_TDM_DEPTH=3 to keep the same lead.

4. Pin the K RoPE value for the SWA copy. The f32 result sits on the exact bf16 tie, and the compiler rematerialises the expression for the second store with the other fma contraction. Explicit fma was not enough on its own; an empty asm is what pins it

## Test Plan

144 op-test configs show the same failure set as pristine main on the same toolchain (all pre-existing). 60 paged-SWA configs: byte-exact warnings 8 → 0. NaN/Inf probe over 16 poison placements: 14 bit-identical, 2 differ only in a quiet NaN's sign bit. All five commits compile cleanly, so the series bisects.

title: [HIP] [JIT] Add a DSv4 paged K gather+dequant kernel
body:
## Summary

Add a HIP kernel for the DeepSeek V4 paged K gather+dequant. The existing Triton kernel does not coalesce and holds ~0.34 TB/s on a 4.2 TB/s device, and it runs twice per chunk in the prefill loop. 

## Suggested fix

The new HIP kernel maps one wavefront to one gathered token, with lane L owning output dims [L8, L8+8). The 64 lanes cover all 512 dims so the store is a single 1024 B line. Lanes 0-55 read the fp8 payload and dequantize, lanes 56-63 pass the bf16 RoPE tail through. The fp8->f32 decode is branchless and parameterized by the exponent bias, so one path serves both e4m3fnuz and OCP e4m3.

## Perf

MI325X (gfx942), CUDA-graph replay, k_cache[*, 64, 584]:

| out shape       | Triton    | new HIP kernel     |       |
|-----------------|-----------|----------|-------|
| [4, 4096, 512]  | 74.6 us   | 13.3 us  | 5.6x  |
| [4, 16384, 512] | 313.5 us  | 32.1 us  | 9.8x  |
| [4, 65536, 576] | 1899.8 us | 126.7 us | 15.0x |

Triton sits at ~0.34 TB/s across all three; this reaches 3.3 TB/s at the larger shapes, against ~4.2 TB/s measured streaming rate on this arch.

Correctness

- Swept all 256 fp8 codes x all 256 UE8M0 scales against the Triton reference, both encodings. OCP e4m3 matches bit for bit; e4m3fnuz matches except 0x3f and 0xbf at scale 2^-126, where the result is bf16-subnormal and flushes to zero — that scale means the whole 64-dim group is already negligible. NaN encodings aren't reachable, since the V4 encoder clamps to FP8_MAX.
- Also checked ragged gather_lens, partial gathers, non-zero offset, and block_size 32 and 64.

title: [FlyDSL] gfx950 FP8 MQA logits indexer kernel
body:
## Motivation

This PR introduces a FlyDSL kernel for computing DeepSeek-V4 sparse attention lightning indexer on `gfx950`. The new kernel is drop-in replacement for the existing Triton/Gluon kernel. For the DSv4 prefill shapes it generally faster than the existing Triton/Gluon kernel. The `gfx942` version was introduced in an earlier PR #3913.

## Technical Details

There are two alternative implementation on `gfx950`

- Direct load kernel similar `gfx942`: Data is streamed directly from DRAM to registers.
- LDS staged kernel where KV slices are stored on LDS and shared among all wavefronts where each wavefront computes it's own disjoint set of query rows. Q fragments and per-row weights are preloaded into registers once per block (similar to the direct load kernel. The LDS staging uses gfx950 specific async global → LDS DMA which writes directly to LDS without passing through VGPRs. XOR swizzle is used for LDS writes and reads to reduce the rate of bank conflicts.

The LDS staged instance can have two or more LDS buffer combined with one or more prefetch stages. Allocation of one LDS buffer more than the prefetch depth (`PD`) enables to reduce the number of required barriers by one (barriers are required to ensure data is ready before running MFMA on it). In practice, the most performant combination is 3 LDS buffers with `PD=2` (only one barrier required).

There is instance auto-selection which selects the best kernel for a given shape. However, similarly to the existing implementation, the auto-selected instance can be overridden with an environment variable. 

There's also one common optimization for both `gfx942` and `gfx950`: when `clean_logits=True`, the baseline implementation uses `torch.fill` to initialize the logits matrix with `-inf` values. Since half of the values are subsequently overwritten by the logits kernel, we have fused the "clean logits" initialization step into the logits kernel. This provides performance boost for small sequence lengths.

## Test Plan

All tests added in PR #3913 are now enabled for `gfx950`. For performance, benchmarked the same DSv4 shapes in PR #3913

## Test Result

All unit tests pass on both `gfx942` and `gfx950` (note: they are not enabled as part of the CI workflow)

title: [FlyDSL] Add QuickAllReduce INT6 and INT5
body:
## Motivation

FlyDSL quick all-reduce only had an INT4 wire format (~19 dB SQNR). This adds
INT6 and INT5, so the mesh covers the full quality/wire range at FlyDSL's speed.

TP8, gfx950, bf16, HIP-graph. Decode 512x5120, prefill 32768x5120. Each row is
the fastest of an ST x grid sweep; SQNR is vs fp32 NCCL.

| Codec | Decode | Decode SQNR | Prefill | Prefill SQNR |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| INT4 | 26.3 µs | 19.2 dB | 524 µs | 19.2 dB |
| INT5 | 28.7 µs | 25.0 dB | 620 µs | 25.0 dB |
| INT6 | 31.2 µs | 30.2 dB | 712 µs | 30.2 dB |

Against HIP QuickReduce at the same bit width (HIP has no INT5):
| Codec | FlyDSL decode | HIP decode | FlyDSL prefill | HIP prefill |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| INT4 | 26.3 µs / 19.2 dB | 29.0 µs / 18.3 dB | 524 µs / 19.2 dB | 1057 µs / 18.3 dB |
| INT6 | 31.2 µs / 30.2 dB | 35.3 µs / 30.4 dB | 712 µs / 30.2 dB | 1137 µs / 30.4 dB |

## Technical Details

INT6 and INT5 are not new engines. The mesh and ring kernels were already
codec-generic, so per review this folds the INT4 and INT6 hosts and kernels into
one and drops `int4` from names that no longer describe the code:
- `quick_allreduce_int4.py` + `quick_allreduce_int6.py` -> `quick_allreduce.py`,
  class `FlyQuickAllReduce`
- `kernels/quick_allreduce_int4.py` + `..._int6.py` -> `kernels/quick_allreduce_mesh.py`
- `kernels/quick_allreduce_int4_ring.py` -> `kernels/quick_allreduce_ring.py`
- `quick_allreduce_int4_ipc.py` -> `quick_allreduce_ipc.py`
- both multi-GPU test files -> `test_flydsl_quick_allreduce.py`
The codec is then a parameter: `MESH_CODECS = ("int4", "int5", "int6", "fp16")`,
one `Codec` each in `quick_allreduce_codec.py`, and a codec-keyed
`MESH_ST_LADDER` behind `mesh_st_ladder(codec, world_size)`. Both new formats
keep INT4's nibble plane byte-identical and add a dense plane on top, so every
region stays on the 64 B fabric sector grid:
- INT5: 1024 B nibbles + 256 B 1-bit plane + 128 B scale = 1408 B, 22 sectors
- INT6: 1024 B nibbles + 512 B 2-bit plane + 128 B scale = 1664 B, 26 sectors
`_Algorithm.single_codec` marks the mesh as carrying one format across both
laps, so it does not inherit the ring's TP8 `rs_codec=int6` / `ag_codec=int4`
default. Mesh only for INT5/INT6; the ring is unchanged, and the communicator
still constructs the mesh INT4 default.

## Test Plan

`op_tests/multigpu_tests/test_flydsl_quick_allreduce.py` on 8 GPUs plus the
flydsl codec and policy tests. Mesh cases are parametrized on codec with
per-format SQNR floors (int4 18 dB, int5 24 dB, int6 25 dB) so a silent
fallback to narrower bits fails instead of passing.

## Test Result


All suites pass. Benchmarks as in the tables above.
Known, tracked separately: below TP8 on an uncached inbox the mesh can publish
the handshake flag before the payload is visible to the peer, because
`_publish` waits with `s_waitcnt vmcnt(0)` (local issue-completion, not peer
visibility). At TP2 with ST=8 and a large grid that costs INT6 ~5 dB and shows
~0.27% of elements differing between two runs of identical input; INT4 has the
same hole, smaller in dB. TP8 (the shipping configuration) is bit-stable, and
the finegrained/default inboxes do not flake.

## Submission Checklist

title: docs: Copilot FlyDSL path instructions and review-pr C5
body:
## Summary
- Copilot code review does not load `.claude/skills` on its own. GitHub's supported hook is path-specific files under `.github/instructions/*.instructions.md` with `applyTo` globs; without `excludeAgent`, Copilot code review uses them ([repository custom instructions](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-on-github/customize-copilot/add-custom-instructions/add-repository-instructions), [Copilot code review](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-on-github/use-copilot-agents/copilot-code-review)). Triton already uses this; FlyDSL PRs had none, so Copilot reviewed kernels with generic mixed-device advice and invented `gcnArchName` probes against `get_gfx_runtime()`.
- Add `.github/instructions/aiter-ops-flydsl.instructions.md` so matching FlyDSL/wrapper/test diffs get the in-repo authoring, cleanup, and aiter-op-test skills, plus the chip_info ISA-gate policy (homogeneous node; do not reimplement arch detection per kernel).

title: [FlyDSL] Expose FP8 attention and gather capability checks
body:
Callers preparing FP8 attention inputs need to reject unsupported architectures and model dimensions before quantization or before gather overwrites a BF16 workspace. Expose two capability queries for that decision:

- `flydsl_flash_attn_fp8_supported(device, num_heads, num_kv_heads, head_dim, head_dim_v, *, dtype=...)` checks fixed device/head configuration without allocating tensors, compiling, launching kernels or reading device values. It reuses the kernel builder's layout and LDS checks for both automatic tile choices. The existing FP8 dispatch gate uses the same query.
- `gather_kv_b_proj_flydsl_fp8_supported(...)` checks FP8 output tensors and descale metadata, sharing validation with the gather launcher. Unsupported devices, malformed weight layouts and mismatched devices return `False`.

Results can be cached while device/layout/dtype/head dimensions and scale metadata remain fixed. Per-call sequence metadata, explicit launch overrides and descale values remain caller/runtime contracts. These interfaces do not catch or retry kernel execution failures.

Used by [ROCm/ATOM#2191](https://github.com/ROCm/ATOM/pull/2191) to select BF16 attention with a warning when FP8 MHA is unavailable or unsupported, before FP8 preparation; FP8-gather rejection can retain FP8 MHA by using BF16 gather followed by dynamic quantization.

Validation on gfx950:

- Combined AITER capability/validation tests and ATOM dispatch regressions: **94 passed, 1 skipped** (unrelated architecture-specific case).
- Metadata tests simulate gfx942/gfx1201, unsupported QK/V widths and LDS limits, invalid head grouping and FP8 formats, and gather output/scale/device mismatches. Existing gather GPU tests confirm predicate/launcher agreement.
- Real GPU checks passed for FP8 QKV + MHA, graph replay with changed inputs, direct FP8 gather + MHA, BF16 gather + fused KV quantization + FP8 MHA, and BF16 attention after simulated gfx942 rejection.
- Black, Ruff and diff checks pass. No full model evaluation was rerun for this change.

title: [Triton/Gluon] Create benchmark for fused_rmsnorm_add_bench
body:
## Motivation

`fused_rmsnorm_add.py` ships a Triton kernel and a gfx1250 gluon kernel, but it doesn't have a benchmark within Triton, so there is no baseline to measure numbers. Because it's been added post Triton 3.4, it does not have any performance history at all. 

The op is not covered by the model benchmarking tool either -- it is absent from both `model_shapes.json` and `KERNEL_DICT`, so it cannot be reached through `bench_models.py`.

## Technical Details

Shape-driven benchmark following a similar family layout:

- same get_x_vals/run_benchmark/parse_args/main structure,
- same triton.testing.Benchmark + perf_report + do_bench(warmup=25, rep=100), and,
- it reuses the tester's generate_inputs rather than duplicating input construction.

It has a smaller flag set compared to previous additions of benchmarks ([PR#5574](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/5574)) since there is no `--backend` (Gluon on gfx1250 and Triton otherwise). No `--pad-to-multiple`, `--quant`, or `--backward` as op has none of those paths. It does keep `add_residual`.

15 default shapes: 

| group | shapes | why |
|---|---|---|
| M scaling at a fixed width | (1 / 1024 / 16384, 4096) | `grid=(M,)`, so M is the occupancy knob |
| `BLOCK_SIZE_N` buckets | (8192, 4 / 128 / 512 / 2048 / 8192 / 16384), (256, 32768) | the 32 floor up to the widest row |
| model hidden sizes | (8192, 2880 / 7168), (4096, 5120), (16380, 1536) | `model_shapes.json` rmsnorm entries |
| divisibility | (8192, 4095) | `N % 16 != 0`, (below) |

N = 4, 128, 512, 1536, 2880, 4096, 5120, 7168, 8192 and 16384 are all rmsnorm widths in this repo's `model_shapes.json` or the tester's own `get_vals()`; (16380, 1536) is a tester shape.

Bandwidth is the meaningful figure here, and that's the default metric for this kernel. 
Memory accounting is similar to ([PR#5574](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/5574)) with the exclusion of the output due to the padding in PR#5574. 

## Test Plan

- Every CLI path exercised: default sweep, `--shape`, all three metrics, all three dtypes, `--add-residual`, `-o`, and both `--shape` guards
- Byte model cross-checked against `rocprofv3 --kernel-trace` on four configurations
- pytest correctness test
- black, ruff checks

## Test Result

Default sweep, bandwidth, gfx950, bf16:

```
       M       N    GB/s  (no res)    GB/s (--add-residual)
       1    4096         3.9                    6.1
    1024    4096      2205.5                 3179.2
   16384    4096      5369.3                 5621.3
    8192       4        13.7                   24.5
    8192     128       460.7                  844.6
    8192     512      1645.7                 2682.8
    8192    2048      4164.8                 4599.2
    8192    8192      5165.8                 5572.6
    8192   16384      5412.8                 5638.2
     256   32768      3216.7                 4258.1
    8192    2880      4805.6                 5132.6
    8192    7168      5279.1                 5470.7
    4096    5120      4425.7                 4866.8
   16380    1536      4758.7                 5032.2
    8192    4095      1717.2                 1943.3
```

`test_fused_rmsnorm_add.py`: 32 passed. `black` and `ruff`: clean

### Byte model cross-check

`rocprofv3 --kernel-trace`, 250 iterations + 25 warmup, against the model above:

| shape | bytes | kernel time | kernel GB/s | % of ~8 TB/s |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8192 x 8192 | 268.45 MB | 42.825 us | 6268.5 | 78.4 % |
| 8192 x 8192, residual | 536.89 MB | 80.032 us | 6708.4 | 83.9 % |
| 8192 x 4096 | 134.23 MB | 22.069 us | 6082.0 | 76.0 % |

The residual and non-residual paths land within 7 % of each other, which is what validates the `HAS_RES` branch of the accounting -- had the `out_res1` write been dropped from the model, the residual row would read ~25 % low. `do_bench` reads above kernel time (27.4 us vs 22.1 us at 8192 x 4096) because it flushes L2 before every timed iteration. An upcoming  `do_bench_cudagraph` can fix and account for this difference.

### One finding the benchmark makes visible

`(8192, 4095)` is in the default list because `N % 16 != 0` costs **3.4x**:

| shape | `BLOCK_SIZE_N` | kernel time | kernel GB/s |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8192 x 4096 | 4096 | 22.069 us | 6082.0 |
| 8192 x 4095 | 4096 | 74.462 us | 1802.2 |

Same kernel, same `BLOCK_SIZE_N`, same byte count to within 0.02 % -- the only difference is that Triton's divisibility-by-16 specialization on `N` and the row strides does not apply. This is *not* row-stride byte alignment: `N = 4088` gives a 16-byte-aligned row stride (8176 B) and is still in the slow tier, while `N = 4080` is fast. Across 13 sampled widths the fast/slow split tracks `N % 16 == 0` exactly.

Not addressed by this PR. The benchmark exists so it can be tracked for future changes or comparisons.

### Register growth

The uncapped `BLOCK_SIZE_N` shows up as register pressure rather than spilling (`FIRST_INPUT_RES=0`, `num_warps=4`):

| `BLOCK_SIZE_N` | 32 | 4096 | 8192 | 16384 | 32768 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| VGPR | 12 | 43 | 63 | 154 | 219 |
| spills | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

There are no spills at any bucket, and the widest rows are not slow -- `(8192, 16384)` is the fastest shape in the sweep. The cost is occupancy, which this streaming kernel tolerates.

- [x] Look over the contributing guidelines at https://github.com/ROCm/TheRock/blob/main/GOVERNANCE.md#pull-requests.

title: [Triton/Gluon] Create benchmark for `Norm/Layernorm`
body:
## Motivation

`norm.py` exposes six public layernorm entry points and a backward pass, and has **no benchmark**.

This matters in practice because we are able to spot regressions when comparing to previous architectures, and have a default way of seeing metrics for various shapes/features of the kernel.

## Technical Details

Shape-driven benchmark following the neighbouring kernel `bench_rmsnorm.py` layout:
- same get_x_vals/run_benchmark/parse_args/main structure,
- same triton.testing.Benchmark + perf_report + do_bench(warmup=25, rep=100),

Existing flags:
| flags | entry point | kernel |
|---|---|---|
| (none) | `layer_norm` | `_layernorm_kernel` |
| `--add-residual` | `layernorm2d_fwd_with_add` | `_fused_add_layernorm_kernel` |
| `--quant dynamic\|smooth` | `..._with_dynamicquant` / `..._with_smoothquant` | `_quant_layernorm_kernel` |
| `--quant … --add-residual` | `..._with_add_dynamicquant` / `..._with_add_smoothquant` | `_quant_fused_add_layernorm_kernel` |

18 default shapes, each with a source:
| category | shapes | source |
|---|---|---|
| M scaling at a fixed compiled variant | (1 … 16384, 4096) | row-count scaling with `BLOCK_SIZE` held constant |
| model hidden sizes | (8192, 512/1536/2880/5120/7168/8192) | `model_shapes.json`: layernorm has no entries of its own but sits where `rmsnorm` does |
| unaligned M and N | (873, 1245) | `test_rmsnorm.py` and `test_fused_rmsnorm_add.py` `get_vals()`; the largest observed 3.8 regression when tested with `rocprofv3 --kernel-trace` |
| tester edge cases | (1, 4), (128, 2), (359, 1), (1, 131072) | `test_layernorm.py::get_vals()` |
| `BLOCK_SIZE` cap boundary | (256, 32768), (256, 65536) | 32768 is exactly the bf16 cap (`65536 // element_size`); 65536 is past it, so the kernel loops over N |

**Memory accounting** tracks each path: 
- quant writes **int8** (`M*N`) plus a per-row `yscale`; 
- smoothquant adds an `xscale` read; 
- residual adds one read and one write;
- `mean`/`rstd` are allocated only by the autograd paths. 
- FLOPs are an effective count (`8*M*N` forward, `12*M*N` backward), approx. twice RMSNorm's `4*M*N` since layernorm also
computes and subtracts a mean.

Default metric is `bandwidth`, and there is no model mode because layernorm is in neither `model_shapes.json` nor `KERNEL_DICT`, so `models="llama3"` is not inherited; `model_benchmarking_shapes` is not required.

## Test Plan

- `--quant` x `--add-residual` x `--dtype`, plus backward x residual x dtype, plus all three metrics, `--shape`, `-o`, and the `--backward --quant` guard
- `pytest op_tests/triton_tests/normalization/test_layernorm.py`
- Reproducibility: full default sweep run twice
- `black`, `ruff`, `py_compile` checks

## Test Result

Forward matrix 18/18 passed; backward 6/6; all metrics, dtypes and guards behave.

**Every path** dispatches the expected kernel, verified by trace:

```
(plain)                        -> _layernorm_kernel                  OK
--add-residual                 -> _fused_add_layernorm_kernel        OK
--quant dynamic | smooth       -> _quant_layernorm_kernel            OK
--quant … --add-residual       -> _quant_fused_add_layernorm_kernel  OK
```

Default sweep, bandwidth:

```
      M         N     GB/s            M         N     GB/s
      1    4096.0     4.98         8192    7168.0  3639.93
    128    4096.0   317.88         8192    8192.0  3665.83
   1024    4096.0  1820.53          873    1245.0   412.19
   4096    4096.0  3250.31            1       4.0     0.01
  16384    4096.0  3732.19          128       2.0     0.31
   8192     512.0  1224.04          359       1.0     0.66
   8192    1536.0  2649.08            1  131072.0    31.08
   8192    2880.0  3157.77          256   32768.0  2081.44
   8192    5120.0  3300.29          256   65536.0  2622.78
```

#### Correction
`144 passed in 5.51s`

### Regression coverage

Not addressed by this PR. This will be filed separately as a compiler issue with ATT traces. All five regressing configurations are now reachable, four of them from the default sweep:

| entry point | shape | Triton 3.4 | Triton 3.8 | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `..._with_add_smoothquant` | M=873 N=1245 | 15.604 µs | 17.224 µs | **+10.4 %** |
| `..._with_add_dynamicquant` | M=873 N=1245 | 13.875 µs | 14.790 µs | **+6.6 %** |
| `..._with_add_smoothquant` | M=16384 N=4096 | 187.903 µs | 196.703 µs | **+4.7 %** |
| backward + add | M=16384 N=4096 | 107.689 µs | 110.303 µs | **+2.4 %** |
| `..._with_add_dynamicquant` | M=16384 N=4096 | 176.992 µs | 181.043 µs | **+2.3 %** |

rocprofv3 --kernel-trace, 250 iters + 25 warmup, with single-average number (10% off head and 10% off tail, average the middle 80%). Across the full 80-shape sweep Triton 3.8 is a net win: median **-7.6 %**, backward **-12.3 %** -- with these five regressing. Plain `layer_norm` at M=16384 N=4096 *improves* 7.2 %, so the effect tracks the fused add+quant kernel, not the shape.

## Submission Checklist

- [x] Look over the contributing guidelines at https://github.com/ROCm/TheRock/blob/main/GOVERNANCE.md#pull-requests.

title: Implement FlyDSL version of fused_qk_norm_mrope_3d_cache_pts_quant_shuffle

## Motivation

Implements a FlyDSL version of the existing fused_qk_norm_mrope_3d_cache_pts_quant_shuffle kernel with the goal of improving performance for larger shapes.

The test file (`op_tests/test_flydsl_fused_qk_norm_mrope_cache_quant_shuffle.py`) verifies the new implementation against the existing HIP implementation. Results match the existing HIP exactly on the tested parameters with `match_hip = True` and differ by bf16 truncation accuracy with `match_hip = False`.

title: [WIP] Add MoonEP prefill and decode planning policies
body:
## Summary

- add a PrefillPolicy that builds a global expert histogram, runs the gfx950 FlyDSL planner, and emits EPLB-style virtual physical IDs for a normal MoRI dispatch
- constrain each destination to EPR resident experts plus B prefetched remote experts; overflow allocations fall back to the expert owner
- add a DecodePolicy that preserves logical owner IDs and performs no histogram exchange, global synchronization, or weight migration
- replace the RCCL all-gather planning dependency with a symmetric-heap direct-push exchange and stream barrier
- provide the reusable symmetric weight pool and prefetch kernel consumed by the ATOM integration

This draft is stacked on the existing gfx950 MoonEP proof-of-concept commits. The new policy-facing work is in the tip commit; the legacy grouped-row path remains in the stack only as historical comparison while ATOM uses MoRI dispatch plus standard `fused_moe`.

ATOM draft: https://github.com/ROCm/ATOM/pull/2333

The ATOM side uses production MoRI v1 for the initial gfx950 closure and switches to MoRI v2 for gfx1250 under the same planning and virtual-ID contract.

## Contract

```text
physical_id = destination_rank * (EPR + B) + destination_slot
```

- `[0, EPR)`: resident experts
- `[EPR, EPR+B)`: prefetched remote experts
- Decode uses `EPR` and leaves IDs unchanged

## Validation

title: [OPUS] fix(opus): prevent DSV4 DPA CI OOM with bounded route workspace buckets
body:
## What

Prevent the DeepSeek-V4-Pro DPA 8K/1K c256 CI workload from exhausting device memory during prefill, using an AITer-only token capacity class for the Opus A8W4 stage2 route workspace.

The affected route-reduce path materializes an MXFP8 workspace with shape:

```text
[token_num * topk, model_dim + model_dim / 8] uint8
```

For a captured DPA prefill step:

```text
token_num = 129216
topk      = 6
model_dim = 7168
row_bytes = 7168 + 7168 / 8 = 8064
workspace = 129216 * 6 * 8064
          = 6,251,986,944 bytes
          = 5.822617 GiB
```

## Root cause

DPA gathers per-rank prefill inputs before routed MoE, so stage2 sees a global token count close to 128K. That count changes slightly between scheduler steps.

Previously, each call allocated the exact route-output size. For this model, changing `token_num` by one changes the request by 48,384 bytes. A slightly larger request cannot reuse a slightly smaller cached allocator block. Repeated dynamic-M steps therefore leave a staircase of fully inactive 5-6 GiB segments while requesting the next size.

```text
dynamic DPA global M
  -> exact-size multi-GiB route workspace
  -> previous inactive segment is slightly too small
  -> allocator obtains another large segment
  -> torch reserved memory grows in ~5.8 GiB steps
  -> physical free memory reaches zero
  -> an in-flight collective reports HSA out-of-resources
```

The collective is where the failure is observed, but it is not the allocation producer. Memory-history allocation stacks and operator logging identify the Opus stage2 `torch.empty` call, and the recorded 6,251,986,944-byte request matches the tensor shape exactly.

## Fix

Map each positive runtime token count to the next power-of-two capacity:

```python
def _route_workspace_token_capacity(token_num: int) -> int:
    token_num = int(token_num)
    if token_num <= 0:
        raise ValueError(f"token_num must be positive, got {token_num}")
    return 1 << (token_num - 1).bit_length()
```

Allocate physical storage with that capacity, while exposing only the exact logical rows to the kernel:

```python
capacity_tokens = _route_workspace_token_capacity(token_num)
storage = torch.empty(
    (capacity_tokens * topk, cols),
    dtype=torch.uint8,
    device=device,
)
route_output = storage[: token_num * topk]
```

The kernel ABI, grid, tile, reduction, logical tensor shape, and numerical path do not change.

This replaces the earlier 1 GiB byte-bucket implementation; it is not retained as a fallback. It also removes the proposed public `stage2_max_token_num` parameter and requires no ATOM change or model-name special case.

## Capacity behavior

The regression test covers the relevant boundaries:

```text
1       -> 1
247     -> 256
256     -> 256
257     -> 512
32768   -> 32768
32769   -> 65536
65536   -> 65536
65537   -> 131072
117626  -> 131072
128332  -> 131072
131072  -> 131072
131073  -> 262144
```

For current DSV4 parameters, capacity `131072` is exactly 5.90625 GiB per rank. The observed large shapes all reuse it:

```text
117626 -> 131072: about 620 MiB padding, +11.4%
128332 -> 131072: about 126 MiB padding,  +2.1%
129216 -> 131072: about  86 MiB padding,  +1.4%
```

## Scope and limitations

This is the smallest AITer-only fix for the confirmed CI failure mode:

- changes one Opus FP8 route-output allocation path;
- does not modify ATOM;
- does not add a DSV4 model-name special case;
- does not change tuned CSV selection, kernel code, launch geometry, or reduction;
- does not reduce KV-cache capacity;
- keeps the kernel-visible view exact.

It stabilizes allocation sizes but is not a complete system memory contract:

- the first large allocation still occurs after KV sizing;
- just above a power-of-two boundary, padding can approach 2x;
- `131073 -> 262144` would require an 11.8125 GiB DSV4 workspace;
- multiple streams or graph pools can require multiple segments of the same capacity;
- the geometric history is below 2x the largest class only when there is one segment per class and no overlapping pools.

A caller-owned workspace pool allocated before final KV sizing remains the most robust long-term design. This PR intentionally keeps the immediate fix limited to AITer.

## Validation

Completed for this exact revision:

- Black check: passed;
- Ruff check: passed;
- Python compile: passed;
- `git diff --check`: passed;
- focused MI355X container test: all 12 boundary mappings plus 0/-1 validation passed.

The common `op_tests/test_moe_2stage.py` script calls the capacity test unconditionally, so the CI entry point exercises it before the operator sweep.

Full CI-equivalent validation for this exact revision also passed on 8 x MI355X with ATOM `bd7a020e` main, expandable segments disabled, `gpu_memory_utilization=0.9`, 8K/1K requests, and concurrency 256:

```text
warmup / formal requests = 512 / 2560
successful requests      = 2560 / 2560
duration                 = 657.12 s
total token throughput   = 32,373.22 tok/s
observed concurrency     = 249.45
OOM / HSA OOR / 5xx      = 0
worst max physical used  = 265.703 GiB
worst min physical free  = 22.281 GiB
```

The eight-rank post-init snapshots reported `allocated=224.65-225.51 GiB` and `reserved=226.04-226.90 GiB`. Runtime allocator profiling was intentionally not injected, so those post-init values are not presented as runtime peaks and this run does not claim an exact active/awaiting-free segment count. The 2-second physical-memory sampling covered the complete warmup and formal workload.

title: [Config] configs(glm5.2): o_proj switches to CK Tile at M=1024, not M=8192
body:
`configs/model_configs/a8w8_blockscale_bpreshuffle_tuned_gemm_glm5.2.csv` keeps CK instances for `o_proj` (N=6144, K=4096) all the way to M=4096 and only moves to `a8w8_blockscale_cktile_192x256x128` at M=8192.

Measured on MI350X (gfx950, 256 CU), **CK Tile is already ahead from M=1024** — three rows earlier.

## Result

| M | shipped | candidate | gain | resolution floor |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1024 | 54.739 µs `ck` | **49.978 µs** `cktile` | **+8.70%** | 5.98% |
| 2048 | 100.818 µs `ck` | **87.913 µs** `cktile` | **+12.80%** | 3.15% |
| 4096 | 184.560 µs `ck` | **148.773 µs** `cktile` | **+19.39%** | 3.10% |

`o_proj` runs in every one of this model's 78 layers, so this is a prefill and large-batch win on a shape that is always hot.

## The boundary is measured, not assumed

This is **not** "CK Tile is better than CK". Below M=1024 this shape dispatches to the asm kernel, and CK Tile loses there badly:

| M | shipped | CK Tile forced | |
|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 256 | 20.092 µs `asm` | 46.028 µs | **−129%** |
| 512 | 33.206 µs `asm` | 46.434 µs | **−39.8%** |

So the claim is narrower and more useful: **the switch is three rungs late.** Rows below M=1024 are untouched.

## Protocol

- Production entry point, not a microbenchmark.
- Arms **interleaved**, 9 repeats × 100 iterations, compared by **median**. Single-shot margins on CK candidates here are misordered, not merely noisy.
- Correctness checked against a dequantized fp32 reference on the first repeat of every arm.
- A margin is only called a win if it clears **both arms' spreads and the control delta** — the floor column above.

### Negative control

Forcing the kernel the heuristic already picks must not change the timing. If it does, the instrument is measuring something other than the kernel.

```
# stage 1 control: M=8192 unforced 70.348 (spread 3.7%) vs forced-same 70.356 (spread 1.6%) -> +0.01%
# stage 1 control: M=8192 unforced 68.737 (spread 9.8%) vs forced-same 70.191 (spread 4.0%) -> +2.11%
```

+0.01% on the low-M run and +2.11% on the high-M run. Both runs used the larger of that and the arm spreads as the bar. Without this arm the M=1024 row would not have been distinguishable from noise on the first attempt; with it, +8.70% against a 5.98% floor is.

## Scope

Three rows. No kernel, no dispatch logic, no ABI change. The table stays uniquely keyed on `(gfx, cu_num, M, N, K)` and its schema is unchanged.

Environment: ROCm 7.2.4, torch 2.10.0+rocm7.2.4, MI350X 8×gfx950/256 CU, quiet box.

title: [Triton/Gluon] [Config] Enable unified-attention skip-mask for gfx950 hd256 FP8 prefill
body:
## Summary

- Enable the existing `SPLIT_UNMASKED_LOOP` fast path for gfx950 head-size-256 FP8 Q / FP8 KV, non-windowed, non-shuffled prefill with `max_seqlen_q >= 256`.
- This is config-only: the kernel and wrapper from [AITER PR #4761](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/4761) are unchanged.
- Add the head-size-256 `Q_GEQ_256` config family while keeping sliding-window and shuffled variants on the non-skip path.
- Restore efficient long-context FP8-Q unified prefill: the exact [SGLang PR #39998](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39998) parent stack regresses badly at long context without this config, while [AITER PR #5598](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/5598) recovers and exceeds the true-stock serving baseline.

## Why

[AITER PR #4761](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/4761) enabled skip-mask only for `D_LEQ_128.Q_GEQ_256.DT_fp8_fp8`. Qwen3.8-27B full-attention layers use `head_dim=256`, so they match `D_GEQ_256` first and never reach the head-size-128 key.

This PR adds `D_GEQ_256.Q_GEQ_256.DT_fp8_fp8` with `BLOCK_M=128`, tile 64, and `SPLIT_UNMASKED_LOOP=true`. Sliding-window and shuffled siblings use the same long-prefill tile without enabling the skip loop. Lookup continues to prefer `D_GEQ_512` for head size 512, while decode continues to prefer `D_GEQ_256.Q_LEQ_1*`.

## Activation requirements

This config is used only when SGLang routes prefill through AITER unified attention:

- `SGLANG_USE_AITER=1`
- `SGLANG_USE_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN=1`
- `attention-backend=aiter`
- FP8 Q conversion from [SGLang PR #39998](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39998)

For full AITER page-size-1 decode, the CUDA-graph page-table fix from [SGLang PR #40410](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40410) is also required. The stock/parent/candidate crossover below used Triton decode for every arm, avoiding the affected unified-decode path while preserving the AITER prefill comparison.

## Controlled stock, parent, and candidate comparison

The primary comparison used the same MI355X host, TP1, Qwen3.8-27B MXFP4 model, FP8 KV, seeds, prompt counts, request shapes, and Triton compiler in every arm.

| Component | Value |
|---|---|
| Triton | `3.8.0+amd.rocm7.2.0.git7cb7b059` |
| Triton wheel SHA256 | `2aa39a413aab73901e1e4b3a166495a17d2325ac9cedf0e8c77a1f0df661b71a` |
| Chunked prefill | 16384 |
| Decode backend | Triton for all arms |
| True stock | [SGLang PR #39598](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39598), legacy `mha_batch_prefill_*` |
| Parent | SGLang [PR #39998](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39998), parent AITER unified Triton config |
| Candidate | Same parent stack plus [AITER PR #5598](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/5598) |
| Stock image | `sha256:6457bcaf548be73cebfd9ca6650e43ecb8ba78d82ce87e1f4b33696075bc7e5e` |
| Parent image | `sha256:0223e66ecfb6c5773cb22ff495dd213f5aaf4c79c897ace8ba9697ce7345bd5d` |
| Candidate image | `sha256:69aa235ad0bdf09674c6bb6bafa0fafc7a4bb36c819e7cf73a3dc062f1aaec9d` |

Each arm ran on HIP 4 and HIP 6 in a crossover schedule. All 48 child benchmark runs completed. Cross-GPU output-throughput variance was below 3% except the candidate 128K/c16 row at 3.83%, which remains explicitly flagged.

Route probes confirmed:

- True stock used legacy `mha_batch_prefill_*`.
- Parent used FP8-Q/FP8-KV unified Triton fallback.
- Candidate selected unified Triton with `BLOCK_M=128` and `SPLIT_UNMASKED_LOOP=true`.
- Every arm used Triton decode.

Short-answer, 60K needle, and sampled GPQA smoke gates passed in every arm.

## Direct unified-attention kernel evidence

The kernel gate uses the production Qwen3.8 geometry: 24 Q heads, 4 KV heads, head dimension 256, page size 1, and FP8 Q / FP8 KV. Both parent and candidate completed 18/18 executable cases with zero runtime errors and zero quantized-reference failures.

Measured after one warmup invocation:

| Prefill shape | Parent config | [#5598](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/5598) config | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Q=16K, KV=16K | 9.16 ms | 2.94 ms | 3.12× |
| Q=16K, KV=64K | 88.18 ms | 15.37 ms | 5.74× |
| Q=16K, KV=128K | 218.02 ms | 32.92 ms | 6.62× |

The short-Q and decode probes remained close, which matches the PR scope: the new key targets long prefill rather than decode.

At Q=16K and KV=16K, the candidate FP8-Q output had approximately 0.9998 cosine similarity to the quantized-input reference and passed the configured tolerance. The same output had approximately 0.9988 cosine similarity and 91.6% head-output argmax agreement versus the original BF16 reference.

## End-to-end serving evidence

Output throughput is the median of the HIP 4 and HIP 6 crossover runs.

| Workload | True stock | [#39998](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39998) parent | [#5598](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/5598) candidate | Candidate vs stock | Candidate vs parent |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 8K/1K c4 | 303.68 | 300.41 | 298.84 | −1.6% | −0.5% |
| 8K/1K c16 | 844.34 | 835.33 | 850.12 | +0.7% | +1.8% |
| 60K/600 c4 | 129.93 | 97.75 | 142.43 | +9.6% | +45.7% |
| 60K/600 c16 | 179.65 | 123.75 | 203.50 | +13.3% | +64.5% |
| 128K/1K c4 | 84.25 | 53.98 | 99.67 | +18.3% | +84.6% |
| 128K/1K c16 | 102.21 | 60.41 | 125.10 | +22.4% | +107.1% |

Variance-adjusted output-throughput geometric-mean deltas:

- [SGLang PR #39998](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39998) parent versus true stock: −24.04%.
- [AITER PR #5598](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/5598) candidate versus true stock: +10.10%.
- [AITER PR #5598](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/5598) candidate versus its exact parent: +44.95%.

The context trend is the important result. The candidate is approximately flat at 8K and improves progressively at 60K and 128K. This is consistent with the direct kernel measurements and demonstrates why the head-size-256 long-prefill config is needed.

## Corrected full-stack validation

A separate corrected page-size-1 stack added [SGLang PR #40410](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40410) and kept Triton `7cb7b059`. Full correctness validation produced:

- GPQA: 48.48% over 198 samples, matching the BF16-Q parent.
- NIAH: 100% at both 64K and 128K over 1,000 total samples.
- MMMU: 59.11% over 900 samples, within the planned two-point tolerance.

The corrected TP1+TP2 40-row text and multimodal sweep completed every expected request. Absolute output-throughput geomeans were:

- Text: 603.49 tok/s.
- Multimodal: 427.99 tok/s.
- Overall: 525.98 tok/s.

These absolute numbers are not a stock-versus-candidate isolation; the crossover table above is the direct PR comparison.

## Complementary Gluon result

On the same corrected Triton `7cb7b059` stack, [AITER PR #4614](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/4614) at `f54d368` plus runtime-stride [commit `89f96298`](https://github.com/vorapolsiloai/aiter/commit/89f9629872726be8c93fcc896d53577c83705dbc) measured 622.82 tok/s on text, 415.83 tok/s on multimodal, and 529.89 tok/s overall.

The implementations are complementary: adjusted Gluon is stronger on text, while [AITER PR #5598](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/5598) remains stronger on important multimodal shapes. Because this PR changes only the Triton config, it remains useful as the fallback even if the Gluon implementation merges.

## Triton compiler sensitivity

An older [AITER PR #5598](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/5598) image used `triton==3.8.0+git4cff872c.rocm10.0.0` and did not contain [SGLang PR #40410](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40410). Its overall 40-row output-throughput geomean was 540.15 tok/s versus 525.98 tok/s for the corrected Triton `7cb7b059` stack, a −2.6% stack-level difference.

This is not a clean compiler-only A/B because [SGLang PR #40410](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40410) also changed. A `4cff872c` run with the page-table fix is needed to isolate the compiler contribution. The older result is not a correctness-valid deployment result because it lacks the page-size-1 fix.

## Interpretation

[AITER PR #5598](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/5598) fixes a severe long-context configuration gap in the FP8-Q parent path:

- 3.12–6.62× faster direct long-prefill kernels.
- +44.95% end-to-end output-throughput geomean versus its exact [SGLang PR #39998](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39998) parent.
- +10.10% end-to-end output-throughput geomean versus true stock.
- Near-neutral behavior at 8K.

It is a low-risk, config-only improvement and remains valuable as the Triton implementation and fallback independently of the Gluon work.

## Test plan

- [x] Validate exact route selection for true stock, parent, and candidate.
- [x] Validate the current `BLOCK_M=128`, tile-64, skip-enabled config.
- [x] Run direct kernel correctness and timing gates on Qwen3.8 production geometry.
- [x] Run the six-row stock/parent/candidate crossover on HIP 4 and HIP 6.
- [x] Verify all 48 child serving runs complete.
- [x] Run short-answer, 60K needle, and sampled GPQA smoke gates in every crossover arm.
- [x] Run corrected full GPQA, NIAH-64K/128K, and MMMU gates.
- [x] Run corrected TP1 and TP2 40-row text and multimodal sweeps.
- [ ] Run the complete AITER unified-attention test matrix on gfx950.

title: [FlyDSL] Allocate split-K scratch buffers from a private MemPool
body:
## Problem

FlyDSL's split-K preshuffle GEMM reduces through a workspace guarded by an
atomic semaphore. Both are cached and reused across launches, keyed on
`(device, stream)` and allocated lazily on the first miss for that key:

```python
@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=128)
def _get_preshuffle_split_buffers(device, stream):
    workspace = torch.empty(...)
    semaphore = torch.zeros(...)
```

A CUDA graph capture always runs on a freshly created stream, so that key is
always new and the first capturing GEMM always misses — allocating inside the
capture region, where memory is served from the graph's private mempool and can
land on the address of an intermediate the same capture already freed. Keying on
the stream is also why the cache cannot be pre-warmed: the capture stream does
not exist until the capture begins.

**The failure surface is the semaphore, not the workspace.** Three things have
to line up:

1. the buffers are allocated inside a capture and inherit a freed
   intermediate's address;
2. some graph sharing that pool is replayed and writes those bytes — the
   allocation alone is harmless, because during capture the producing kernel is
   only recorded, never run;
3. the GEMM graph reading them is an lru **hit**. Only the graph that missed
   recorded `torch.zeros`' memset, so only that one re-zeroes the semaphore on
   every replay. Every later graph shares the buffer with no memset of its own.

`splitk_reduce_epilogue` counts relatively: each CTA does `atomic_add(sem, +1)`,
the one that sees `arrival == split_k - 1` reduces, and it restores with
`atomic_add(sem, -split_k)` rather than storing 0. A dirty slot therefore never
matches, **the reduction never runs**, and that tile's output keeps whatever it
held. The workspace being clobbered is harmless by comparison — every launch
rewrites the planes it is about to reduce.

## Reproduction

Pure torch, no aiter, no model — the buffer is an lru cache keyed like aiter's:

```python
@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=128)
def get_scratch(device, stream):
    return torch.zeros(N, device=device)

get_scratch(dev, torch.cuda.current_stream(dev))        # eager warmup: another key

with torch.cuda.graph(decoy, pool=pool, stream=side):
    t = src * 2.0; t_ptr = t.data_ptr(); t.sum(); del t  # freed; its kernel stays

with torch.cuda.graph(g1, pool=pool, stream=side):
    out1.copy_(src + get_scratch(dev, side))             # MISS: allocates, records memset
with torch.cuda.graph(g2, pool=pool, stream=side):
    out2.copy_(src + get_scratch(dev, side))             # HIT: same buffer, no memset

assert get_scratch(dev, side).data_ptr() == t_ptr
decoy.replay(); g1.replay()      # out1 = 3.0  -- g1's own memset reruns
decoy.replay(); g2.replay()      # out2 = 9.0  -- nothing cleans it
```

```
plain    cache 2 miss/1 hit  aliased=True   g1=3.0  g2=9.0  <- WRONG
MemPool  cache 2 miss/1 hit  aliased=False  g1=3.0  g2=3.0
```

`9.0 = 3.0 + 6.0`, the decoy's own intermediate. The same three-graph shape
driving the real kernel (`M=1 N=2048 K=2048 split_k=4`) gives 64/2048 wrong
outputs with `max_err=778.5` — one dirty semaphore slot x `tile_n=64` columns —
and 0/2048 with this branch.

## Why it needs a specific snapshot to show up

Reaching the defect needs a capture on a stream the cache has never seen:

| Condition | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| The FULL-graph capture runs on a stream no warmup ran on, so the cache always misses inside the capture | vLLM's V2 model runner called `torch.cuda.graph(graph, self.pool)` with no `stream=`, which puts the capture on torch's process-wide singleton `default_capture_stream` — a different stream from the one `graph_capture()` runs warmup on. Fixed upstream by vllm-project/vllm#53818; older snapshots still have it. PIECEWISE capture was never affected: it captures on the current stream. |
| The split-K scratch is allocated lazily on that first miss | this PR |

vLLM captures every batch size into one shared `graph_pool` and replays them in
turn during decode, so conditions 2 and 3 above are met by construction once the
first one is.

## Fix

Take the buffers from a per-device `torch.cuda.MemPool`, which is not part of
the graph private pool's reuse chain, so the address cannot be inherited from a
freed intermediate:

```python
with persistent_alloc(device):
    workspace = torch.empty(...)
    semaphore = torch.zeros(...)
```

Cache keys, kernels, the split-K protocol, tuned configs and the steady-state
path are unchanged. The pool is entered only on a cache miss — once per
`(device, stream)` — so the hot path is bit-identical.

The same lazy-allocation pattern guards five sibling scratch caches, which take
the same helper: the a16w16 split-K semaphore/signal buffers (gfx950 and its
gfx1250 twin), the ASM a16w16 counter, the a8w8 zero-bias buffer, and topk's MoE
workspace. `mla_reduce`'s `_get_splitk_scratch` is deliberately left alone — its
key carries no stream, so a first miss inside a capture needs a shape
combination no eager launch has used; its docstring now says so instead of
claiming to be capture-safe.

The a8w8 zero-bias buffer is the one with no protocol behind it: the kernel only
reads it, so nothing hands it back at zero and a clobbered one silently adds the
intermediate's values as bias on every replay. Unfixed, an lru-hit graph reads
`6.0` there; fixed, `0.0`.

### Replaces the ASM a16w16 mechanism from #4916

That PR fixed this hazard on the ASM path by giving every recorded launch its
own ring slot and recording a `zero_` per launch, so a replay starts from zero
whatever the counter held. Measured here, that node costs **2.2–2.4 us per
launch** — independent of the counter's size, so it is the node itself, not the
bytes — plus a fixed 16 MiB per device allocated whether or not the process ever
captures a graph. On a 10.9 us decode GEMM that is +20%.

Both kernels hand the counter back at zero on their own (verified: 0/1024 and
0/256 nonzero after six launches), so nothing has to re-zero it between
launches. What neither survives is another graph in the same pool owning the
counter's address — which is what this PR removes instead of tolerating.

`check_graph` dirtied the counter with `fill_(2)` from outside to stand in for
that state. The workspace belongs to the GEMM and nothing outside it writes
there, so the decoy graph it now uses produces the dirt the way a capture
actually does. #4916's own repro command passes:

```
$ python3 op_tests/test_gemm_a16w16.py --graph -mnk 64,256,5120 32,512,8192 -d bf16 -o fp32
graph dim: (64, 256, 5120)  replay vs eager: [checkAllclose atol=0.01 rtol=0.01 passed~]
graph dim: (32, 512, 8192)  replay vs eager: [checkAllclose atol=0.01 rtol=0.01 passed~]
all graph capture/replay checks passed
```

@JohnQinAMD — flagging this for your review since it reworks your fix.

**torch floor.** `use_mem_pool` can only win inside a capture on torch 2.10 or
newer: older allocators scan `captures_underway` in registration order, so the
graph pool registered at capture begin always wins, while 2.10 scans it in LIFO
order (`c10/cuda/CUDACachingAllocator.cpp::get_pool`). On an older torch the
helper warns once per device when it is entered during a capture, and the
capture test is skipped rather than failed. Thanks to @valarLip for measuring
what that looks like on 2.9.1.

## Verification (gfx950, torch 2.10.0+rocm7.2.4)

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Three-graph repro driving the real GEMM | unfixed: g2 64/2048 wrong, `max_err=778.5`. This branch: 0/2048. |
| Pure-torch repro above | unfixed: `g2=9.0`. This branch: `g2=3.0`. |
| `op_tests/test_graph_alloc.py` | 3 passed |
| Every cached accessor's `segment_pool_id` is the private pool's | 6/6; dropping any one site's wrapper fails the test by name |
| #4916's repro command (`test_gemm_a16w16.py --graph`) | passes |
| Cost of a recorded per-launch memset node | 2.2–2.4 us, same for a 1 KiB and a 4 KiB counter |
| Pool is one per device under 16 concurrent first callers | 1 pool |
| Pool routing when the buffer's device is not the current device | without `device=`: 0 bytes routed. With `device=`: routed. |
| 4 graphs sharing one pool, split-K a8w8 GEMM whose buffer first misses inside capture, 40 cross-replays | rel_err 0.0013–0.0016, no NaN/inf, identical to the eager result |

`op_tests/test_graph_alloc.py` is a plain pytest regression on allocator /
CUDA-graph pointer semantics -- there is no kernel, no shape sweep and nothing
to time, so it does not follow the op-test benchmark template.

title: [CK] fix(moe): handle 64-aligned A16W16 shards in CK dispatch
body:
## Motivation

We found a startup failure while running Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-PTPC-FP8 with native MTP in ATOM standalone on MI308X, using TP=2 and EP=1. The target model is FP8, but the checkpoint's MTP draft MoE uses BF16 weights. Tensor parallelism reduces its intermediate dimension to 320.

Without a tuned configuration, AITER selected a CK stage1 kernel with `NPerBlock=128` for this intermediate dimension. CK's non-padded MoE GEMM requires `N % NPerBlock == 0`; `320 % 128 != 0`, so initialization failed with:

```text
RuntimeError: wrong! device_gemm with the specified compilation parameters does not support this GEMM problem
```

This PR fixes the default kernel selection rather than requiring a model-specific CSV workaround or changing the draft model's precision.

## Technical Details

- Update `A16W16_gemm1_heuristic_dispatch` in `csrc/ck_gemm_moe_2stages_codegen/gen_instances.py`.
- Preserve the existing small-dimension rule and also select the existing N64/V1 specialization when `inter_dim % 128 == 64` (for example, 320 or 448).
- Keep the selected M tile unchanged, including BM64/BM128/BM256. BM32 already uses N64 and is unchanged.
- Preserve the previous choices for 128-aligned dimensions. Dimensions not divisible by 64 are not newly supported by this change; CK's existing argument validation still applies.
- Do not change kernel arithmetic, tensor layouts, explicit tuned-kernel lookup, or gfx950-specific dispatch.
- No stage2 change is needed for the tested shapes: its BF16/FP16 K64 alignment is satisfied by intermediate dimensions 320 and 448. Full two-stage output tests cover this interaction.

## Test Plan

Add `op_tests/test_moe_a16w16_default_dispatch.py`:

1. Bypass tuned CSV selection using `AITER_BYPASS_TUNE_CONFIG=1` and clear cached dispatch metadata before/after each case.
2. Cover BF16 and FP16, M tiles 32/64/128/256, and intermediate dimensions 192/256/320/384/448. The 320/448 cases cover the regression; the other dimensions cover existing paths.
3. Exercise the production BF16 MoE shape without a block-size override:
   - tokens: 4, 512, 8192
   - model dimension: 2560
   - intermediate dimension per TP rank: 320
   - experts: 512; top-k: 10
   - W1: `[512, 640, 2560]`; W2: `[512, 2560, 320]`
4. Compare **all output elements**, not sampled rows, with an independent PyTorch reference using FP32 linear operations/accumulation and BF16 or FP16 intermediate activation rounding. Check finite output and `rtol=0.02, atol=0.002`.
5. Skip GPU tests outside gfx942, the platform validated here.

Run from the AITER repository on gfx942, with a fresh JIT directory so old shared libraries cannot hide the code-generation change:

```bash
dispatch_test_cache=$(mktemp -d /tmp/aiter-moe-dispatch.XXXXXX)
HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 MAX_JOBS=16 \
  AITER_JIT_DIR="$dispatch_test_cache" \
  python3 -m pytest -q op_tests/test_moe_a16w16_default_dispatch.py
```

## Test Result

- Environment: MI308X/gfx942, ROCm 7.2.4, Python 3.12, PyTorch 2.10.0+ROCm.
- Before the fix: reproduced the CK unsupported-GEMM failure for BM128/intermediate=320; the production 512-token case also failed with the old compiled kernel.
- After the fix: the initial BF16-only suite passed all 23 cases using a newly compiled extension, including the full 8192-token production-shape comparison.
- Extended BF16/FP16 suite: **43 passed in 113.54 seconds**. BF16 used the freshly rebuilt extension from the initial run; FP16 compiled its own extension in the same isolated JIT directory. No model-specific CSV workaround was used.
- No before/after performance claim is made. Previously valid shape dispatches retain their existing specializations; the affected default path previously failed instead of producing a benchmarkable result. Model-level performance has not been re-measured with this source fix.

## Submission Checklist

- [ ] Look over the contributing guidelines at https://github.com/ROCm/ROCm/blob/develop/CONTRIBUTING.md#pull-requests.
