title: [Triton/Gluon] [Perf] Cut per-iteration address math and cndmask in the non-preshuffle MQA logits decode kernel
body:
## Summary

Two instruction-level optimizations to the non-preshuffle (`Preshuffle=False`) Gluon decode kernel. Both are unconditional; the shape gate on the first one is a correctness condition, not a toggle.

Stacked on #5614 so the diff shows only these two commits; the base will retarget to `main` when that merges. Nothing here changes the preshuffle path, the varctx kernel, or the Triton JIT kernels.

**1. Hoist the KV block index and in-block offset out of the loop.** The kernel recomputed `token // KVBlockSize` and `token % KVBlockSize` over a `ChunkK`-wide vector every iteration. `KVBlockSize` is a `constexpr` power of two, so that should be one shift and one AND per register, but it expanded to 64 instructions because `context_idx` is loop-variant and the compiler cannot fold through it. `context_idx` advances by `ChunkK` and the gate requires `ChunkK % KVBlockSize == 0`, so the modulo is loop-invariant and the quotient grows by a constant. Both now come from the first tile and the loop only adds. The identity does not require `context_idx` to be `KVBlockSize`-aligned — `residual_context` can be anything — and `KVBlockSize > ChunkK` leaves the quotient without a constant stride, so those shapes keep the general form.

**2. Mask the logits after the head reduce, not before.** The kernel wrote `-inf` into the whole `(ChunkQ, ChunkK)` accumulator before reducing over heads, costing one `v_cndmask` per accumulator register: 32 in the loop and 32 more in the epilogue. Masking the reduced logits needs four and is the same value, since summing `ChunkQ` copies of `-inf` is `-inf` and unmasked columns are untouched. **The preshuffle kernel already masks after its reduce at all four of its store sites**; only the plain path did it the expensive way. Removing the `-inf` write also unblocks packed FP32 in the epilogue.

## ISA

`ChunkQ=32, ChunkK=256, Preshuffle=False, KVBlockSize=64, WavePerEU=2`:

| | in-loop integer address ops | `v_cndmask` | `v_mul_f32` | `v_pk_add_f32` | `v_pk_mul_f32` | `v_pk_fma_f32` | VGPR |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| #5614 head | 168 | 98 | 132 | 35 | 0 | 0 | 186 |
| + commit 1 | **76** | 98 | 132 | 35 | 0 | 0 | 188 |
| + commit 2 | **76** | **42** | **68** | **18** | **16** | **16** | 190 |

Commit 2 also removes the `s_nop 5` that sat after the first VALU read of the accumulator — an MFMA-to-VALU RAW hazard that no longer applies once the epilogue is restructured.

Neither commit improves register pressure. VGPR goes 186 to 190 and all three allocate 192, so occupancy stays at 2 waves/SIMD. The two loop-carried index vectors in commit 1 cost slightly more than the div/mod temporaries they replace.

## Testing

Environment: gfx950, 256 CU at 2.4 GHz, mclk 2000 MHz, ROCm 7.2.4, PyTorch `2.10.0+rocm7.2.4.git3d3aa833`, Triton 3.7.0. One physical GPU pinned, verified at 0% utilisation, 0% VRAM and no KFD process before the run; clocks not locked.

```bash
ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES=7 PYTHONPATH=. python -m pytest -q op_tests/test_pa_mqa_logits_offset.py
# -> 62 passed, unchanged from #5614
```

Performance, `N=131072`, `H=32`, `D=128`, `next_n=1`, `KVBlockSize=64`, `ChunkK=256`, `WavePerEU=2`, one process per point.

**Method.** Three worktrees — base, base+commit 1, base+both — run back to back inside each round, with the arm order rotated every round, eight rounds. The statistic is the **median of the per-round paired ratio**, not a ratio of per-arm medians: clocks are not locked on this box and the baseline drifts several percent over an eight-minute window, which only pairing cancels. `Preshuffle=True` is untouched by both commits, so base and head run the same kernel there and its paired ratio is the noise floor; it was measured separately with the same round structure.

Brackets are the min and max of the eight per-round ratios.

| Batch | commit 1 | commit 2 | both | control (noise floor) |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 16 | −0.58% [−1.63, −0.23] | **−2.83%** [−4.03, −1.11] | **−3.57%** [−4.85, −2.28] | +0.09% [−0.43, +0.84] |
| 64 | −0.40% [−15.64, +0.04] | **−1.02%** [−1.39, −0.69] | **−1.36%** [−16.22, −1.10] | +0.01% [−0.49, +0.15] |
| 128 | −0.12% [−0.36, +0.18] | **−0.69%** [−0.85, −0.48] | **−0.80%** [−0.92, −0.65] | +0.06% [−0.13, +0.11] |

Absolute medians, us:

| Batch | base | + commit 1 | + both | `Preshuffle=True` |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 16 | 47.92 | 47.60 | **46.16** | 43.94 |
| 64 | 234.29 | 233.53 | **231.05** | 220.56 |
| 128 | 458.97 | 458.50 | **455.36** | 444.10 |

**Commit 2 carries almost all of the gain.** Commit 1 only just clears the noise floor at batch 16 and sits inside it at batch 128; it is worth keeping because it costs nothing and the instruction count genuinely drops, not because it is a measurable speedup on its own.

**Batch 1 does not resolve and no claim is made for it.** Sixteen paired rounds at `num_iters=501`: plain moves −0.97% with an IQR of [−3.08%, +0.28%], but the unchanged preshuffle control moves +0.61% with an IQR of [−0.75%, +9.18%]. The kernel is 7 us there and launch overhead dominates.

### Shape coverage

`HoistKvAddr` is `KVBlockSize > 1 and ChunkK % KVBlockSize == 0`, so commit 1 has a gated-off path. Both sides were measured at the same production scale, three paired rounds:

| KVBlockSize | ChunkK | `HoistKvAddr` | b=16 | b=128 |
| ---: | ---: | :---: | ---: | ---: |
| 16 | 256 | on | −2.88% | −0.66% |
| 64 | 256 | on | −3.57% | −0.80% |
| 128 | 256 | on | −3.95% | −0.89% |
| 256 | 256 | on | −5.02% | −1.38% |
| 128 | 64 | **off** | −2.21% | −1.38% |
| 256 | 128 | **off** | −0.58% | −0.35% |
| 1 | 256 | **off** | −2.96% | — |

No shape regresses. The gated-off shapes still gain, because commit 2 is unconditional and only commit 1 is gated. `KVBlockSize=1` takes the branch where `logical_kv_idx_next` is never defined and `KVBlockSize > ChunkK` takes the branch where it is defined but the hoist is off, so all three paths commit 1 introduces are exercised. `op_tests/test_pa_mqa_logits_offset.py` already parametrises `block_size ∈ {1, 16, 64, 128} × chunk_k ∈ {64, 256}`, which covers the same gate split for correctness; this is the production-scale confirmation.

Across every campaign — three-arm 72, control 48, batch 1 64, shape sweep 66, plus 180 from an earlier loosely-paired run — all 430 processes were 0-mismatched against the fp32 reference with no NaN or Inf.

## Re-measured after the rebase

The numbers above replace an earlier set taken on `8add88cf7`, before #5614 picked up the SplitKV grid change in `f2d4101` and `6e5e7f9`. That change moved the baseline a long way — batch 16 from 58.41 to 47.92 us (−18.0%), batch 64 from 274.84 to 234.29 (−14.8%), batch 128 from 470.86 to 458.97 (−2.5%) — so the old absolutes are not comparable and everything was re-run on the new base.

The relative gains reproduce: −3.15% / −1.47% / −0.41% before, −3.57% / −1.36% / −0.80% now. Batch 128 was previously at the edge of what the measurement could resolve; tight pairing narrows the noise floor there to ±0.13% and makes it a readable result. That is a change in method, not in the code.

The ISA counts and the numerics analysis are unchanged, because the kernel is byte-identical to what was measured before — the only edit since was removing the two environment-variable toggles.

## Numerics

Commit 1 is **bit-identical**: 0 of 2097152 logits differ at batch 16.

Commit 2 is not, because folding a multiply and an add into `v_pk_fma_f32` skips the rounding of the intermediate product. 410363 of 2097152 logits move, by at most `3.05e-05` on a `±273` range. Against an fp64 reference the two versions are equally far from the truth:

| | max abs err | mean abs err | rms err |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| before | 3.839734e-03 | 4.615302e-04 | 6.016148e-04 |
| after | 3.839734e-03 | 4.615247e-04 | 6.016279e-04 |

The error floor is the fp8 quantisation of `q` and `k`, not the fp32 epilogue, and the change between the two versions is 15x below it.

## Note for AOT users

The plain kernel's instruction stream changes, so cached `.hsaco` artifacts for `Preshuffle=False` have to be regenerated from this branch. This is in addition to the regeneration #5614 already requires for its `i32` to `i64` stride change. #5614's own SplitKV grid change does not require it — `SplitKV` is a runtime `i32` argument, not a `constexpr`.

## Approaches measured and rejected

Recorded so they are not retried. Each was implemented, verified bit-correct, and measured on an idle gfx950.

| Approach | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Hand-driven LDS staging with gfx950's `ds_read_b64_tr_b8` transpose read, replacing `convert_layout(k.T)` | 38–54% slower. The hardware transpose read is emitted (32 of them for 20 `ds_read_b128`), but all LDS ops together are only 6.1% of stalls while the `s_barrier` and `s_waitcnt` the round trip forces are 38%. Same barrier count, same LDS bytes, and the regression holds at `ChunkK=128` where both variants fit two workgroups in 64 KB, so it is neither synchronisation nor occupancy — it is 53 LDS instructions against 37. Branch `maki/mqa-plain-tr-20260920`. |
| Pairing the two adjacent in-loop logits stores into one burst | 13% slower, with VGPR, spills, LDS and occupancy all identical before and after. Moving the store across the `_amd_iglp_sched_group_barrier` groups displaces the hand-written software pipeline. Branch `maki/mqa-batched-store-20260918`. |
| `ChunkK=128`, which does reach 4 waves/SIMD at 114 VGPR | 491.5 us against 471.1 for `ChunkK=256`. |
| Raising occupancy through `WavePerEU` | `WavePerEU=4` reaches 4 waves/SIMD but spills 128 B: 670.9 us against 470.2 at batch 128. `WavePerEU=8` is 1825.9 us. |
| Hand-packing the epilogue `v_mul_f32` into `v_pk_mul_f32` | Superseded — commit 2 gets it from the compiler for free. The lines involved are 0.69% and 1.15% of stalls, so a hand-written version was never worth it either. |

## Remaining headroom, for context

The trace says what is left, and neither item is instruction count. `s_barrier` from the LDS transpose round trip is 18.4% of stalls, and memory is 48.4%. On the memory side the fp32 logits write is 3% of the bytes but 11 percentage points of achievable bandwidth: an isolated reproduction of this kernel's exact access pattern reaches 70.2% of spec with the write removed and 59.0% with it, while the kernel itself measures 62.9%, i.e. already slightly ahead of a no-compute reproduction of its own memory pattern. Store granularity is not the lever — at matched byte counts, bursting four 512 B stores together is 7.3 points worse than one per stage.

After these two commits the plain path still trails preshuffle by 5.1% / 4.8% / 2.5% at batch 16 / 64 / 128, down from 9.1% / 6.2% / 3.3%. The rest is structural: the LDS round trip, and VGPR 190 against 92 with occupancy 2 against 5.

title: [Triton/Gluon] Unified attention: opt-in prefill configs for head sizes 129+
body:
## Motivation

This PR covers a Triton regression raised in https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/issues/4137: Unified attention prefill regressed on gfx950 for head sizes 129 and above. On the Qwen3.5-397B debug shape the kernel went from about 4ms on Triton 3.6 to 16ms on 3.7 and 12ms on 3.8. This is due to three separate problems:

**Register pressure.** At `BLOCK_M=128` a head size in 129-255 pads to a 256-element accumulator, and the kernel needs about 470 VGPRs (it uses no LDS at all). `waves_per_eu=2` caps the budget at 256, so the excess spills to scratch inside the KV loop.

**An LLVM scheduler regression in Triton >= 3.7.** The same config that fit on 3.6 does not on 3.7+, which is what turned this from latent to visible. TTIR and TTGIR are byte-identical across the three versions and the LLVM IR instruction mix is the same; only the scratch size differs, so it is the AMDGPU machine scheduler producing longer live ranges, not anything in Triton's own passes.

**Config shadowing.** Because the lookup gives the leftmost axis priority, `D_GEQ_256` outranks `Q_GEQ_256`, so head sizes 256+ in prefill were picking a `BLOCK_M=16` entry meant for decode. That is why `d=256` was slower than `d=192` despite doing less work per program.

The goal is to fix all three without changing the default behavior so when a fix eventually lands in Triton, this change does not end up regressing the performance. The tuned configs trade occupancy for registers against one measured shape family, so they are exposed as an opt-in rather than made the default.

## Technical Details

Two files change: the gfx950 `DEFAULT.json` and `unified_attention_utils.py`.

**An opt-in config section.** A new `attn_2d.OPT_IN` section holds the retuned prefill entries and is merged into the lookup only when `AITER_TRITON_UA_FAST_PATH=1`. With the variable unset nothing changes: the section is never consulted, and all five pre-existing sections of `DEFAULT.json` are byte-identical to before. The core fix in these entries is `waves_per_eu=1`, which lifts the VGPR budget from 256 to 512 and eliminates the spill. It is scoped to head sizes 129+ (`D_GEQ_129` / `D_GEQ_256` keys) because sizes below that never spilled, and halving their occupancy target only costs them speed.

**The AMD backend workaround.** On top of the register fix, the opt-in entries can pass `amdgpu-sched-strategy=iterative-minreg` through Triton's `llvm_fn_attrs` option. This overrides the AMDGPU machine scheduler with a register-minimising strategy, recovering a further ~25% on large caches. It is not unconditionally good, so it sits in a `LARGE_KV` sub-block behind three guards:

- **Cache size.** Under `2**31` elements the backend indexes the cache with 32-bit buffer ops instead of 64-bit global loads. Against that different code the attribute costs about 3x rather than saving 25%. The guard counts elements, so if what the backend really tests is bytes, a borderline cache is declined rather than wrongly taken.
- **Dtype.** The overrides pay off for fp8 and cost bf16 about sixfold, so only the `DT_fp8_fp8` keys carry them.
- **Triton support.** `llvm_fn_attrs` is read off the backend's own options rather than inferred from a version number, and the block is skipped with a warning where the option does not exist.

## Test Plan

A standalone harness replays the Qwen3.5-397B debug shape and swaps configs through the lookup:

- **Coverage sweep** across head sizes 64-512, both prefill and decode, small (128-block) and large (4795-block) KV caches, fp8 and bf16, with the flag both unset and set. Each run reports the matched config entry, p50 latency, and the compiled kernel's scratch (register spill) bytes.
- **Guard tests** that exercise each of the three `LARGE_KV` gates: large cache with the option supported (applies), small cache (size guard declines), and a backend without `llvm_fn_attrs` (support guard declines). Also asserts the `LARGE_KV` sub-block never leaks into the launched config.
- **Numerics check** comparing the opt-in base and the large-KV overrides for bitwise-identical output, since the overrides only move scheduling and occupancy.
- **Regression guard on the default** by diffing every pre-existing section of `DEFAULT.json` against `HEAD` to confirm the flag-off path is untouched.

## Test Result

All pre-existing `DEFAULT.json` sections are byte-identical to `HEAD`; the only addition is `attn_2d.OPT_IN`. The guard tests pass (overrides apply only on a large fp8 cache with a supporting Triton, and never leak), and the opt-in base and large-KV overrides are bitwise identical.

gfx950, fp8, prefill. Small cache is 128 blocks, large is 4795. Each cell is p50 latency in ms (±0.1-0.2 ms run to run), with kernel scratch (register spill) in bytes in parentheses; "unchanged" means the opt-in section holds no entry for that head size, so the flag has no effect.

| head size | off, small cache (ms) | off, large cache (ms) | on, small cache (ms) | on, large cache (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 64, 128 | 2.5-2.9 | 2.5-3.1 | unchanged | unchanged |
| 160, 192, 224 | 5.2-5.3 (132 B) | 12.1-12.2 (288 B) | 5.3 (0 B) | 4.6 (20 B) |
| 256 | 10.0 | 12.5 | 5.2 (0 B) | 4.7 (20 B) |
| 512 | 24.8 | 28.9 | unchanged | unchanged |

bf16, same shape, large cache is 2400 blocks. bf16 stays on the opt-in base config, since the large-KV overrides do not apply to it:

| head size | off, small cache (ms) | off, large cache (ms) | on, small cache (ms) | on, large cache (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 192 | 11.7 (236 B) | 31.1 (920 B) | 7.1 (0 B) | 8.7 (0 B) |
| 256 | 25.0 | 34.8 | 7.2 (0 B) | 8.7 (0 B) |

Spill drops from up to 920 B to at most 20 B on every affected head size (0 B except on the fp8 large cache, where the minreg override leaves 20 B). The `d=256` bf16 row is the shadowing fix on its own; the `d=192` row is the register fix, worth 3.6x on the large cache. Decode is untouched under both settings, as are head sizes 64, 128 and 512.

## Notes and follow-ups

- The opt-in section has four entries where two would do. `D_GEQ_256` shadows `D_GEQ_129.Q_GEQ_256`, so the config has to be repeated at each `D` bound, and again split by dtype because only fp8 takes the `LARGE_KV` block.
- These configs were tuned against one shape family. `waves_per_eu=1` trades occupancy for registers, which is why this is opt-in rather than the default.

## Submission Checklist

title: [Triton/Gluon] [HIP] [JIT] Add Windows support
body:
## Motivation

aiter has no Windows support: `__init__.py` force-enables `AITER_TRITON_ONLY` on `win32`, and the JIT layer assumes Linux-only tooling (`rocminfo`, `libamdhip64.so`, `/dev/null`, `rm -rf`, ELF linker flags). This wires the JIT and Python layers up to the Windows ROCm stack so CK- and HIP-based ops compile and run there.

## Technical Details

Toolchain discovery - ROCm tools ship as `.exe`/`.bat` wrappers on Windows, so executable lookup goes through a suffix-aware `_find_executable`, and `_find_rocm_home` falls back to `HIP_PATH`. `get_cxx_compiler` returns hipcc, the only compiler on Windows that can build both the .cpp and .hip sources.

GPU info - `chip_info` uses `hipinfo` in place of `rocminfo`, with a parser per output format, and loads the version-suffixed `amdhip64*.dll`. `--offload-arch=native` shells out to offload-arch, which cannot detect the GPU on Windows, so `native` resolves via `_detect_native()` instead.

Build system - ELF/GNU-ld-only flags (`-fPIC`, `-mcmodel=large`, `--gc-sections`, `-fvisibility=*`, `_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI`) are excluded on Windows; `_ninja_path` escapes drive-letter colons, which ninja otherwise reads as rule separators; PE links against `pythonXYZ.lib`; `-D_USE_MATH_DEFINES` is added since the UCRT only declares `M_SQRT2` & friends under it. `compile_lib` drives hipcc with ninja instead of make.

Stale-lock fix - `FileBaton._pid_alive` no longer probes with `os.kill(pid, 0)` on Windows: CPython maps that onto `TerminateProcess`, so the liveness check would kill the very builder it was checking on.

Several shell idioms are also replaced with portable equivalents that are more robust on Linux too: `os.system("rm -rf")`, `os.popen("cat /proc/sys/kernel/numa_balancing")`, `echo ... | hipcc -`, and the shelled-out `hipcc` and `hipconfig` calls in `csrc/cpp_itfs/utils.py`.

`check_LLVM_MAIN_REVISION` needed more than the shell change. Its probe relies on CTAD, and at hipcc's default standard on Windows it failed on a template-argument error rather than on the `__host__ __device__` rule it is meant to measure, so the function returned the same value whatever the toolchain did. The probe is now pinned to `-std=c++20`, the standard the modules are built with. On Linux clang already defaults to `gnu++17`, so the answer there is unchanged.

`arch_info.get_arch()` now probes Triton on first call instead of at import. Since #5590 the flash-attention Triton backend imports `tuned_config_utils`, which imports `arch_info`, so importing it on a host with no GPU driver raised and then fell through to the `jax` fallback. This is what fails the Windows Smoke Test on `main`.

## Test Plan

Windows 11, RDNA4, TheRock ROCm 7, Python 3.12. Each op runs in its own subprocess against a torch reference, both from the repo and from a `pip install .`'d wheel.

## Test Result

| Op | Result |
|---|---|
| `rms_norm` | OK |
| `rmsnorm2d_fwd` | OK |
| `silu_and_mul` | OK |
| `topk_softmax` | OK |
| `rotary_embedding_fwd` | OK |

`import aiter` builds and loads the full CK/HIP path - previously Windows exited before any op was loaded.

Not covered: ops whose modules run a CK-tile blob generator (layernorm2d, the CK GEMMs, flash-attn). Those generators emit hundreds of specializations and dominate build time on Linux equally, so this is not a Windows-specific gap, but that path is untested here.

## Submission Checklist

- [x] Look over the contributing guidelines at https://github.com/ROCm/ROCm/blob/develop/CONTRIBUTING.md#pull-requests.

title: [Triton/Gluon] [Kimi-K3] Optimize speculative KDA decode on gfx950
body:
## Summary

Optimize the Triton fused KDA decode path used by Kimi K3 speculative decoding
on gfx950.

This PR:

- fixes an in-place convolution-state race
- adds speculative-sequence support to fused KDA decode
- adds a parallel-V spec-7 kernel for the K3 gfx950 shape
- separates recurrent processing from output/state finalization
- reduces memory stalls through prefetching, load hoisting, and pipelining
- adds correctness and state-determinism coverage

The implementation is self-contained and preserves a generic fused fallback for
shapes that do not match the specialized spec-7 dispatch.

## Conv-state race fix

Some launch layouts use more threads than convolution channels, causing multiple
lanes or waves to access the same convolution-state vectors.

The previous kernel shifted each Q/K/V cache in place immediately after
computing that component. Without cross-wave synchronization, one wave could
overwrite convolution history while another wave was still reading the original
taps, producing nondeterministic output and corrupted convolution state.

The updated kernel:

1. loads and computes all Q/K/V convolution values
2. executes a workgroup barrier
3. shifts and stores the Q/K/V convolution state

This enforces load → barrier → store ordering without allocating an additional
state buffer.

The determinism test now compares output, convolution state, and SSM state
across repeated launches, ensuring that state-only races are also detected.

## Speculative decode support

The fused decode interface now accepts:

- per-sequence accepted-token counts
- two-dimensional speculative SSM-state indices
- separate convolution-cache slot indices
- an optional preallocated output tensor

For speculative sequences, the kernel restores the recurrent and convolution
state from the accepted-token checkpoint. It then processes all draft
candidates and writes each resulting SSM state to its destination slot.

The generic fused path remains available for unsupported architectures and
shapes.

## Parallel spec-7 kernel

For the K3 gfx950 shape:

- `H=2`
- `K=V=128`
- convolution width `W=4`
- seven speculative tokens plus one target token
- expanded convolution-state length of 10

the optimized path partitions the recurrent state across 16-element V tiles.

The first kernel:

- loads convolution history from the accepted checkpoint
- keeps the rolling history in registers
- processes all speculative candidates
- writes candidate SSM states directly
- writes unnormalized output tiles
- preserves the convolution carry needed for finalization

A second kernel:

- commits the expanded convolution state once
- computes the gated RMSNorm across the full V dimension
- writes the final BF16 output

This avoids repeatedly committing convolution history inside the recurrent
candidate loop while reducing per-program recurrent-state pressure.

## Triton optimizations

The specialized path also:

- hoists invariant convolution weights and decay parameters
- prefetches gate and beta alongside Q/K/V loads
- pipelines token-dependent loads with `num_stages=2`
- adds safe PID, index, bound, and positive-stride assumptions
- applies `tl.multiple_of` and `tl.max_contiguous` to aligned offsets
- uses two warps with a 16-element V tile

ATT profiling showed that moving from one to two warps reduced per-wave VGPR
usage from 118 to 86. VMEM waits remained the dominant stall source, motivating
the invariant-load hoisting and gate/beta prefetch.

## Performance

All results use the median latency from three independent trials.

### Normal decode

Shape: `Hloc=12`, `D=128`, `W=4`, one token per sequence.

Baseline:

1. `causal_conv1d_update_split_qkv`
2. `fused_sigmoid_gating_delta_rule_update`
3. `rmsnorm_gated_bf16`

Optimized path: single generic fused Triton kernel.

Method: `triton.testing.do_bench`, 50 warmups and 200 repetitions per trial.

- B1: 108.0 → 28.0 µs, 3.86× (-74.07%)
- B2: 107.0 → 27.1 µs, 3.95× (-74.67%)
- B4: 106.2 → 27.1 µs, 3.92× (-74.48%)
- B8: 100.7 → 25.8 µs, 3.90× (-74.38%)
- B16: 97.9 → 29.7 µs, 3.30× (-69.66%)
- B32: 95.7 → 38.4 µs, 2.49× (-59.87%)
- B64: 99.3 → 60.7 µs, 1.64× (-38.87%)
- B128: 106.8 → 101.1 µs, 1.06× (-5.34%)
- B256: 190.2 → 188.4 µs, 1.01× (-0.95%)
- B512: 353.9 → 350.5 µs, 1.01× (-0.96%)

The generic fusion provides approximately 3.9× speedup at B1–B8 and remains
at parity or better through B512. B256 and B512 are effectively neutral within
run-to-run variation.

### Spec-7 decode

Shape: `H=2`, `K=V=128`, `W=4`, seven speculative tokens plus one target
token per sequence.

Baseline:

1. `causal_conv1d_update`
2. `fused_recurrent_kda`
3. `rms_norm_gated`

Optimized path:

1. parallel-V convolution and recurrent KDA kernel
2. convolution-state commit and gated-RMSNorm finalize kernel

Method: CUDA graph replay, 100 warmups and 500 repetitions per trial.

- B1: 33.88 → 27.36 µs, 1.24× (-19.25%)
- B2: 33.36 → 27.08 µs, 1.23× (-18.82%)
- B4: 33.44 → 29.00 µs, 1.15× (-13.28%)
- B8: 34.24 → 29.76 µs, 1.15× (-13.08%)
- B16: 35.92 → 31.04 µs, 1.16× (-13.59%)
- B32: 37.60 → 35.04 µs, 1.07× (-6.81%)
- B64: 46.08 → 41.12 µs, 1.12× (-10.76%)
- B128: 67.20 → 58.24 µs, 1.15× (-13.33%)
- B256: 106.44 → 99.64 µs, 1.07× (-6.39%)
- B512: 188.32 → 178.32 µs, 1.06× (-5.31%)

The optimized spec-7 path is faster in every trial across B1–B512, reducing
latency by 5.31% to 19.25%.

## Validation

- 24 targeted tests passed
- normal single-token and multi-token decode covered
- speculative accepted-token checkpoints covered
- output, convolution state, and SSM state verified

title: [HIP] [JIT] [Build] Add GLM-5.3-Flash IQ2R 2-bit MoE support
body:
## Summary

- add an IQ2R compiler and model-neutral overlay contract for GLM-5.3-Flash (glm5_next / Glm5NextForConditionalGeneration)
- convert the routed experts in layers 3-44 from the source block-FP8 checkpoint into AITER's native-basis IQ2R representation
- generalize the IQ2R MoE runtime for GLM's independent 4096 hidden / 2048 expert-intermediate widths, 288 experts, top-k 8 routing, and clamped SwiGLU parameters
- add resumable shard validation, Redline calibration-artifact loading, synthetic gfx950 correctness coverage, and checkpoint/overlay contract tests

## Dependency and provenance

Stacked on and requires ROCm/aiter#5678. Until that PR merges, GitHub's comparison against main also includes the dependency commits; the GLM-5.3-Flash work itself is the final commit in this branch.

The IQ2R format, calibration contract, and gfx950 execution design are adapted from Redline's O0 implementation. AITER remains self-contained at build and runtime.

## Model and scope

This PR targets **zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash**, not the plain GLM-5.3 model:

- architecture: Glm5NextForConditionalGeneration
- 45 transformer layers, with dense layers 0-2 and routed MoE layers 3-44
- hidden size 4096
- routed expert intermediate size 2048
- 288 routed experts, top-k 8
- source expert weights use block FP8 with 128x128 scales

The initial runtime is gfx950 TP1/EP1. Only routed expert weights are replaced. Attention, dense MLPs, shared experts, and the MTP checkpoint layer retain the source model's base quantization.

Production-quality compilation requires a valid Redline-format diagonal second-moment calibration artifact containing paired gate/up-input and activated down-input importance. Uniform importance is deliberately exposed only as a one-layer diagnostic mode and is stamped as not O0 quality.

## Validation

Run after rebasing onto AITER #5678:

    38 passed, 70 skipped across op_tests/test_iq2r_*.py
    14 passed, 1 skipped in focused compiler/checkpoint/overlay/workspace tests

title: [Triton/Gluon] [Kernel] Add fused SiLU-and-multiply backward
body:
## Summary

Add a fused Triton backward operation for `silu(gate) * up` with concatenated
`[gate, up]` input layout.

Closes #5541.

## Motivation

AITER already provides the SiLU-and-multiply forward operation, but training
currently builds its backward from multiple eager PyTorch operations. This PR
adds the matching fused backward while keeping the implementation in the
existing activation family.

## Changes

- Add `_silu_and_mul_backward_kernel` beside the existing SiLU-and-multiply
  forward kernel and reuse the shared `_sigmoid_exp2` device helper.
- Add `silu_and_mul_backward(grad_output, x, out=None)` to
  `aiter.ops.triton.activation`.
- Evaluate SiLU and both gradient products in FP32 before converting to the
  input dtype.
- Support FP16, BF16, and FP32, arbitrary leading dimensions, strided
  `grad_output`, optional preallocated output, empty rows, and non-current-GPU
  launches.
- Add a config-aware kernel `repr`, unit tests, a benchmark, and the measured
  gfx950 tuning configuration.
- Reuse a shared `select_leq_config` helper for upper-bound config tables and
  migrate the two existing local copies in `fused_clamp_act_mul` and
  `fused_add_rmsnorm_pad`.
- Route the touched config reads through `resolve_config_dir()` and document
  the shared selector in the config rulebooks.
- Correct the shared VGPR table parser for benchmark labels containing units.

## Hardware support and tuning

This PR supports **gfx950 only**. It does not ship or claim support for gfx942;
an unsupported architecture fails required-config resolution with the missing
architecture-specific path.

The measured config is stored at:

```text
aiter/ops/triton/configs/gfx950/triton/fusions/silu_and_mul_backward/DEFAULT.json
```

`width` below is the gate/up width, so `x.shape[-1] == 2 * width`.
`select_leq_config` chooses the smallest matching `N_LEQ_*` entry and otherwise
uses `any`:

| Width | `BLOCK_M` | `BLOCK_N` | `num_warps` | `num_stages` |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `<= 64` | 32 | 64 | 4 | 1 |
| `<= 128` | 32 | 128 | 4 | 1 |
| `<= 256` | 16 | 256 | 4 | 1 |
| `<= 512` | 8 | 512 | 4 | 1 |
| `> 512` | 4 | 1024 | 4 | 1 |

`BLOCK_M` and `BLOCK_N` are the row and column tiles. At launch, `BLOCK_M` is
capped by the next power of two of the row count; widths above 1024 use
multiple column tiles. `num_warps` and `num_stages` control launch scheduling.
The kernel `repr` records the effective `BLOCK_M` and `BLOCK_N` specialization.

## Performance

Measured at commit `74dcacab94842bac67e59b50e202ecea2b129672`.

- GPU: AMD Instinct MI350X VF (`gfx950`)
- ROCm: 7.2.4
- HIP runtime: 7.2.53211
- Python: 3.10.12
- PyTorch: `2.13.0+rocm7.2`
- Triton: 3.7.0
- dtype: BF16
- Timing: `triton.testing.do_bench`, `warmup=25 ms`, `rep=100 ms`, arithmetic mean

Commands:

```bash
for width in 4096 12288; do
  for metric in time bandwidth; do
    ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 PYTHONPATH=. \
      python op_tests/op_benchmarks/triton/bench_silu_and_mul_backward.py \
      --width "${width}" --dtype bf16 --provider all --metric "${metric}" \
      --warmup 25 --rep 100
  done
done
```

Each provider is measured by an independent `do_bench` invocation. `aiter`
measures the allocation-inclusive public API (`out=None`),
`aiter-preallocated` allocates `out` before timing, and `torch` is an
FP32-intermediate eager implementation of the same derivative. There was no
previous AITER backward operator, so the eager implementation is the functional
baseline rather than a before/after AITER kernel baseline.

### Latency and speedup

| Rows | Width | Preallocated `out` (us) | `out=None` (us) | FP32 eager (us) | Speedup: preallocated / `out=None` |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 4,096 | 10.095 | 7.806 | 89.599 | 8.88x / 11.48x |
| 128 | 4,096 | 6.817 | 6.939 | 87.115 | 12.78x / 12.55x |
| 2,048 | 4,096 | 32.894 | 33.041 | 234.537 | 7.13x / 7.10x |
| 8,192 | 4,096 | 107.258 | 107.228 | 1,032.173 | 9.62x / 9.63x |
| 1 | 12,288 | 11.821 | 10.054 | 104.233 | 8.82x / 10.37x |
| 128 | 12,288 | 9.110 | 11.659 | 104.813 | 11.50x / 8.99x |
| 2,048 | 12,288 | 89.151 | 89.169 | 757.152 | 8.49x / 8.49x |
| 8,192 | 12,288 | 256.765 | 256.638 | 3,079.848 | 11.99x / 12.00x |

Geometric-mean speedup over the FP32 eager reference is **9.73x** with a
preallocated output and **9.92x** through the allocation-inclusive public API.
For rows >= 2048, the two AITER paths differ by at most 0.45%; sub-percent
differences are measurement noise, not evidence that allocation improves the
kernel. Small cases are launch/API-latency bound.

### Effective bandwidth

Logical BF16 traffic is three input reads plus two output writes per gate/up
pair:

```text
5 * rows * width * sizeof(bfloat16) = 10 * rows * width bytes
```

Utilization uses AMD's published MI350X peak theoretical HBM bandwidth of
[8.0 TB/s per GPU](https://www.amd.com/en/products/accelerators/instinct/mi350/mi350x.html),
or 8,000 GB/s in decimal units.

| Rows | Width | Logical bytes | Preallocated GB/s (% peak) | `out=None` GB/s (% peak) | FP32 eager logical GB/s (% peak) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 4,096 | 40,960 | 4.1 (0.05%) | 5.2 (0.07%) | 0.5 (0.01%) |
| 128 | 4,096 | 5,242,880 | 769.1 (9.61%) | 755.5 (9.44%) | 60.2 (0.75%) |
| 2,048 | 4,096 | 83,886,080 | 2,550.2 (31.88%) | 2,538.9 (31.74%) | 357.7 (4.47%) |
| 8,192 | 4,096 | 335,544,320 | 3,128.4 (39.10%) | 3,129.3 (39.12%) | 325.1 (4.06%) |
| 1 | 12,288 | 122,880 | 10.4 (0.13%) | 12.2 (0.15%) | 1.2 (0.01%) |
| 128 | 12,288 | 15,728,640 | 1,726.5 (21.58%) | 1,349.1 (16.86%) | 150.1 (1.88%) |
| 2,048 | 12,288 | 251,658,240 | 2,822.8 (35.29%) | 2,822.3 (35.28%) | 332.4 (4.15%) |
| 8,192 | 12,288 | 1,006,632,960 | 3,920.4 (49.01%) | 3,922.4 (49.03%) | 326.8 (4.09%) |

The eager path uses the same logical-byte denominator for comparison, but it
performs additional physical traffic for FP32 casts, intermediates, separate
pointwise kernels, concatenation, and the final BF16 cast. Its reported value
is useful/logical bandwidth, not measured HBM traffic. The local GPU is exposed
as a virtual function, and the 8.0 TB/s figure is an advertised theoretical
full-GPU peak rather than sustained application bandwidth.

### Roofline estimate

Per gate/up pair, the fused kernel transfers 10 logical bytes and performs
approximately 11 ordinary FP32 operations plus one `exp2`, or about
**1.1 FLOP/byte** when the transcendental is excluded from the FLOP count.
AMD publishes 144.2 TFLOP/s peak FP32 vector performance and 8.0 TB/s peak HBM
bandwidth for MI350X, giving an estimated roofline ridge point of
`144.2 / 8.0 = 18.0 FLOP/byte`.

Because 1.1 FLOP/byte is far below 18.0 FLOP/byte, the conventional roofline
predicts a bandwidth-bound kernel at sufficiently large shapes. The largest
cases reach about 39-49% of advertised peak HBM bandwidth. This is an estimate:
`exp2` throughput, non-payload traffic, virtualization, and QoS are not modeled.

## Validation

MI350X/gfx950 targeted correctness, including width 1, strided gradients,
explicit output, empty rows, unsupported gfx942 config behavior, and a
non-current-GPU launch:

```bash
GPU_ARCHS=gfx950 PYTHONPATH=. pytest -q \
  op_tests/triton_tests/fusions/test_silu_and_mul_backward.py
```

Result: `53 passed`.

Kernel and config-loader regression suite:

```bash
GPU_ARCHS=gfx950 PYTHONPATH=. pytest -q \
  op_tests/triton_tests/fusions/test_silu_and_mul_backward.py \
  op_tests/triton_tests/fusions/test_fused_clamp_act_mul.py \
  op_tests/triton_tests/normalization/test_fused_add_rmsnorm_pad.py
```

Result: `1223 passed, 874 skipped`.

Activation-family regression suite:

```bash
GPU_ARCHS=gfx950 PYTHONPATH=. pytest -q \
  op_tests/triton_tests/test_activation.py \
  op_tests/triton_tests/fusions/test_fused_silu_mul.py
```

Result: `419 passed, 228 skipped`.

Width-one benchmark smoke test:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=. python \
  op_tests/op_benchmarks/triton/bench_silu_and_mul_backward.py \
  --rows 3 --width 1 --provider all --metric time --warmup 5 --rep 20
```

Result: all providers completed.

VGPR path:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=. python \
  op_tests/op_benchmarks/triton/bench_silu_and_mul_backward.py \
  --rows 1 --width 64 --provider aiter --metric time \
  --warmup 1 --rep 1 --print-vgpr
```

Result: `_silu_and_mul_backward_kernel_BLOCK_M_1_BLOCK_N_64`, 11 VGPR, no
VGPR spill.

Ruff 0.16.0, Black 26.5.1, `compileall`, JSON parsing, and
`git diff --check` pass for all changed files.

## Documentation, dependencies, and compatibility

- The public wrapper documents the config parameters and gfx950-only support.
- The shared config selector is documented in `configs/CLAUDE.md`, the Triton
  maintainer guide, and the scoped review instructions.
- No new third-party dependency.
- No breaking change to an existing public API.
- The forward path remains the existing `aiter.silu_and_mul` operation.

title: [FlyDSL] M3 index score flydsl
body:
A FlyDSL kernel for MiniMax-M3's decode index scorer: for each 128-token page of the index K cache, the max over tokens of q.k * scale, with a per-query causal cutoff. It replaces the Triton decode scorers in ATOM outright -- both `_decode_index_score_tiled_kernel` (TP) and `_context_score` (indexer CP) are deleted there, so this is the only decode scorer that ships.

The design rests on one measured fact about gfx950 MFMA 16x16x32: a lane's four accumulators are four consecutive M rows at a single N column. Choosing A=K so that M=token therefore puts the reduced axis inside one lane's registers, and the cross-lane tree Triton spends on `tl.max(qk, axis=0)` -- DPP shifts, swizzles and barriers -- disappears. Only the C half of that mapping had evidence in the repo; A and B were inferred, so test_flydsl_mfma_lane_mapping.py asserts all three with positional codes chosen to be exact in bf16 and asymmetric enough that a transposed or mis-gathered mapping cannot pass unnoticed.

Being memory bound, most of the work was in the load path:

- K reads are non-temporal (`buf_copy_atom` gained a cache policy). A KV cache read once and never revisited buys no reuse from L1 but pays a line fill per access. Over a 32000-page random gather: fp8 3.29 -> 5.02 TB/s, bf16 4.12 -> 5.48 TB/s.
- Page ids are fetched up front as independent loads instead of one per page with a wait before its K address can be formed, and K loads carry across the page boundary so a wave never drains and refills. ATT tracing had attributed 52.5% of latency to s_waitcnt against only +0.26% over-fetch, i.e. the cost was a serial dependency chain run once per page, not bytes.
- Out-of-range pages are clamped and masked at the store rather than branched around: a guarded second copy of the panel loop cost 1068 instructions per page against 622.
- The page-loop depth is picked from batch and max_block -- never from the contents of seq_lens, which a cudagraph replay is free to change underneath. Worth 4-12% at long sequence and up to 71% *worse* at short, where dividing the CTA count leaves 256 CUs underfed.
- iglp_opt(0) is requested only when a wave has more than one feature tile. Of four scheduling spellings tried it was the only one ever better than the backend's own, and the sign tracks tile count rather than length or dtype.

Two knobs stay off by default because they only pay at shapes that are not the production point: `token_waves` (splits a page's token panels across waves; -7% at q=1, +17% at the serving point) and the pre-shuffled K layout.

Correctness is judged by a pure-torch oracle transcribed from the contract, not from any kernel -- a reference sharing the implementation's assumptions cannot catch the implementation's bugs. That independence is now the whole safety net, since the Triton arm it once cross-checked against is gone: 298/298 pass, 206 skipped as illegal. The bench keeps flydsl-against-floor; at serve_b32_q8_s128k bf16 that is 178.6 us against a 194.2 us floor.

End to end on MiniMax-M3-MXFP4 (TP4, cudagraph, 5-shot GSM8K), the substitution holds accuracy on both arms: indexer CP on 0.9348, CP off 0.9393, against a 0.9363 reference -- each within one standard error, and the two arms are separately meaningful because world/rank fold in as compile-time constants and compile to distinct kernels.

title: [Triton/Gluon] [FlyDSL] [GDN] Segmented affine-scan K5 for long prefills
body:
## Motivation

Stock FlyDSL K5 assigns one program per `(sequence, head, V tile)` and walks 64-token chunks serially. A single 16k Qwen3.8 TP8 sequence therefore launches only 128 programs. Segmenting recovers occupancy on long, narrow prefills without changing the prepare or `o` kernels.

### Isolated kernel (gfx950)

`python op_tests/op_benchmarks/triton/bench_gdn_segment_scan.py` — H=16, indexed varlen, idle GPU:

| seq_lens | N | stock | segmented | delta |
| --- | --: | --: | --: | --: |
| 8192    | 1 | 253.3 µs | 150.7 µs | −40.5% |
| 16384   | 1 | 507.2 µs | 275.6 µs | −45.7% |
| 32768   | 1 | 952.3 µs | 504.4 µs | −47.0% |
| 16384×2 | 2 | 575.7 µs | 492.0 µs | −14.5% |
| 8192×4  | 4 | 400.6 µs | 487.9 µs | +21.8% |

The N=4 row is why the dispatch gate keeps packed batches on FlyDSL.

## Technical Details

The per-chunk hidden-state update is affine in the incoming state: for `h` shaped `[V, K]`,

```text
h' = h @ A + b
```

A long sequence is split into segments of `ceil(total_chunks / 16)` chunks. Each segment is an independent affine map, recovered without materializing a dense operator per chunk:

1. **Summaries.** Run the same recurrence over each segment twice in one launch: start at `h=0` with `u` to get `b_seg`, and start at `h=I` with `u=0` to get `A_seg`. `A_seg` is stored as `[V, K]` with `K=V=128`.
2. **Scan.** A short sequential kernel composes those maps along the sequence and writes each segment's true incoming state, including `h0` / `state_indices` for indexed varlen pools.
3. **Output.** Rerun every segment from that state and write the stock K5 contract: chunk snapshots `h`, `v_new`, and optional final state (in-place into the SSM pool when the FlyDSL wrapper would).

`T_FLAT` is a runtime kernel argument so packed batches of different lengths do not retrigger Triton constexpr compiles. The segment kernels use `BV=64` and the scan `BV=16`, both tuned on gfx950 over the gated shapes.

The FlyDSL wrapper (`chunk_gated_delta_rule_fwd_h_flydsl_opt`) intercepts before BV selection when all of the following hold:

- `B=1`, `K=V=128`, `use_g`, not `use_gk`, head-major log2-scaled `g`, `save_new_value`
- total chunks ≥ 128 ≈ 8k tokens
- `N<=2`, or `N==3` with total chunks ≥ 512 and max seq chunks ≥ 256

Varlen needs `prefill_metadata` so CPU `seq_lens` are available. Prepare (`gdn_prepare_fwd_flydsl`) and `chunk_fwd_kernel_o_opt_vk` are unchanged.

## Test Plan

- [x] `pytest op_tests/test_gdn_segment_scan.py` on gfx950 (MI355).
- [x] Serving A/B on Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B-Quark-MXFP4 TP8, 8×MI355X, `gdn_prefill_backend=aiter_flydsl`.
- [x] Matched 32k N=1 profiler traces.

## Test Result

### Unit tests (gfx950)

`pytest op_tests/test_gdn_segment_scan.py` — 6 passed:
| Test | What it checks |
| --- | --- |
| `test_gdn_segment_scan_matches_flydsl` | N=1, 1024 tokens, vs stock FlyDSL K5 |
| `test_gdn_segment_scan_packed_n2_matches_flydsl` | packed N=2 varlen + in-place state pool |
| `test_gdn_segment_scan_mixed_segment_counts_matches_flydsl` | mixed lengths, one-segment tail still gets `h0` |
| `test_wrapper_dispatches_n1_and_skips_n4` | dispatches N=1 when the chunk gate is lowered; N=4 packed never calls the segmented kernel |
| test_gdn_segment_scan_single_segment_indexed_pool_matches_flydsl | one segment per sequence still resolves the pool through `state_indices` |
| test_wrapper_packed_n2_matches_stock_flydsl                      | FlyDSL wrapper's segmented route vs its own stock route, packed N=2      |


### E2E serving (8k/32k, OSL 1024)

E2E Qwen3.8-2.4T MXFP4 on 8xMI355X vs a stock/control is (tok/s):

ISL / max_conc | Med TTFT | Med ITL | Out tok/s
-- | -- | -- | --
8k c=1 rr=0.8 | +0.6% | 0% | −1.5%
8k c=2 rr=0.8 | −1.6% | 0% | −2.0%
8k c=4 / c=8 rr=0.8 | −0.6 / −0.7% | 0% | +0.4 / −2.6%
8k c=1 rr=1.0 | +0.2% | 0% | −1.6%
8k c=2 rr=1.0 | +1.7% | 0% | 0%
8k c=4 / c=8 rr=1.0 | −0.1 / +0.1% | 0% | −2.2 / −2.7%
32k c=1 rr=0.8 | −2.5% | 0% | −0.2%
32k c=2 | −2.2% | 0% | −0.4%
32k c=4 | −2.0% | 0% | +0.5%
32k c=8 | −2.7% | 0% | +0.9%

With MBT=32k, 8k c≥4 packs N≥4 and stays on FlyDSL; rr=0.8 8k often misses the 128-chunk gate. **32k −2.0 to −2.7% median TTFT is the measured win.** 8k is flat within noise.

### Serving traces (32k, N=1, c=1, rr=1.0, OSL 8)

Same image pair, FlyDSL GDN prefill on both arms. Control: `stock_flydsl`, `chunk_gdn_fwd_h_flydsl_opt`. Candidate: `segment_scan`, `_gdn_segment_kernel` + `_gdn_segment_scan_kernel`.
| | Stock | Segmented |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Median TTFT | 1076.85 ms | 1046.23 ms (**−2.8%**) |
| GPU total | 1.096 s | 1.068 s |
| K5 GPU | 66.1 ms (69×) | 36.6 ms (**−45%**) |

K5 is ~6% of 32k prefill GPU, so −45% kernel is a ~3% TTFT ceiling. Matches the 32k cells.

title: [FlyDSL] [fused_moe] Do not route MXFP4 MoE to CK-Tile when inter_dim % 256 != 0
body:
# [fused_moe] Do not route MXFP4 MoE to CK-Tile when `inter_dim % 256 != 0`

Kernel-level defect report: ROCm/aiter#5233. This PR is the host-side mitigation. If the
CK-Tile stage-2 scale indexing is fixed there, the guard added here becomes dead and should be
dropped in favour of the kernel fix.

## Problem

MXFP4 MoE (`QuantType.per_1x32`, `q_dtype_w = fp4x2`) returns badly wrong results whenever
`inter_dim % 256 != 0` — e.g. `inter_dim = 384`, which is what a `moe_intermediate` of 3072
gives at TP8. There is no error, no warning and no NaN; only the output is wrong.

rel L2 per stage against `torch_moe_stage1` / `torch_moe_stage2`, token=32, model_dim=6144,
E=256, topk=8, block_m=32, split_k=2, with stage 2 fed the reference stage-1 output so the two
stages are isolated:

```
 inter     path    stage1    stage2
   256   cktile  0.003933  0.004314
   384   cktile  0.003986 10.280723   <-- broken
   384   flydsl  0.000003  0.004304
   512   cktile  0.003995  0.004376
   640   cktile  0.003990  8.005772   <-- broken
   640   flydsl  0.000002  0.004379
   768   cktile  0.003996  0.004297
```

The same pattern holds at E=129 topk=5.

## Root cause

CK-Tile stage 2 reduces over `inter_dim` and indexes its E8M0 weight scales in groups of 8
blocks (8 x 32 = 256 elements). The host pads the scale group dimension up to a multiple of 8
(`shuffle_scale` / `e8m0_shuffle`), so at `inter_dim % 256 != 0` the scale tensor handed to the
kernel has a wider group stride than the kernel assumes and stage 2 consumes the wrong scales.
Stage 1 reduces over `model_dim` and is unaffected.

This is a kernel indexing bug, not just a read of uninitialised pad bytes: pre-filling the w2
scale pad with a known byte before `e8m0_shuffle` changes the error but does not remove it
(at 384, uninitialised -> nan, `0x7F` -> 10.239, `0x00` -> 0.686; at 512 all three are 0.0038).

## Fix

Both changes are host-side. The CK-Tile HIP/CK source is not in this repository, so this PR
stops the broken shape from reaching the kernel rather than fixing the kernel.

**`aiter/fused_moe.py`.** `get_2stage_cfgs` gains `cktile_mxfp4_ok`, which gates the two CK-Tile
MXFP4 dispatch sites and routes the affected Swiglu shapes onto the same a16w4 FlyDSL kernels
SiTUv2 already uses. The guard also requires that a FlyDSL branch can actually accept the shape,
so `fp16` activations — which have no FlyDSL mxfp4 kernel here — keep their current routing
instead of being left with no backend at all.

The takeover is limited to the numerically validated path: BF16 output, BF16 activation,
SEPARATED weights, both weights marked shuffled, 128-aligned `inter_dim`, and 256-aligned
`model_dim`. FP16 output and FP4/FP8 activation families are not made newly eligible by this
guard. If no safe FlyDSL route exists, `_fused_moe_impl` and `cktile_moe_stage2` raise
`NotImplementedError` before CK-Tile can return a corrupt result.

Unsafe tuned, custom, and online-tuned CK-Tile stage-2 rows — including the
`swiglu_mxfp4_bf16_cktile` alias — are discarded before their early return and fall back to the same heuristic selection. The runtime check in `cktile_moe_stage2`
is the final guard for direct callers.

**`aiter/ops/shuffle.py`.** The `is_guinterleave=False` branch allocated the padded scale buffer
with `torch.empty` and never wrote the pad, so a kernel reading a whole 8-group tile consumed
stale device memory (E8M0 `0xFF` is NaN). It now fills with `0x7F` (E8M0 1.0), matching the
`is_guinterleave=True` branch. This removes the nondeterminism, not the corruption.

## Already-256-aligned shapes are unaffected

`get_2stage_cfgs` returns a field-identical `MOEMetadata` at inter_dim 256 / 512 / 768 — both
stage callables, every bound `functools.partial` keyword, `block_m`, `ksplit` and all flags —
compared against the same function with `cktile_mxfp4_ok` forced to `True`.

Dispatch tests cover the aligned and non-aligned `inter_dim` matrix, all six bf16/fp4/fp8
activation and SEPARATED/INTERLEAVE layout pairs, `model_dim=1152`, unsafe tuned CK-Tile metadata,
the packed-activation runtime guard, an explicit `AITER_KSPLIT=2` reroute, and standard-layout
scale padding. Aligned MXFP4 and non-FP4 calls remain allowed.

## Cost of the re-route

The re-routed shapes land on the FlyDSL heuristic fallback, because `tuned_fmoe.csv` has no rows
for a non-256-aligned `inter_dim` on this path (fallback count in a serving run goes 48 -> 72).
On MiniMax-M3-MXFP4, TP8, MI355X, against the same 512-padded baseline (`vllm bench serve`,
ISL 8192 / OSL 1024, concurrency 64, 2x2 interleaved paired runs):

| intermediate | kernel | output correct | throughput vs 512-padded |
|---|---|---|---|
| 512 (padded) | CK-Tile | yes | baseline |
| 384 | CK-Tile | **no** | +12.89 % |
| 384 | FlyDSL (this PR) | yes | +4.26 % |

The gap is tuning, not a kernel limitation: it closes by adding tuned rows for non-256-aligned
`inter_dim`, or by fixing the CK-Tile stage-2 scale indexing so the shape can stay on CK-Tile.

## Test plan

`op_tests/test_moe_mxfp4_inter_dim_dispatch.py` contains the dispatch and safety cases. It is at
the `op_tests` top level and has a `pytest.main` entry point, so the standard direct-python Aiter
CI runner executes it. `op_tests/flydsl_tests/test_moe_mxfp4_inter_dim_align.py` keeps the three
GPU numerics cases for FlyDSL toolchains that can compile the a16w4 port.

Reverting only the original dispatch guard fails the three dispatch and three numerics cases:

```
dispatch  inter_dim=128  expected flydsl, got stage1=cktile stage2=cktile
dispatch  inter_dim=384  expected flydsl, got stage1=cktile stage2=cktile
dispatch  inter_dim=640  expected flydsl, got stage1=cktile stage2=cktile
numerics  inter_dim=128  rel L2 18.193647   (gate: < 5e-2)
numerics  inter_dim=384  rel L2 10.408027
numerics  inter_dim=640  rel L2  7.897558
```

The aligned dispatch and CK-Tile runtime cases ensure the safety checks do not reject supported
shapes.

## Limitations

* The numbers above were produced on aiter 0.1.19 with this change applied on MI355X (gfx950),
  not on a `main` build. `main`'s FlyDSL a16w4 kernel source needs a newer flydsl than the 0.2.4
  in the test image: `aiter/ops/flydsl/kernels/moe_2stage_a16wmix/gemm1.py` fails codegen with
  `TypeError: s_waitcnt() got an unexpected keyword argument 'lgkmcnt'`. This is pre-existing and
  unrelated — `main` at `0598b04fc` with zero patches fails the shipped
  `test_flydsl_moe_a16wfp4.py` the same way. On `main` this change rests on the predicate
  equivalence above, the dispatch test (which needs no kernel), and inspection.
* gfx950 only for end-to-end numerics. No gfx942, expert-parallel (`is_ep=True`), or INTERLEAVE
  numerics coverage.
* `inter_dim` below 256 is covered by dispatch and safety tests but not by an end-to-end model run.
* Shapes with no compatible FlyDSL route now fail explicitly; only the kernel fix can make them
  executable on CK-Tile.

## Downstream

vllm-project/vllm#55104 aligns the ROCm AITER W4A4 MoE intermediate size to 128 and depends on
this PR. It is kept as a draft until this one lands, because without this guard that alignment
change silently corrupts decode output (clean-corpus perplexity 10.936 -> 41.325).

title: [HIP] Lift the 2 GiB limit on mla_reduce_v1 final output and LSE
body:
`mla_reduce_v1` rejected any call whose final output or final LSE spanned 2 GiB or more. The limit was real: both stores went through a buffer descriptor based at the tensor pointer with a 32-bit signed byte offset carrying the full `(seq, head)` index, so a larger tensor would have silently wrapped. It is easy to reach — bf16 output at `nhead=128` and `batch=16384` is exactly 2 GiB, so `-n 128,1 -b 16384` failed on every context length, on both the opus and asm decode paths.

`seq_idx` and `head_idx` are wave-uniform in all four store sites, so they now go into the 64-bit descriptor base and only the per-lane element offset stays in the 32-bit voffset. This is the same treatment the partial-output buffer already gets a few lines above, and it brings the buffer-store paths in line with `mla_reduce_v1_impl_*` massive's plain-pointer variant, which was already 64-bit. With nothing large left in the voffset, both host-side span checks and the `kMaxSpanBytes` constant are gone.

## Validation

The four previously rejected configurations now run and match the torch reference on both paths:

```
PYTHONPATH=. python3 op_tests/test_mla_persistent.py -d bf16 -kvd bf16 -n 128,1 -b 16384 -c 224 2048
```

## No regression

Folding the offset into the base means the descriptor is rebuilt per sequence instead of hoisted out of the loop, so the cost was measured on the shape where the reduce carries the most weight relative to the decode (`-n 96,4 -c 256`, over a thousand partials against a ~30 us kernel), five runs each, comparing medians:

| | before | after | delta |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `-b 32` | 31.186 us | 31.190 us | +0.01% |
| `-b 64` | 36.027 us | 35.958 us | -0.19% |

Both directions sit inside the run-to-run spread and the two distributions overlap almost entirely. A single-shot comparison had suggested up to +1.2%, which the repeats did not reproduce.

title: [FlyDSL] [gfx950] Add explicit page strides and 64-bit rebase for FP4 MQA logits
body:
## Summary

Extend the existing gfx950 FlyDSL paged MXFP4 MQA scorers with shared-pool page strides and 64-bit physical-page rebasing. This changes addressing, not FP4 arithmetic or the default dense layout. Consumer: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57517.

The public runtime wrappers read `kv_cache.stride(0)`, `kv_scale.stride(0)`, and `block_tables.stride(0)`; optional stride arguments belong to the build/compile APIs. Cache strides are bytes for uint8 tensors; table stride is int32 elements. `_i32_buffer(..., byte_offset=...)` rebases the descriptor before page-local loads.

The scorers now also accept 128-row pages while retaining the 256-token compute chunk. Scale writers/readers use four equal token groups instead of a hard-coded 16-row group, preserving the existing 64-row ABI and correctly packing the two 64-token warp regions of a 128-row page. Both 64- and 128-row decode and prefill cases match the exact FP4-dequant reference at cosine 1.000000. The default decode and prefill correctness sweeps now include 128-row page cases.

The original offset is **4,608,000,000 bytes = 4.608 GB = 4.292 GiB**, not 4.6 GiB. #4609 migrated existing scorers to the fx API; it did not first introduce FP4 scoring.

## FP8 -> FP4 indexer micro-benchmark

This is the primary performance comparison for the scorer: the previous paged
FP8 indexer pipeline gathers paged K/scales into contiguous buffers and then
runs FP8 MQA logits; the FP4 path reads the paged cache directly in one kernel.
Both operate on the same synthetic indexer shape and exclude model GEMMs,
attention, scheduler and CPU/server overhead.

MI355X/gfx950, H=64, D=128, page=64. These results were measured inside the
Sep-10 ROCm 10 nightly (`sha256:72e90adf360c...`), with Torch
`2.12.0+rocm10.0.0` and Triton
`3.8.0+git4cff872c.rocm10.0.0`. The FP8 arm uses the exact merged #5603 source
(`a84bd368`); the FP4 arm adds only this PR's three runtime scorer files. Each
shape uses five independent processes, with 10 warmups and 50 timed iterations
per process; medians are shown. FP8 total includes paged gather and FP8 logits;
FP4 is the single direct-paged scorer.

| Shape | B | Query rows / request | Context | FP4 us | FP8 gather us | FP8 total us | FP8 / FP4 | FP4 vs BF16 cos | FP8 vs BF16 cos | FP4 vs FP8 cos |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1x512x64K | 1 | 512 | 65,536 | **259.82** | 8.41 | 315.00 | **1.21x** | 0.987314 | 0.999301 | 0.985827 |
| 1x1Kx64K | 1 | 1,024 | 65,536 | **450.64** | 8.48 | 591.55 | **1.31x** | 0.987140 | 0.999295 | 0.985643 |
| 1x1Kx128K | 1 | 1,024 | 131,072 | **864.12** | 13.90 | 1166.32 | **1.35x** | 0.987143 | 0.999293 | 0.985628 |
| 4x256x16K | 4 | 256 | 16,384 | **126.85** | 8.35 | 184.82 | **1.47x** | 0.987142 | 0.999295 | 0.985647 |
| 8x128x8K | 8 | 128 | 8,192 | **63.57** | 8.99 | 111.17 | **1.75x** | 0.987139 | 0.999295 | 0.985643 |
| 1x8Kx8K | 1 | 8,192 | 8,192 | **414.53** | 4.31 | 536.86 | **1.30x** | 0.987229 | 0.999298 | 0.985725 |

Across this exact-stack sweep, FP4 is **1.21x–1.75x** faster than FP8
gather+score. FP4-vs-FP8 is computed directly from both output vectors over the
same valid windows. Every shape also reports `cos=1.000000` against the exact
FP4-dequant reference, separating kernel correctness from the expected
quantization difference.

```bash
for spec in \
  "1 512 65536" "1 1024 65536" "1 1024 131072" \
  "4 256 16384" "8 128 8192" "1 8192 8192"; do
  read -r bs nq ctx <<< "$spec"
  for repeat in {0..4}; do
    python - "$bs" "$nq" "$ctx" "$repeat" <<'PY'
import sys
from op_tests.test_flydsl_pa_mqa_logits_fp4_prefill import run_case
bs, nq, ctx, repeat = map(int, sys.argv[1:])
run_case(
    bs,
    [[ctx] * nq for _ in range(bs)],
    seed=42 + repeat,
    bench=True,
    iters=50,
    warmup=10,
    parallel_unit_num=max(512, bs * nq),
)
PY
  done
done
```

The existing op-test calls the FP8 reference pipeline `ATOM
cp_gather+fp8_logits`; that test name and implementation remain unchanged.
Decode uses H=64, D=128, page=64 and the new graph-stable auto-CTA schedule.
The search covered 16–4096 CTAs at 8K/32K/64K/128K; each final row is the
median of five independent processes with 20 warmups and 100 timed iterations.
FP4 and FP8 are measured in the same process on identical inputs.

| Context | Decode batch | Auto CTA | FP4 us (range) | FP8 us | FP8 / FP4 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 8K | 1 | 64 | 4.21 (3.62–4.27) | 4.17 | **0.99x** |
| 8K | 2 | 96 | 4.34 (3.75–4.43) | 4.31 | **0.99x** |
| 8K | 4 | 256 | 4.48 (3.95–4.58) | 4.35 | **0.97x** |
| 8K | 8 | 256 | 4.54 (3.94–4.58) | 4.50 | **0.99x** |
| 8K | 16 | 512 | 4.84 (4.80–4.91) | 4.82 | **1.00x** |
| 8K | 64 | 512 | 8.36 (8.09–8.62) | 11.89 | **1.42x** |
| 128K | 1 | 256 | 4.04 (3.99–4.59) | 4.14 | **1.03x** |
| 128K | 2 | 512 | 5.45 (4.86–5.50) | 5.50 | **1.01x** |
| 128K | 4 | 1280 | 7.37 (7.26–8.05) | 12.36 | **1.68x** |
| 128K | 8 | 1280 | 11.87 (11.07–12.04) | 20.79 | **1.75x** |
| 128K | 16 | 2048 | 17.60 (17.37–17.99) | 33.27 | **1.89x** |
| 128K | 64 | 4096 | 56.53 (55.46–57.02) | 165.55 | **2.93x** |

At 8K, the tuned grid removes the fixed-512 low-batch penalty: B1–B16 are
within 3% of FP8 and B64 is 1.42x faster. At 128K, B1/B2 are at parity and
B4–B64 are 1.68x–2.93x faster; B64 drops from 70.44 us with 512 CTAs to
56.53 us with the tuned grid. The selection uses only host-known row and
maximum-context buckets, so it adds no device-to-host synchronization and is
stable under graph replay. Explicit `parallel_unit_num` remains an override.

## Correctness / regression

Local MI355X, gfx950, GPU 7. Four-commit branch: functional kernel commit `d6807379`, consolidated test/benchmark commit `0030d058`, CI coverage fix `063f3eb5`, and auto-CTA tuning commit `6ab04df3`; all are authored by LiuYinfeng01. Torch `2.12.0+git6bbd260`, HIP `7.2.53211`; original validation used image Triton `3.7.1`; the complete correctness suite and standard shape sweep were rerun with the upstream CI Triton `3.8.0+amd.rocm7.2.0.git111ff227` pin. The strided-page test now enables graph replay and page-map/scale sensitivity checks by default, while non-gfx950 runners print `[skip]` and exit 0. No NVIDIA validation is implied.

```bash
python op_tests/test_flydsl_pa_mqa_logits_fp4.py
python op_tests/test_flydsl_pa_mqa_logits_fp4_prefill.py
python op_tests/test_flydsl_pa_mqa_logits_fp4_strided_pages.py \
  --json-output address-results.json
```

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Existing decode sweep | PASS; cosine 1.000000, existing error/mask checks |
| Existing prefill/variable-qlen sweep | PASS; cosine against FP4 reference 1.000000, BF16 comparison and `-inf` masks retained |
| Random dense vs shared-pool | PASS; identical payloads, separately contiguous dense K/scales, bit-identical dense/strided outputs |
| Independent FP4-dequant oracle | PASS; rtol=2e-4, atol=2e-3; nonuniform signed Q/K and per-group scales |
| Small, 2 GiB and 4 GiB boundary, original 4.608 GB offset | PASS; sequentially bounded allocations, nonzero layer/Q/scale offsets |
| Multiple requests, shuffled pages, padded table rows | PASS |
| Nonzero/empty windows, tail contexts, output guards | PASS |
| Prefill **and decode** graph capture/replay | PASS; logical outputs poisoned between replays |
| Deliberately wrong page map / scale permutation | Detected; restored inputs pass |
| Total recorded layout/path/execution comparisons | 40 PASS; includes original constant 8192.0 regression |
| Non-gfx950 default invocation | SKIP; prints `[skip]` and exits 0 |
| CTA tuning and paired final A/B | 1,792 correctness-passing records; 5-process final medians |

Negative control: running the new small strided case against upstream scorer files from `246efe9105ba` produced a GPU memory-access fault (exit 134). The patched source passes the same test. Do not run this negative control in a shared serving process.

## Appendix: stride/rebase performance non-regression

Following the same-change isolation used in #5285: only the three scorer files differ between baseline `246efe9105ba` and patched source; same dependencies, GPU and test. Three alternating process-level repetitions, 20 warmups, 100 timed iterations each; table reports the median of the three event-time averages. Dense K/scales and tables are genuinely contiguous and valid on both versions.

**Scope: public scorer API including internal schedule and output reset, CUDA graph replay; not kernel-only and not vLLM.** Rows=32, requests=3, context upper bound=8192 with ragged/empty windows, H=64, D=128, page=64.

| Path | Before us | After us | Latency change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Prefill | 36.564 | 36.442 | -0.33% |
| Decode | 37.704 | 37.779 | +0.20% |

Observed ranges overlap (prefill before 36.277–36.635, after 36.070–36.681 us; decode before 37.628–37.764, after 37.197–37.856 us). This auxiliary check only shows that shared-pool addressing did not materially regress the already-existing FP4 scorer; it is not the FP8 -> FP4 speedup table above.

title: [FlyDSL] [Kernel] gfx950 FP8 sparse MLA prefill and decode (FlyDSL)
body:
## Motivation

DSA-style sparse attention on gfx950  FlyDSL kernels for both prefill and decode phases, plus the split reducer decode needs.

## Kernels

`flydsl_sparse_mla_prefill` takes `q_nope` and `q_rope` separately: the caller already holds them split and the kernel reads them into different LDS regions, so concatenating first would copy the larger half for nothing. Below 96 tokens it splits the topk range across CTAs, because one CTA covers one token and a short prefill otherwise leaves most of the device idle. The partials it emits are the layout the sparse-decode reducer already consumes. Above that the grid fills the device on its own and a `const_expr` selects the single-split path, which emits the same IR as before split-K. The 96-token bound is the shared decode reducer's supported scope, not a tuning constant.

Both entry points take 1 to 16 heads. The MFMA tile is 16 rows wide, so the head count is a runtime kernel argument rather than a padded staging copy: rows past it re-read head 0, in bounds and dropped by the store predicate. GLM-5.2 has 64 heads, so 16 is TP4 and 8 is TP8, and refusing the latter would have excluded the configuration the end-to-end runs used. The kernel takes the same time at 8 heads as at 16, because KV traffic does not scale with the head count.

`flydsl_sparse_mla_decode` adds a split-K reducer. `sparse_mla_decode_workspace_shape` sizes its scratch, so a caller can allocate once and reuse across layers.

`mla_reduce_kernels.py` and `kernels/mla_reduce.py` gain the split-reduce entry points decode needs. One pre-existing path does change: `_resolve_actual_max_splits`, which `flydsl_mla_reduce_v1` calls, used to answer a graph-capture lookup straight from a pointer-keyed cache. A freed buffer hands its address to the next tensor, so a recycled key could return a stale split bound. Entries now carry a weak reference to the storage and a capture-time hit is honoured only while that storage is alive at the same base; a recycled key reports a miss, which the launch path already rejects with a message asking the caller to warm the buffer. Eager behaviour is unchanged.

## Measurements

MI355X gfx950, torch `2.9.1+rocm7.2.0`, tilelang `0.1.7.post3`. fp8 e4m3 `q` and KV, fp32 softmax and accumulation, bf16 out, `P` requantised to fp8 for the PV MFMA. `q` reaches TileLang already in fp8, so the baseline is not charged for a conversion it would not do in service.

One harness throughout: 200k-row KV pool, uniformly random topk, minimum of five HIP-graph replays. SNR is against an fp32 oracle on the pre-quantisation inputs, so it includes the fp8 input error and is the same oracle for every kernel. That error dominates, which is why TileLang, Triton and FlyDSL land within 0.1 dB of one another. The inputs are Gaussian, so the softmax over the 2048 selected keys is close to uniform -- the worst case for quantising `P`, and not what real top-k selection produces. On scores with realistic structure the same kernel measures several dB higher and the split count stops mattering: 16 splits scores +0.04 to +0.30 dB against 1 split there, against -1.0 dB on these inputs. Read the absolute figures as a floor, not as production accuracy. Triton is sgl-project/sglang#30575, run unmodified, using that PR's `triton_sparse_mla_fwd` for prefill and `triton_sparse_mla_decode` for decode. aiter's own sparse-MLA ASM prefill is gfx1250-only, so `mla_decode_fwd` appears in the decode table only.

### Prefill

| `T` | TileLang | Triton | FlyDSL | vs TileLang | vs Triton |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 13.52 us | 10.94 us | 7.82 us | 1.73x | 1.40x |
| 4 | 14.56 us | 11.48 us | 8.20 us | 1.78x | 1.40x |
| 16 | 20.25 us | 13.96 us | 10.42 us | 1.94x | 1.34x |
| 64 | 34.02 us | 34.30 us | 20.91 us | 1.63x | 1.64x |
| 96 | 41.90 us | 55.77 us | 25.66 us | 1.63x | 2.17x |
| 128 | 56.82 us | 58.46 us | 54.66 us | 1.04x | 1.07x |
| 256 | 102.43 us | 87.48 us | 59.30 us | 1.73x | 1.48x |
| 512 | 193.90 us | 103.66 us | 98.15 us | 1.98x | 1.06x |
| 1024 | 356.01 us | 200.32 us | 208.63 us | 1.71x | 0.96x |
| 2048 | 610.52 us | 391.42 us | 380.40 us | 1.60x | 1.03x |
| 4096 | 1185.05 us | 764.04 us | 752.28 us | 1.58x | 1.02x |
| 8192 | 2312.95 us | 1474.37 us | 1492.33 us | 1.55x | 0.99x |
| 16384 | 4562.58 us | 2901.64 us | 2968.91 us | 1.54x | 0.98x |
| 32768 | 9030.53 us | 5775.87 us | 5924.40 us | 1.52x | 0.97x |

14/14 against TileLang. Against Triton: ahead below 512, level within 2-4% from 2048 up where both are bandwidth-bound, 4% behind at 1024. Before split-K the first five rows against Triton were 0.24x, 0.25x, 0.26x, 0.64x and 0.61x. SNR spans 27.46-28.57 dB with the three kernels within 0.7 dB of each other.

### Decode

Sizes speculative decode at c<=16 produces -- draft `1,2,4,8,16` and verify `6,12,24,48,96`. aiter is `mla_decode_fwd`, each decode token issued as one request whose page table is its topk, with unity fp32 `q_scale`/`kv_scale` so the numerics match bare fp8.

| `seq` | TileLang | Triton | aiter ASM | FlyDSL | vs TL | vs TR | vs aiter |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 13.51 us | 8.91 us | 15.92 us | 6.47 us | 2.09x | 1.38x | 2.46x |
| 2 | 13.96 us | 9.09 us | 15.74 us | 6.72 us | 2.08x | 1.35x | 2.34x |
| 4 | 14.54 us | 9.57 us | 15.24 us | 7.23 us | 2.01x | 1.32x | 2.11x |
| 6 | 15.03 us | 10.68 us | 16.75 us | 7.76 us | 1.94x | 1.38x | 2.16x |
| 8 | 15.69 us | 10.35 us | 13.38 us | 8.30 us | 1.89x | 1.25x | 1.61x |
| 12 | 18.68 us | 11.05 us | 17.28 us | 9.63 us | 1.94x | 1.15x | 1.79x |
| 16 | 20.20 us | 11.88 us | 18.03 us | 10.36 us | 1.95x | 1.15x | 1.74x |
| 24 | 23.19 us | 15.56 us | 20.19 us | 12.97 us | 1.79x | 1.20x | 1.56x |
| 48 | 28.19 us | 24.52 us | 25.11 us | 19.78 us | 1.43x | 1.24x | 1.27x |
| 96 | 42.11 us | 39.54 us | 39.44 us | 32.87 us | 1.28x | 1.20x | 1.20x |

30/30, and decode output is bitwise deterministic across repeated runs at every size. Triton is the closest of the three.

aiter is about 1.6 dB more accurate on these inputs, and it is worth saying where that comes from, because it is not a scale tensor. Modelling the same arithmetic one step at a time: FP8 inputs with everything else exact give 31.8 dB; quantising `P` to FP8 for the PV MFMA costs 2.75 dB and lands at 29.06, which is where aiter measures. Quantising `P` against a running maximum rather than the row's final one costs a further 0.36 dB, and doing that once per split costs 1.25 dB more, putting TileLang, Triton and FlyDSL at a modelled 27.45 against a measured 27.54. So aiter is not doing something extra -- it sits at the FP8-`P` limit, and pays about 2.4x the time for it. The gap is also specific to these inputs: FP8 `P` against BF16 `P` is worth 3.92 dB here, 2.63 dB at a 1.2-bit score spread, and 0.02 dB at 12.6 bits.
27.3-28.2 dB for Triton -- which is consistent with it reading a scale tensor
per operand that the others do not. Its seq=96 SNR was not reproducible across runs, so it is left out rather than quoted.

### Sensitivity to the KV pool

The prefill margin over TileLang depends on gather locality, and the two kernels do not react to it the same way:

| `T`=1024, pool | TileLang | FlyDSL | speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2048 rows (1.2 MB) | 303.96 us | 119.35 us | 2.55x |
| 8192 rows (4.7 MB) | 337.19 us | 136.06 us | 2.48x |
| 32768 rows (18.9 MB) | 352.42 us | 166.44 us | 2.12x |
| 131072 rows (75.5 MB) | 355.63 us | 200.13 us | 1.78x |
| 200000 rows (115.2 MB) | 356.08 us | 203.55 us | 1.75x |

TileLang moves 17% across that range, FlyDSL 72%: FlyDSL is near the bandwidth roofline (6.4 TB/s of effective KV read at `T`=4096 against a 5.15 TB/s streaming-copy ceiling) and pays in full when locality degrades, while TileLang is not bandwidth-bound at these sizes. `T`=4096 behaves the same way, 2.61x down to 1.58x. Since a token reaches only its own sequence's KV, the figure tracks context length: roughly 2.0-2.1x at 32k, 1.6-1.8x at 128k. The tables above use the conservative end.

### Known gaps

FlyDSL trails Triton by 2-4% around `T`=768-1024 and I do not have the mechanism. It is not occupancy: the kernel sits at 152 VGPRs, which pins it to 3 CTAs per CU independently of LDS, and padding LDS from 44.5 KB to 69.5 KB or sweeping `waves_per_eu` over 1-4 changes nothing at any `T`.

## Tests

`op_tests/flydsl_tests/`, four files, 35 tests: accepted shapes, the rejection path for every wrong dtype/shape/arch/contiguity case, the split scratch's capacity and its identity under reuse, and the compile-cache domain.

```
$ python3 -m pytest op_tests/flydsl_tests/test_flydsl_sparse_mla_prefill.py \
    op_tests/flydsl_tests/test_flydsl_sparse_mla_decode.py \
    op_tests/flydsl_tests/test_flydsl_split_cache_identity.py \
    op_tests/flydsl_tests/test_flydsl_compile_cache_domain.py -q
35 passed, 2 warnings in 9.56s
```

Black and Ruff 0.16 clean on all changed files.

## Note for reviewers

#5167 also adds a `flydsl_sparse_mla_prefill`, written independently, with a
different signature -- single concatenated `q` plus `indptr`, `attn_sink` and `split_kv`, BF16, `D`=512 -- where this one takes `q_nope`/`q_rope` separately, fp8, `D`=576, and has no varlen or sink support. They are not drop-in replacements and whichever lands second collides on the name in `aiter/ops/flydsl/__init__.py`. Worth deciding which shape the namespace should carry before either merges; I am happy to adapt.
