title: [Triton/Gluon] Add fused Qwen3-Next GDN prefill (gfx950 Gluon) with fp8 group-quant epilogue
body:
A single fused op for the Qwen3-Next gated delta-net *prefill* chain (causal_conv1d_split_qkv -> fused gating -> fp32 chunked delta scan -> gated RMSNorm -> per-head group-128 FP8 quant), replacing the four-kernel path with a tight set of Gluon launches that fuse the work intra-kernel and drop the intermediate HBM traffic. The FP8 activations a block-FP8 out_proj consumes are emitted by the epilogue launch (no separate quant kernel).

Support is reported, not asserted: fused_gdn_prefill_qkvz_supported gates on gfx950, Triton >= 3.8 (Gluon dialect), and an in-range (tokens, batch)/dtype contract, so callers fall back to the four-kernel chain instead of crashing. Prefill spans a wide token range, so it dispatches one of four autotuned M-tile schedules. The Gluon/HIP tiles import lazily on dispatch, keeping the module and the support predicate importable on any platform.

Tests: pure-torch fp32 sequential-scan reference (deliberately not the chunked algorithm) at the kernel's bf16 rounding boundaries; 9/9 pass on MI355X (gfx950, Triton 3.8). Includes an op benchmark.

### Motivation
  The Qwen3-Next GDN (gated delta-net) **prefill** is a four-kernel chain today:
  `causal_conv1d_split_qkv` → fused gating → the fp32 chunked delta-rule scan →
  gated RMSNorm + per-head group-128 FP8 quant. Four launches means the large
  intermediate tensors (split qkv, conv output, gated core) round-trip through HBM
  between every step.

  This PR adds a single fused Gluon op, `fused_gdn_prefill_qkvz`, that folds that
  work intra-kernel: split + conv + SiLU + QK-norm + gating-prep in one launch, the
  fp32 chunked scan, and a gated-RMSNorm + group-128 FP8-quant **epilogue**. The win
  is the intra-launch fusion and the dropped intermediate HBM traffic. The FP8
  activations a block-FP8 `out_proj` consumes are emitted by the epilogue launch, so
  there is no separate quantization kernel.

  This is the **prefill sibling of the decode kernel** (ROCm/aiter#5520): same
  Qwen3-Next GDN math, but it consumes ragged variable-length batches
  (`cu_seqlens` + `has_initial_state`) and runs the fp32 chunked scan instead of the
  single-token recurrent update.

  ### Design
  - **Reported, not asserted.** `fused_gdn_prefill_qkvz_supported(...) -> (bool, reason)`
    gates on **gfx950** (CDNA buffer addressing / inline asm / explicit register
    layouts) and **Triton ≥ 3.8** (the tiles are the Gluon dialect; some ROCm 3.7
    builds import `triton.experimental.gluon` but fail to compile it, so the gate is a
    version check, not just an import probe). Callers fall back to the four-kernel
    chain instead of crashing.
  - **Lazy tile import** on the dispatch path, so the module and the support predicate
    stay importable on any platform (older Triton, non-gfx950, CUDA).
  - Prefill spans a wide token range, so it dispatches one of **four autotuned M-tile
    schedules** over the covered region (`tokens ∈ [1024, 16384]`, `batch ∈ [1, 64]`).
  - Constraints inherited from the epilogue: `head_k_dim == head_v_dim == 128`, group
    size 128, `num_v_heads == 2·num_k_heads`.

  ```python
  (normalized_bf16, conv_state, delta_state, quantized_fp8, scales) = fused_gdn_prefill_qkvz(
      projected_qkvz, projected_ba, conv_state, delta_state,
      cache_indices, cu_seqlens, has_initial_state,
      conv_weight, conv_bias, a_log, dt_bias, norm_weight,
      scale=head_k_dim ** -0.5, eps=norm.eps,
  )   # conv_state / delta_state advanced in place
  ```

  ### Files changed (9 files, +4655)
  | File | + | What |
  |------|---|------|
  | `aiter/ops/triton/gated_delta_net/fused_gdn_prefill_qkvz.py` | 308 | Public op + `_supported()` gate + tile
  dispatch (`_select_tile_key`) |
  | `aiter/ops/triton/_gluon_kernels/gfx950/gated_delta_net/fused_gdn_prefill_qkvz/` | 3761 | 4 Gluon M-tile schedules
  (`_tile_m1024_3071`, `_tile_m3072_16384`, `_tile_m12289_16384_b1_5`, `_tile_m12289_16384_b6_15`) + package `__init__`
  |
  | `aiter/ops/triton/gated_delta_net/__init__.py` | 6 | Export `fused_gdn_prefill_qkvz` / `_supported` |
  | `op_tests/triton_tests/test_fused_gdn_prefill_qkvz.py` | 416 | Correctness vs pure-torch fp32 reference |
  | `op_tests/op_benchmarks/triton/bench_fused_gdn_prefill_qkvz.py` | 164 | Latency benchmark |

  ### Accuracy — run command
  Correctness is checked against a **pure-torch fp32 sequential-scan reference**
  (deliberately *not* the chunked algorithm the kernel uses, so agreement is
  meaningful), matched to the kernel's bf16 rounding boundaries. Needs a gfx950 +
  Triton ≥ 3.8 ROCm environment.

  ```bash
  # from the aiter checkout, on an MI350-series (gfx950) host:
  python3 -m pytest -q op_tests/triton_tests/test_fused_gdn_prefill_qkvz.py
  ```
  Result on MI355X (Triton 3.8): **9 passed** — all 4 M-tiles compile+run+match the
  reference, both `has_initial_state` paths, determinism, and the unsupported-reason
  path. Numerics: fp8 activation ~1.3–7% (fp8 level), `conv_state` exact, recurrent
  state ~0.4%.

  ### Perf

  **Kernel vs the four-kernel chain it replaces** (MI355X, num_k=4 / num_v=8 /
  head=128; latency ms, median; speedup of the fused kernel):

  | shape k:v:b:s |     m | 4-kernel chain (ms) | fused (ms) | speedup |
  |---------------|------:|--------------------:|-----------:|--------:|
  | 4:8:1:4096    |  4096 |               0.691 |      0.222 |   3.1×  |
  | 4:8:2:4096    |  8192 |               0.834 |      0.302 |   2.8×  |
  | 4:8:4:2048    |  8192 |               0.782 |      0.287 |   2.7×  |
  | 4:8:1:8192    |  8192 |               0.867 |      0.324 |   2.7×  |
  | 4:8:1:2048    |  2048 |               0.616 |      0.215 |   2.9×  |
  | 4:8:2:1024    |  2048 |               0.677 |      0.176 |   3.8×  |
  | 4:8:8:1024    |  8192 |               0.744 |      0.209 |   3.6×  |
  | 4:8:2:8192    | 16384 |               1.072 |      0.509 |   2.1×  |

  (2.1–3.8× faster; widest at small-seq/large-batch where launch overhead dominates,
  narrowest at m=16384 where it is compute-bound.)

  **End-to-end through sglang** (Qwen3-Next-80B FP8, MI355X, TP4), prefill-focused
  (ISL 6144 / OSL 8) so TTFT surfaces the prefill win:

  | metric | stock | fused | Δ |
  |--------|------:|------:|---|
  | Median TTFT (ms) | 647.9 | 471.6 | **−27%** |
  | Input throughput (tok/s) | 92.8k | 125.4k | **+35%** |
  | GSM8K | 0.955 | 0.950 | parity |

  A balanced 1k/1k concurrency sweep (1→32) is TTFT-neutral-to-better (−12–16% at low
  concurrency, −2–6% at high), decode-neutral (TPOT identical), GSM8K parity
  (0.953 / 0.950). The sglang consumer wiring is a companion PR.

title: [Triton/Gluon] [gfx942] Enable sparse_mla_fwd on gfx942
body:
Enables `sparse_mla_fwd` on gfx942, on top of #4919.

The Gluon kernel needs no change to run there — the `gl.amd.cdna4` intrinsics it
uses (`async_copy`, `mfma`, `buffer_load`/`buffer_store`) all lower fine on
gfx942 under Triton 3.7.1. The arch gate was the only thing in the way, plus two
launch-config values sized against gfx950's LDS budget.

### Why the tile has to change

gfx942 (CDNA3) has **64 KB of LDS per workgroup against gfx950's 160 KB**. The
bf16 KV tile alone is `BLOCK_K * (kv_lora_rank + LDS_PAD) * 2 B`, so the gfx950
tile of 64 asks for 68 608 B and will not launch:

```
OutOfResources: out of resource: shared memory, Required: 68608, Hardware limit: 65536
```

`BLOCK_K=32` is the largest that fits.

**`num_warps` is decoupled from `BLOCK_K` in the same change.** It was derived as
`BLOCK_K // 16`, so capping the tile for LDS would have dropped num_warps from 4
to 2 as a *side effect* rather than as a tuning decision. Keeping it at 4 is
worth **1.19× → 1.55×** on the prefill shapes, so it is worth making explicit.

### `dot_precision="fp8"` is rejected on gfx942

This one is a genuine hardware limit and was the only real surprise. The fp8 dot
path feeds the cache's own code points to the matrix core, which needs **OCP
e4m3 MFMA — that arrives with CDNA4**. CDNA3 has fp8 MFMA in the fnuz encoding
only, so OCP code points read back wrong.

It was **silently wrong (rel-err 7.5e-1) rather than faulting**, which is why
this raises now, naming the alternative. `dot_precision="bf16"` dequantizes the
tile on its way into LDS and works on every arch and every cache format —
including the fp8 caches, which is what production uses here.

### gfx950 is unchanged

`_arch_block_k` → 64, `_arch_num_warps` → 4, `lds_limited` False, and
`FP8_DOT_ARCHS` contains gfx950, so every value and branch resolves exactly as
before. I do not have gfx950 hardware, so that claim is by construction rather
than by test — worth a second pair of eyes.

### Validation

On MI325X (gfx942), TP4, GLM-5.3-Flash at 131 k context. This matters on that
model because its NoPE MLA has `qk_rope_head_dim = 0`, which has no AITER path
today, so vLLM falls back to a vendored Triton gather+dot — the single largest
kernel in the model in both phases.

`op_tests/triton_tests/attention/test_sparse_mla.py`:

```
32 passed, 12 skipped in 23.61s
SKIPPED [12] fp8 matrix-core dots need OCP e4m3, absent on gfx942
```

Kernel bucket, from a real torch profile at concurrency 12 (rank 0):

| phase | bucket | Triton (vLLM) | this kernel | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| decode | per step | 3.099 ms | 0.400 ms | **7.74×** |
| prefill | per call | 10 988 µs | 10 330 µs | 1.06× |

End-to-end, 131 k in / 1024 out, same image both arms with only the dispatch
switched:

| conc | out tok/s before → after | delta |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 80.92 → 91.36 | **+12.90%** |
| 4 | 110.96 → 121.09 | +9.13% |
| 8 | 129.61 → 137.74 | +6.27% |
| 12 | 141.29 → 147.94 | +4.71% |
| 16 | 143.24 → 149.89 | +4.64% |

**Won 7/7 rows, mean +7.14% output throughput, zero failed requests.** gsm8k
(5-shot, full 1319 questions) is neutral: 0.9719 vs 0.9712 strict-match, against
a ±0.0046 standard error.

The gain being largest at low concurrency is the signature of this kernel rather
than noise: the operator is batch-independent, so replacing it takes a roughly
constant ~2.7 ms off every decode step, which is 16.6% of TPOT at concurrency 2
but 4.9% by concurrency 16.

### Note on prefill

The 1.06× prefill figure is the honest one, measured in a profile. A
microbenchmark using `randperm` top-k indices reports 1.55× for the same shape,
but that flatters it — random indices give the Triton gather far worse locality
than production does (11.0 ms real vs 15.7 ms synthetic for the same shape),
while this kernel gathers whole 512 B rows and is locality-insensitive. **Prefill
microbenchmarks on this operator should not be trusted without a profile.**

title: [OPUS] Key the MXFP8 BMM tuned lookup on cu_num
body:
## Motivation

MI350P and MI355X are both `gfx950`, but have 128 and 256 CUs respectively. The MXFP8 BMM tuned lookup currently keys only on `(gfx, b, m, n, k)`, so it cannot distinguish them. This can cause a kernel tuned for 256 CU to be selected on a device with 128CU. The CK batched gemm already keys on both gfx and cu_num (`aiter/ops/batched_gemm_op_a8w8.py:84`), as well as opus A16W16 (`aiter/ops/opus/policy.py:51`). Opus MXFP8 BMM does not.


## Changes

- Key both MXFP8 BMM loaders on `(gfx, cu_num, b, m, n, k)`.
- Resolve `cu_num` inside the lookup functions, alongside `gfx`, without changing call sites.
- Update `opus_bmm_mxscale_tune.py` to record `cu_num` in generated rows.
- Backfill the 77 existing `gfx950` rows with `cu_num=256`.
- Preserve compatibility with CSVs that do not have a `cu_num` column. They continue using the old `(gfx, b, m, n, k)` key and print a warning message.
- Add `index_tuned_by_cu_num` for merged tables containing both rows both with and without CU. The update_config_files function joins the per-model CSVs and fills a missing cu_num with 0 (`aiter/jit/core.py:385`). The index_tuned_by_cu_num function removes defaulted 0 cu_num from the keys.

title: [FlyDSL] [MoE] Raise the stage-2 invalid-row sentinel from 2 GiB to 4 GiB
body:
## Motivation

  The stage-2 CShuffle atomic epilogue does not branch around padding rows. It gives them a deliberately out-of-bounds byte offset and relies on the buffer descriptor's
  num_records check to drop the atomic (mixed_moe_gemm_2stage_common.py:4479). That sentinel was hardcoded to 0x7FFF0000, i.e. 2 GiB − 64 KiB.

  The guard that moves stage 2 off buffer atomics, requires_flydsl_stage2_reduce (moe_kernels.py:107-111), only fires above 4 GiB, because it is written against the
  32-bit addressing limit. Nothing covered the sentinel's own, much lower limit.

  So for any output in (0x7FFF0000, 0xFFFFFFFF] the sentinel is a valid address. Padding rows stop being discarded and instead atomically accumulate into a live token
  row. For model_dim=7168 with bf16 output the row stride is 14336 bytes and 0x7FFF0000 = 149792 * 14336 exactly, so those writes land on the start of row 149,792 and
  stay inside it.

  This is reachable today: the DSv4 a8w4 large-token case at token=262144 produces a 3.500 GiB output.

##  Technical Details

  One immediate constant, raised to 0xFFFF0000 (4 GiB − 64 KiB).

  The 64 KiB of headroom exists because the epilogue adds a column offset to the stored value (byte_off_i32 = row_byte_off_i32 + col_byte_off_i32, :4930), and
  use_buf_atomic requires row_stride <= 16384. Worst case is 0xFFFF0000 + 16382 = 4,294,918,142 < 2^32, so the uint32 voffset cannot wrap.

  Worth stating explicitly, because it is easy to misread: crossing 2^31 is not the failure. Buffer voffset and num_records are compared as unsigned 32-bit, the
  kernel's i32 arithmetic carries no nsw/nuw, and the FlyDSL wrapper (flydsl/expr/rocdl/__init__.py:663-675) passes the value through without sign extension. Only the
  discard mechanism was broken, not the addressing.

  No symbol, tile shape, occupancy, LDS budget, autotune input, or dispatch logic changes. Rows with accumulate=False, need_fp8_out, or row_stride > 16384 are
  unaffected.

  Known limitation, not fixed here. requires_flydsl_stage2_reduce still tests > 0xFFFFFFFF while the sentinel now fails above 0xFFFF0000, leaving a 65,535-byte window.
  For model_dim=7168 bf16 that exposes tokens 299,589–299,592. A static check over all 21 tuned-config CSVs found no shipped shape in that window, nor in the old 2 GiB
  window. The durable fix is to restore a real row-level predicate in precompute_row (:4809), which currently returns row_pred=None on the buffer-atomic path so
  mfma_epilogues.py:403 emits no guard.

title: [Bugfix][MLA] Fix reduce_partial_map over-allocation when max_split_per_batch is set
body:
## Motivation

On one rank, MLA decode can cut that rank's local KV into chunks and run them on
different CUs (the metadata kernel's `num_clusters` / `num_cu`).
`max_split_per_batch` caps how many of those extra KV fragments one batch is
allowed. The fp32 `reduce_partial_map` / `logits` buffer is the scratch to merge
those CU partials back.

DCP is separate: each GPU already holds only 1/`dcp_world_size` of the sequence.
Ranks do not share this split-K buffer. DCP only makes the per-GPU allocation
worse because that GPU's decode sees gathered query heads
(`nheads x dcp_world_size`) and still split-Ks its local KV across its own CUs.

An inference framework — in our case vLLM's ROCm MLA attention backend — cannot
allocate that scratch lazily, because the buffers have to exist before a
cudagraph is captured. So it uses aiter's ask-allocate-fill interface: ask
`get_mla_metadata_info_v1` for the sizes, allocate exactly those, then let
`get_mla_metadata_v1` build the schedule into them. Whatever step one returns is
what gets reserved.

So passing `max_split_per_batch` should return a smaller size. It does not:
sizing returns the same buffer whether you pass `1`, `256`, or `-1`.
`get_mla_metadata_info_v1` computes the cap-aware bound, then discards it with a
`max()` against the uncapped estimate. This is the other half of #3855, which
fixed the same expression but left the `max()`.

For Kimi-K3 MLA decode (TP8, DCP8, fp8 asm) that is **9.35 GiB to 2.38 GiB** of
fp32 scratch, 6.97 GiB per GPU. Before the fix a batch-48 decode died on every
rank with `torch.OutOfMemoryError: Tried to allocate 9.35 GiB`.

## Technical Details

`max()` becomes `min()`. Three constraints on where it applies:

- **fast_mode only.** With `fast_mode=False` and `intra_batch_mode=False` the
  planner is `get_mla_metadata_v1_1` (`metadata.cu:149`), which takes no cap.
- **Raw KV batch count**, not the sparse-expanded one (`v1_2_device.cuh:860`).
- **Scaled by `qk_batch_ratio`** when the head count is not natively served, via
  the same gate the planner uses (`v1_2_device.cuh:910-928`).

Callers passing no cap are unaffected: the branch needs
`max_split_per_batch > 0`, default `-1`.

`reduce_partial_map` entries, gfx950, `nhead=128`, `qo_len=4`:

| batch | uncapped | cap=1 | cap=256 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 1024 | 5 | 260 |
| 64 | 1276 | 320 | 512 |

Not addressed: `max_work` / `work_info_set` are still sized from the uncapped
estimate, and `intra_batch_mode` ignores the cap entirely.

## Test Plan

```bash
pytest op_tests/test_mla_metadata_split_cap.py op_tests/test_mla_metadata_split_cap_fill.py

# also run standalone, which is how aiter CI invokes op_tests files
python3 op_tests/test_mla_metadata_split_cap.py
python3 op_tests/test_mla_metadata_split_cap_fill.py
```

Two files because a sizing formula can otherwise only be checked against itself.
The first pins the arithmetic and the native-support gate across gfx950, gfx942
and gfx1250. The second allocates exactly what sizing returns, runs the planner
into it with the same cap and dtypes, and checks the populated extents fit.

## Test Result

```
op_tests/test_mla_metadata_split_cap.py       31 passed
op_tests/test_mla_metadata_split_cap_fill.py  27 passed
```

Measured fills against the bound, printed by the fill test so the numbers land
in CI:

| shape | partials / bound |
|---|---:|
| batch 1, cap 256 | 256 / 260 |
| batch 8, cap 256, qlen 1 | 262 / 263 |
| batch 512, cap 256 | 506 / 2040 |
| nhead 48 (folded), cap 16 | 48 / 60 |

The qlen=1 row is the tight one, a single entry of headroom.

title: [FlyDSL] perf(hca): the gfx1250 hca_compress optimization
body:
…nfig table

The Phase 1 / Phase 2 split gave compress_forward's K loop runtime bounds, so it could not unroll and each iteration serialised into a load -> softmax -> load dependency chain. Splitting the cost three ways (all-sentinel plan, one active boundary, full plan) showed the kernel was spending 3.1us on a single block's latency chain against only 2.8us of throughput for all 128 boundaries, which is also why larger k_split_num_waves used to help: it only shortened the chain.

Phase 2 now covers the wave's whole K range with the Phase 1 prefix masked to -inf. A masked step is an exact no-op (score=-inf forces w_k=0 and m_new=m_old, so the accumulator is scaled by exp(0)=1 and incremented by 0), and the trip count becomes the compile-time K_PER_WAVE, so the loop unrolls and the scheduler batches all K loads. Two smaller latency fixes go with it: the state-cache `slot` load moves into the Phase 1 loop, where LICM sinks it to the preheader so waves that read no state cache never pay for that dependent round trip; and Kernel B's kv_compressed load moves above the sentinel guard, since its address needs only pid and the guard was chaining it behind the plan load.

On prefill bs=64 (16K tokens, gfx1250) compress_forward goes 19.1us -> 9.2us and the 2-kernel path 22.6us -> 12.9us, measured A/B in one process run.

hca_per_n_config_gfx1250 shipped as "Initial values -- need hardware tuning" and selected slice_size=512 above plan_capacity 1024, which does not build at all because VEC=16 exceeds what the Phase 1 f32 loader handles -- decode bs=1024 failed outright. It is retuned from measured medians and VEC=16 now fails at build time with a clear message instead of a bare assert.

Validated against the torch reference across hca_main prefill bs=1/4/16/64 and decode bs=2/64/1024 with mtp=0/3; decode bs=1024 goes from a build failure to 70.7us.

title: [HIP] [Bugfix] Give the 4096<n<=6144 RMSNorm bucket a grouped-quant shape
body:
## Problem

`rmsnorm_quant` / `add_rmsnorm_quant` choose `thread_data_size` from the hidden
size, and the kernel requires a quant group to be a whole number of threads:

```cpp
AITER_CHECK(group_size >= 0 && (group_size % thread_data_size == 0 && ...
```

The `4096 < n <= 6144` bucket picks `thread_data_size = 24`. Neither 32 nor 128
divides 24, so **every grouped quant at those widths failed the check instead of
running**:

```
[AITER] csrc/kernels/rmsnorm_quant_kernels.cu:504 operator() group_size not support: 32
```

On gfx950 a width sweep through the fused path showed 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024,
1280, 2048, 2560, 4096 and 8192 all working and only 5120 aborting — for MXFP4
and MXFP8 alike. 5120 is DeepSeek-V4.1's `hidden_size`, so its per-layer norms
could not use a fused RMSNorm+quant at all.

## Fix

Branch that bucket on `group_size` and reuse the pair the `n <= 8192` bucket
already uses for a grouped quant — `(512, 16)` below 160 CUs, `(1024, 8)` at or
above — whose 16 and 8 divide every group this op supports. Per-token quant
(`group_size == 0`) keeps the 24-wide default, so nothing that worked before
changes shape.

Both template instantiations already exist for the 8192 bucket, so this adds no
compile time. The two non-quant dispatch macros are deliberately untouched: they
hardcode `group_size = 0`, so the branch would be dead code there.

## Test

`op_tests/test_rmsnorm2dFusedAddQuant.py` gains 5120 in its default `-n` sweep.
No default width landed in the `4096 < n <= 6144` bucket, which is how a bucket
with no grouped-quant kernel went unnoticed; modes 7 (`per_1x128`) and 8
(`per_1x32`) now reach it.

## Verification, gfx950 / MI355X

Before, at n=5120: both grouped modes abort. After:

| mode | n=4096 | n=5120 | n=8192 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7, `per_1x128` fp8 | 3.1%, max abs delta 32.0 | **3.1%, max abs delta 32.0** | 3.1%, max abs delta 32.0 |
| 8, `per_1x32` fp4x2 | 0.7%, max abs delta 3.0 | **0.6%, max abs delta 3.0** | 0.6%, max abs delta 3.0 |

Those torch-vs-hip spreads are what the adjacent widths already report on this
test; the point is that 5120 now sits in family with them instead of aborting.
Per-token quant at 5120 is unchanged, and MXFP4 at 5120 — the pre-existing
casualty of the same gap — works again.

title: [Triton] Account for sliding_window in bench_unified_attention metrics
body:
## Purpose
`bench_unified_attention.py --metric throughput`/`bandwidth` ignore `sliding_window`. The FLOP count uses the full causal triangle and the byte count uses the full KV length, so windowed attention reports numbers **above the hardware roofline** and cannot be compared against it. Example (MI325 / gfx942): head_size 256 sliding, window 1024, seqlen 32768 reported ~2598 TFLOPS — above the bf16 (1307) and fp8 (2615) matrix roofs. Fixes #5662.

## Change
- **FLOPs:** count windowed causal pairs — query `i` attends to `min(sk - sq + i + 1, window)` keys — instead of the full triangle.
- **Bandwidth:** cap the KV bytes streamed at the union of all query windows, `min(sk, sq - 1 + window)`.
- The non-windowed path is byte-for-byte unchanged.

## Test Result
Formula validated against hand-computed values:
- no-window prefill/decode: identical to the previous formula.
- window decode (sq=1): pairs and KV = `min(ctx, window)`.
- window prefill (S=32768, W=1024): pairs = `W(W+1)/2 + (S-W)·W` = 33,030,656 (vs 536,887,296 full-causal — the fix removes a **16.3×** over-count); KV read = full `S` (all keys are read across the window union in prefill).

## Notes
End-to-end this makes windowed throughput/bandwidth roofline-comparable (e.g. the Gemma-4 sliding-window layers). AI assistance (Claude Code) was used; a human will review. Not a duplicate — no open PR addresses the windowed metric. Companion to the fp8 reference fix (#5663).

title: [Triton] Tune unified attention configs for Gemma-4 on gfx942 (MI325)
body:
## Purpose
The head-size-aware `select_2d_config` / `select_3d_config` branches for `head_size` 256/512 in `unified_attention.py` were tuned on gfx950 and applied to gfx942 unchanged. On gfx942 (MI325) the default `BLOCK_M=16` badly under-tiles the large Gemma-4 heads (256/512) and `waves_per_eu=2` under-utilises HBM, leaving the two Gemma-4-31B attention shapes far below roofline. This adds gfx942-gated overrides only; every other arch (gfx950/gfx1201/gfx1151/rdna) is byte-for-byte unchanged, mirroring the existing `gfx1151` override precedent.

## Change
- `select_2d_config`, `head_size>=512` and `>=256` prefill: `BLOCK_M 16->64`, `waves_per_eu 2->1`.
- `select_3d_config`, `head_size>=512` decode: `waves_per_eu 2->1`.
- Register Gemma-4 31B shapes in `model_shapes.json` (full: head 512 GQA 32/4; sliding: head 256 GQA 32/16, window 1024).

## Test Result (MI325 / gfx942, fp8 KV, roofs 1307 TFLOP/s bf16 / 6 TB/s)

| Regime | Before | After | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| full512 prefill (2k/8k/32k) | 79/79/80 TFLOPS | 166/193/218 | 2.1–2.7x |
| full512 decode b1/16/64 (8k) | 399/1482/1919 GB/s | 450/1994/2409 | up to 1.35x |
| slide256 prefill (8k/32k, window-corrected) | 159/160 TFLOPS | 265/234 | 1.5–1.7x |

## Correctness
- fp8-KV `-test` passes for both shapes at `max_diff=0.0156` (prefill) / `0.0005` (decode), using the reference fix in the companion PR.
- `pytest op_tests/triton_tests/attention/test_unified_attention.py`: **1024 passed, 1120 skipped**; head-128 path unaffected. Changes are tiling/occupancy only (numerically neutral).

## ⚠️ Rebase needed before merge
This branch is based on the commit our workspace pins and validated against; `main` has since refactored `unified_attention.py` substantially (this branch is ~234 commits behind). The configs and numbers above are validated on the pinned base — they must be ported onto the current `select_2d_config` / `select_3d_config` and re-validated on `main` before this merges. Opened as a draft for that reason.

## Notes
AI assistance (Claude Code) was used for the sweep, implementation, and validation; a human will review and re-validate before merge. Not a duplicate of the gfx950 tuning (#4044/#4918) — this is the gfx942 counterpart. Depends on the fp8 `-test` reference fix (#5663) to reproduce the correctness numbers.

Bump the Triton build used by AITER CI from commit `111ff227` to `7cb7b059` by pointing the wheel index at the temporary `release_0914` channel, so the new build is validated before it is promoted to the standard `_release` channel. This branch is for CI validation only.

- `.github/scripts/install_triton.sh` and `.github/scripts/download_triton_wheel.sh`: switch the Triton wheel index channel from `_release` to `release_0914`, so the index URL becomes `https://pypi.amd.com/triton/release_0914/rocm-<ver>/simple/` (both the default and the rocm-core-derived paths). The pinned `triton==3.8.0` and `triton-kernels==1.0.0` versions are unchanged — only the channel moves, which is what advances the underlying Triton build from `111ff227` to `7cb7b059`.

title: [Triton/Gluon] [HIP] [JIT] Add optimized FlashKDA prefill kernels for gfx950
body:
## Motivation

This PR adds and optimizes a native HIP/MFMA FlashKDA prefill implementation for `gfx942` and `gfx950`.

The work is motivated by the following upstream integration changes:

- ATOM switched the Kimi K3 prefill path to aiter KDA:
  https://github.com/ROCm/ATOM/commit/16c20d3048ea4cf99d1cfc30fa8cbb01ffca12a9
- The aiter Triton KDA implementation was significantly improved:
  https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/4683

After the Triton update, the original native HIP implementation was no longer competitive across the full K3 prefill workload range. This PR reworks the native preparation, recurrence, and output data flow to recover and extend the performance advantage on gfx950.

The primary optimization target is the public Kimi K3 TP8 prefill configuration:

```text
global heads = 96
tensor parallel size = 8
Hq = HV = 12 per rank
K = V = 128
```

The final gfx950 implementation was evaluated across:

- single-sequence prefill from 128 to 16K tokens;
- both fresh and resumed FP32 recurrent state at every tested length;
- uniform multi-sequence batches;
- ragged packed batches;
- multi-sequence resumed prefill;
- public zero-environment backend selection;
- ROCm graph capture and replay.

Across the 20-cell prefill matrix and three random seeds, native HIP is faster than Triton in all 60 measured seed-cells. The geometric mean speedup is `1.403x`, with speedups ranging from `1.030x` to `1.830x`.

This PR additionally adds grouped value attention (GVA) as a functional extension of the native operator. GVA is not the primary performance claim of this PR.

Pure autoregressive decode is outside the scope of this PR. Kimi K3 decode continues to use its existing specialized fused recurrence kernel rather than `chunk_kimi_delta_attn`.

The native implementation is adapted from the HIP/MFMA backend of [MoonshotAI/FlashKDA](https://github.com/MoonshotAI/FlashKDA), source revision `7557ca0`, under the MIT license. The aiter integration, packed-sequence ABI, gfx950 optimizations, dispatch policies, and GVA extension are maintained in this PR.

## Technical Details

### Native operator integration

This PR adds an architecture-specialized FlashKDA forward implementation for `gfx942` and `gfx950` and integrates it with:

- aiter JIT compilation;
- architecture-specific source selection;
- the aiter tensor ABI and pybind layer;
- the public `chunk_kimi_delta_attn` interface;
- ROCm graph capture and replay.

The native path supports the Kimi K3 prefill contract:

- BF16 Q, K, V, and raw gate inputs;
- FP32 or BF16 beta;
- FP32 `A_log` and `dt_bias`;
- `K = V = 128`;
- fused Q/K L2 normalization;
- fused gate processing;
- fused beta sigmoid;
- lower-bounded safe gate processing;
- V-first recurrent state;
- optional FP32/BF16 initial state;
- optional final-state output;
- dense and packed variable-length prefill;
- `int32` and `int64` packed sequence offsets at the Python boundary.

### Preparation fusion and data reuse

The native implementation uses two logical stages:

- K1 prepares the per-chunk operands required by the recurrence.
- K2 performs the recurrent scan and output calculation.

K1 fuses preparation work that would otherwise require multiple launches or repeated global-memory traffic, including:

- Q/K decay transformations;
- restored K operands;
- cumulative gate terms;
- beta activation;
- local inverse/Neumann terms;
- recurrence operands shared with K2.

K1 publishes these values in a layout selected for the corresponding K2 implementation. K2 reuses the prepared operands rather than reloading and recomputing them independently.

K1 and K2 remain separate physical kernels in the general path. The optimization is primarily fusion within K1 and producer/consumer reuse between K1 and K2, with selective fusion inside individual K2/output paths where the workload geometry makes it profitable.

### Shape-adaptive recurrence

The original plain C-split algorithm is retained as one valid route, but it is no longer used for every workload.

The gfx950 policy selects among several recurrence strategies:

- plain C-split;
- direct context processing;
- affine context scan;
- hybrid direct/scan processing;
- persistent and worklist-based variants.

The route is selected from sequence count, sequence length, packed geometry, recurrent-state mode, and the optional maximum-sequence-length hint.

The main algorithmic changes are:

- use a direct path when the recurrence can be completed efficiently without materializing a global scan structure;
- represent long-sequence chunks as affine state transformations so chunk-local producer work can run in parallel;
- restrict the serial scan to the compact cross-chunk state dependency;
- replay the chunk outputs in parallel after the scan;
- use hybrid routing for heterogeneous packed workloads;
- avoid unnecessary prefix construction on eligible paths;
- reuse activated beta, decay values, and recurrent operands between producer and replay stages;
- use persistent worklists to improve load balance for irregular packed inputs.

This keeps the inherently serial portion of the recurrence small while exposing preparation and output work to GPU parallelism.

### gfx950-specific implementation

The gfx950 implementation adds CDNA4-specific tuning, including:

- architecture-specific MFMA fragments and operand layouts;
- fused BT16 preparation;
- BT32 and BT64 merge paths;
- optimized register and LDS state exchange;
- multi-arena recurrence pipelines;
- packed-sequence prefix and worklist handling;
- direct global and K-split context paths;
- affine A/B producer and compact scan paths;
- persistent replay;
- specialized output replay paths;
- graph-stable, shape-based dispatch policies.

The resulting policy covers short launch-bound inputs, long low-batch inputs, large uniform batches, ragged packed inputs, and resumed prefill.

### Public backend routing

The public `chunk_kimi_delta_attn` wrapper supports:

- `backend="auto"`:
  use native HIP for supported calls on `gfx942`/`gfx950`, otherwise fall back to Triton;
- `backend="native"`:
  require native HIP and report an explicit rejection reason for unsupported inputs;
- `backend="triton"`:
  force the current Triton implementation;
- `backend="baseline"`:
  select the original Triton chunked implementation.

With no backend or KDA environment override, supported K3 prefill calls select native HIP automatically.

A host-provided `max_seqlen_upper_bound` is supported for packed inputs. This allows graph-safe route selection without copying device sequence metadata back to the host.

### Native ABI

The implementation provides validated raw-pointer entry points for the latency-sensitive dispatch path:

- raw v1 preserves the original equal-head interface;
- raw v2 appends the graph-safe maximum-sequence-length hint;
- raw v3 appends the Q/K head count required by GVA.

The v2 and v3 interfaces preserve the preceding ABI argument layout.

The adapter validates:

- tensor shapes and dtypes;
- dense and packed sequence geometry;
- recurrent-state layout;
- workspace capacity;
- GVA head ratios;
- active device;
- stream ownership;
- architecture support;
- graph-safe routing bounds.

### GVA functional support

The native operator additionally supports grouped value attention when:

```text
HV >= Hq
HV % Hq == 0
```

Value, gate, and state heads are mapped to Q/K heads using:

```text
qk_head = value_head // (HV / Hq)
```

The GVA implementation covers:

- ratio-2 and ratio-4 head mappings;
- dense and packed layouts;
- fresh and resumed prefill;
- optional final-state output;
- empty packed sequences;
- descriptor and raw-v3 equivalence;
- ROCm graph capture and replay.

GVA is an operator-level compatibility feature. The primary performance results in this PR use the current public Kimi K3 equal-head geometry, `Hq=HV=12`.

### Test and benchmark integration

Correctness tests are integrated into the standard pytest hierarchy:

```text
op_tests/triton_tests/chunk_delta_attn/test_flash_kda_native.py
op_tests/triton_tests/chunk_delta_attn/test_flash_kda_native_python_api.py
```

Performance coverage is integrated into the standard benchmark hierarchy:

```text
op_tests/op_benchmarks/triton/bench_flash_kda_native.py
```

The benchmark compares public zero-environment HIP routing against the forced Triton path using identical inputs. It records:

- eager and ROCm graph correctness;
- output and final-state relative RMS;
- p10, p50, p90, mean, and standard deviation;
- raw paired timing samples;
- HIP win fraction;
- speedup over Triton;
- kernel route and graph topology;
- CSV and JSON artifacts.

A thin reproducibility runner is provided at:

```text
scripts/run_flash_kda_gva_acceptance.sh
```

The runner delegates correctness and performance validation to the canonical pytest and benchmark files. It also uses an isolated JIT directory and records the tested Git revision, environment, logs, benchmark output, and native module checksum.

## Test Plan

### Correctness

Run the standard Python API and native GPU tests:

```bash
python -m pytest -q \
  op_tests/triton_tests/chunk_delta_attn/test_flash_kda_native_python_api.py \
  op_tests/triton_tests/chunk_delta_attn/test_flash_kda_native.py
```

The tests cover:

- public API validation;
- native admission and fallback behavior;
- raw v1/v2/v3 dispatch;
- dense and packed variable-length prefill;
- fresh and resumed recurrent state;
- equal-head attention;
- GVA ratio-2 and ratio-4 mappings;
- empty packed sequences;
- native versus Triton numerical agreement;
- native versus FP32 recurrence reference;
- descriptor versus raw-v3 equivalence;
- public automatic routing;
- ROCm graph capture and replay.

### Primary equal-head performance matrix

The primary performance comparison uses the public K3 TP8 configuration:

```text
Hq = HV = 12
K = V = 128
state = None or FP32 [N, 12, 128, 128]
execution = ROCm graph replay
```

The following single-sequence lengths are crossed with both state modes:

```text
128, 256, 512, 1K, 2K, 4K, 8K, 16K
```

State modes:

```text
fresh:   initial_state=None
resume:  nonzero FP32 initial_state
```

Additional packed coverage:

```text
batch-16x1K fresh
batch-64x256 fresh
ragged-16K fresh
resume-4x4K FP32
```

The formal comparison uses:

```text
backends:                    public zero-env HIP vs forced Triton
seeds:                       42, 43, 44
warmup:                      20 iterations
measurements:                120 per backend/cell/seed
execution:                   ROCm graph replay
measurement order:           alternating and position-balanced
paired bootstrap resamples:  10,000
relative-RMS tolerance:       0.04
```

A performance cell passes only when:

1. HIP p50 is faster than Triton for every seed.
2. The paired HIP win fraction is greater than 50% for every seed.
3. The upper bound of every per-seed paired-p50 95% bootstrap confidence interval is below zero.
4. The upper bound of the cross-seed paired-p50 95% bootstrap confidence interval is below zero.

The regular benchmark entry point can be used for reproduction:

```bash
python op_tests/op_benchmarks/triton/bench_flash_kda_native.py \
  --suite core \
  --heads 12 \
  --value-heads 12 \
  --backend native \
  --backend triton \
  --execution graph \
  --public-k3 \
  --warmup 20 \
  --repeat 120 \
  --seed 42 \
  --tolerance 0.04 \
  --require-arch gfx950 \
  --require-compute-units 256
```

The same benchmark is repeated for seeds `43` and `44`, and for each single sequence length with a nonzero FP32 initial state.

### GVA functional coverage

GVA is validated separately with:

```text
Hq=2, HV=4
Hq=2, HV=8
```

The GVA tests verify numerical correctness, state layout, public routing, raw-v3 dispatch, packed metadata, and graph replay. GVA performance is not used as the primary performance claim of this PR.

## Test Result

Test environment:

```text
Host:      smci355-ccs-aus-n12-25.cs-aus.dcgpu
GPU:       MI355X / gfx950, 256 compute units
PyTorch:   2.10.0+rocm7.2.4.git3d3aa833
ROCm:      7.2.53211
Execution: ROCm graph replay
```

### Correctness

```text
81 passed in 578.35s
```

For the primary equal-head performance matrix:

```text
logical cells:              20
seeds per cell:             3
total measured seed-cells:  60
p50 wins:                   60 / 60
speedup range:              1.030x - 1.830x
speedup geometric mean:     1.403x
```

All per-seed and cross-seed paired-p50 bootstrap confidence intervals have an upper bound below zero.

The weakest cell is `single-512-fresh`:

```text
worst-seed speedup:          1.030x
worst-seed HIP win fraction: 70.8%
pooled paired p50 delta:     -1.839 us
95% confidence interval:     [-2.620, -0.920] us
```

Even for this launch-bound case, the upper confidence bound remains below zero.

Speedup is defined as:

```text
speedup = Triton p50 / native HIP p50
```

For the following tables, latency is the median of the three per-seed p50 measurements. “Worst speedup” is the minimum speedup observed across seeds 42, 43, and 44.

### Single-sequence fresh/resume cross coverage

| Length | HIP fresh p50 | Triton fresh p50 | Worst fresh speedup | HIP resume p50 | Triton resume p50 | Worst resume speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 128 | 31.201 us | 34.600 us | 1.103x | 31.840 us | 38.481 us | 1.206x |
| 256 | 34.260 us | 40.720 us | 1.182x | 34.580 us | 45.881 us | 1.323x |
| 512 | 49.740 us | 51.360 us | 1.030x | 49.640 us | 56.760 us | 1.134x |
| 1K | 66.960 us | 78.180 us | 1.163x | 67.461 us | 82.601 us | 1.216x |
| 2K | 85.881 us | 118.641 us | 1.376x | 86.001 us | 122.641 us | 1.424x |
| 4K | 117.841 us | 208.382 us | 1.765x | 118.981 us | 212.242 us | 1.783x |
| 8K | 208.462 us | 352.583 us | 1.691x | 205.982 us | 354.543 us | 1.719x |
| 16K | 368.483 us | 621.285 us | 1.684x | 366.123 us | 620.106 us | 1.693x |

Subgroup geometric means across all three seeds:

| State | Seed-cells | Geometric-mean speedup | Minimum speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Fresh single sequence | 24 | 1.350x | 1.030x |
| Resumed single sequence | 24 | 1.421x | 1.134x |

### Batched and ragged prefill coverage

| Workload | HIP p50 | Triton p50 | Worst speedup | Worst HIP win rate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| batch-16x1K fresh | 183.582 us | 333.543 us | 1.812x | 100% |
| batch-64x256 fresh | 189.382 us | 323.683 us | 1.708x | 100% |
| ragged-16K fresh | 366.143 us | 461.124 us | 1.256x | 100% |
| resume-4x4K FP32 | 335.363 us | 409.324 us | 1.216x | 100% |

The four batched/ragged cases have a combined geometric-mean speedup of `1.478x`, with a minimum speedup of `1.216x`.

### Numerical and graph validation

Across the 60 primary performance seed-cells:

```text
maximum output relative RMS:      4.936e-3
maximum final-state relative RMS: 4.207e-3
configured tolerance:             4.000e-2
```

The following contract checks also passed:

- public zero-environment routing selected native HIP;
- public routing was storage-bitwise identical to explicit native routing;
- eager and graph-replay output were storage-bitwise identical;
- eager and graph-replay final state were storage-bitwise identical;
- input initial state remained unchanged;
- output and final-state dtype contracts were preserved;
- expected native and Triton graph routes were observed.

### GVA result

GVA functional coverage passed for ratio-2 and ratio-4 configurations, including dense/packed layouts, fresh/resumed state, raw-v3 dispatch, and graph replay.

These GVA results establish functional support only. The primary performance claim remains the equal-head Kimi K3 TP8 prefill matrix above.

Runtime performance reported in this PR was measured on gfx950. The gfx942 implementation is included, but gfx942 runtime performance is not part of this result set.

## Submission Checklist

- [ ] Look over the contributing guidelines at https://github.com/ROCm/ROCm/blob/develop/CONTRIBUTING.md#pull-requests.
```

title: [Kernel][Perf] split-K long-context decode for shuffled fp8 SWA path
body:
## Summary

Adds `aiter/ops/triton/attention/pa_decode_shuffle_perf.py`, a flash-decoding
(split-K) variant of the sliding-window shuffled-fp8 paged decode. The one-pass
kernel (companion PR, `pa_decode_shuffle.py`) runs one program per (sequence, kv
head) and walks the whole windowed key range serially, which underfills the device
at long context. This splits that range into `partition_size` chunks across the grid
and reduces the per-partition softmax state in a second pass. It is gated to engage
only where it actually helps and never regresses the short-context path.

## Motivation

At long context the one-pass per-program key walk gets long while the grid
(`num_seqs * num_kv_heads`) is too small to fill the GPU, so most CUs sit idle. The
asm decode path solves this with page-split kernels, but the asm path can't take a
window (the gfx942/950 `pa/*.co` kernels are prebuilt code objects with no `.s`
source or PA asm generator in the tree, and the registry has only a causal-mask flag,
no window). So the realistic lever for the windowed shuffled-cache path is the triton
kernel, parallelising context the same way the asm page-split kernels do.

## Changes

- New `pa_decode_shuffle_perf.py` with
  `paged_attention_decode_shuffle_swa_perf(...)`: a partition kernel + a reduce
  kernel, plus a one-pass fallback that runs the same algorithm as the companion
  one-pass kernel.
- The split is bounded to `[seq_len - window, seq_len)`, so a windowed layer only
  partitions the keys it actually attends. `max_seq_len` is taken as a host int
  (vLLM already tracks it), so no per-step `.item()` device sync.
- fp32 scratch is reused across decode steps (one buffer per device/shape) so the
  split path doesn't allocate every step.
- Gating (`_pick_n_part` + `_arch_allows_split`): the auto path splits only when the
  grid underfills or the serial walk is long (>= a threshold of partitions), AND only
  on arches where the split is measured to win end to end (gfx950 by default;
  override with `AITER_PA_SHUFFLE_SPLIT_ARCH`). Short context, a full grid, or a
  non-listed arch stays one-pass, so it is identical to the one-pass kernel there.
  `force_split` overrides the gating and is used by the tests to exercise both code
  paths on any arch.

## Performance

Decode tok/s, clock-locked (`perf_determinism`), Mistral-family SWA model
(`sliding_window=4096`), `--max-model-len 8192`, fp8 shuffled KV, `ROCM_AITER_FA`.
Before = one-pass kernel (companion PR), After = this split-K kernel.

MI355X (gfx950), ROCm 7.13 (where the split is enabled by default):

| Configuration | Before (one-pass) | After (split-K) | Improvement |
|---|---|---|---|
| batch 32, ctx ~590 (< window, stays one-pass) | 3573 | 3559 | parity (no split) |
| batch 8, ctx ~6700 (> window, n_part ~16) | 382-385 | 762-820 | ~2.0-2.1x |

At long context split-K is ~2.0-2.1x over one-pass and recovers decode to ~84-90% of
the bf16 baseline (909-913 tok/s); at short context it stays one-pass (parity). The
numbers above are from the 0.19.1 image with the 0.19.1 dispatch.

Re-confirmed on vLLM built from source at main d980a3cc
(0.23.1rc1.dev480+gd980a3cc6, same node, clock-locked), routing through the corrected
main dispatch, zephyr-7b-beta: short (batch 32, ctx ~590) bf16 3679 / one-pass 3470 /
split-K 3452 (parity, stays one-pass); long (batch 8, ctx ~6700, n_part ~16) bf16
~743 / one-pass ~387 / split-K 731 and 786 on two warm runs (~1.9-2.0x over one-pass,
recovering to ~parity with bf16). The first windowed split-K call pays a one-time
triton JIT for the partition grid (544 tok/s cold vs ~759 warm); one-pass and bf16
are stable to ~1%.

MI300X (gfx942), ROCm 7.2.1 (kept one-pass by the arch gate; numbers are with the
gate forced off, to show why):

| Configuration | Before (one-pass) | After (forced split-K) | Improvement |
|---|---|---|---|
| batch 32, ctx <window | ~949 | ~1005 | ~1.06x (within run-to-run spread) |
| batch 8, ctx ~6700 (> window) | ~244 | ~228 | ~0.93x (slightly behind) |

Isolated kernel microbenchmark on gfx942 (clock-locked) is a real win: parity at
short window, ~1.3-1.4x at win1024/ctx2048, ~4.6-6.4x at win4096/ctx8192 and full
causal. But on a dense 7B at these shapes the decode-attention kernel is a small slice
of the step next to the QKV/O projections and the MLP, so the isolated win does not
surface end to end and the extra reduce launch makes it parity-to-slightly-behind.
That is why the auto path keeps gfx942 on one-pass. gfx950's bf16 decode is much
faster (909 vs ~276 tok/s at the same long shape), so the underfilled one-pass kernel
is a far larger fraction of the step there and the split has real headroom.

## Testing

Numerics harness against the independent fp8 reference, both fp8 dtypes
(`e4m3fn`, `e4m3fnuz`), both code paths (`force_split` on and off), full case matrix
(head 128, GQA 32/8 and MQA, block 16/32, windowed and full, per-tensor and per-token)
plus long-context cases that exercise 4-16 partitions. Split-K reproduces the one-pass
result within the fp8 tolerance, so the reduce is not a correctness regression. This
is the same case matrix and ALL_PASS result as the companion one-pass kernel PR.

- MI300X (gfx942): ALL_PASS both dtypes, max abs <= 1.81e-2 vs a 0.18-0.35 quant floor.
- MI355X (gfx950): ALL_PASS both dtypes, max abs <= 1.55e-2 vs the same floor.

- [x] Tested on MI300X (gfx942)
- [x] Tested on MI355X (gfx950)
- [x] Performance benchmarks run (tables above)

## Documentation

Layout, split scheme, and gating are documented in the module docstrings.

title: [Kernel][Triton] sliding-window decode over shuffled fp8 paged KV
body:
## Summary

Adds `aiter/ops/triton/attention/pa_decode_shuffle.py`, a paged decode kernel
that reads the shuffled fp8 KV layout used by the asm `pa_fwd` / `paged_attention_common`
path and applies a sliding-window mask.

## Motivation

The shuffled fp8 layout is written by `reshape_and_cache_shuffle` and consumed at
decode by the asm paged-attention entry point, which takes no window argument. So a
model with sliding-window attention can't use the shuffled cache: the only windowed
fp8 decode is the NHD `paged_attention_v1` path, which uses a different (non-shuffled)
layout. There was no kernel that both reads the shuffled layout and honors a window,
so SWA layers either fall back to NHD or silently compute full attention. This is the
correctness gap the kernel closes; the vLLM side that routes to it is a companion PR.

## Changes

- New `pa_decode_shuffle.py` with `paged_attention_decode_shuffle_swa(...)`. It
  mirrors the shuffled indexing exactly (x = 16 // elem_size, = 16 for fp8):

  ```
  K: [num_blocks, num_kv_heads, head_size // x, block_size, x]
  V: [num_blocks, num_kv_heads, block_size // x, head_size, x]
  ```

  dequantizes fp8 KV to fp32 with the per-tensor or per-token K/V scales (A16W8,
  same as the asm path: query stays 16-bit, only KV is fp8), runs an online-softmax
  decode, and masks keys outside `[seq_len - window, seq_len)`. One program per
  (sequence, kv head); decode only (one query token per sequence).
- No change to existing kernels or call sites; this only adds the new file.

## Performance

Not a perf change. This is a correctness/enablement kernel (windowed shuffled-fp8
decode that did not exist before). The split-K performance variant is a separate PR.

## Testing

Standalone numerics harness against an independent fp8 reference, both fp8 dtypes
(`e4m3fn`, `e4m3fnuz`), across the full case matrix: head 128, GQA 32/8 and MQA,
block 16 and 32, windowed and full, per-tensor and per-token scales.

- MI300X (gfx942), ROCm 7.2.1, torch 2.10: ALL_PASS both dtypes. Max abs error
  kernel-vs-fp8-reference 7.7e-3 to 1.81e-2, while the fp8 quantization noise itself
  is 0.19 to 0.35, so the kernel error sits well under the quant floor.
- MI355X (gfx950), ROCm 7.13, torch 2.10: ALL_PASS both dtypes, max abs error
  <= 1.55e-2 against the same 0.18-0.35 quant floor.

The kernel is plain triton and arch-generic; the two arches cover both fp8 encodings.

- [x] Tested on MI300X (gfx942)
- [x] Tested on MI355X (gfx950)
- [ ] Performance benchmarks (n/a, correctness kernel)

## Documentation

Layout and masking are documented in the module docstring. No user-guide change.

## Dependencies

No new third-party dependencies (triton + torch only).

## Breaking Changes

None. New file only.

title: [CK] [Bugfix] ck_batched_gemm_bf16: derive operand strides from the tensors
body:
### Motivation

The CK `batched_gemm_bf16` wrapper computes all six strides from the operands' logical
shapes:

```cpp
int StrideA = K;  int StrideB = K;  int StrideE = N;
int BatchStrideA = M * K;  int BatchStrideB = N * K;  int BatchStrideE = M * N;
```

That is correct only when all three operands are contiguous in those shapes. CK takes
these as ordinary runtime scalars and supports arbitrary values, so the kernel was never
the limitation — the wrapper simply did not ask the caller what it had allocated.

Two consequences, both reachable from Python with ordinary tensors:

- **A non-contiguous output is written as if it were contiguous.** No error is raised and
  the arithmetic is right, but the results land at the wrong addresses and the returned
  tensor's strides describe a layout the memory does not have. Silent, and it corrupts
  whatever the caller reads next.
- **A weight tensor in `(batch, K, N)` orientation** makes `BatchStrideB = N*K` read well
  past the end of the allocation, surfacing as a HIP illegal memory access rather than as
  a layout error. In our case that wedged the HIP context, which is a good deal harder to
  diagnose than a rejected argument.

This is already known in-tree, and documented as a limitation rather than fixed —
`op_tests/test_batched_gemm_bf16.py` skips the CK path for the transposed input with the
comment *"on the mbn (transposed mbk) input it returns wrong results"*.

### Technical details

Strides are read from the tensors. What the CK descriptors cannot express is rejected
loudly instead of being mis-placed: each operand must be unit-stride in its innermost
dimension, the batch and contraction dimensions must agree, and a stride that would not
fit in the `int` the descriptors take is refused rather than silently truncated.

Second commit: the test stops skipping. Both halves of the defect are reachable by
different calls, so there are two entries — `batched_gemm_bf16_CK` allocates its own
contiguous output and can therefore only exercise the input strides, while placement needs
the op called directly with a preallocated output whose outer strides are not those of a
contiguous `[b, m, n]`. That output is built the same way as the triton path's rather than
with `empty_like`, whose layout preservation depends on the source being non-overlapping
and dense, and its non-contiguity is asserted so a later change cannot quietly leave the
case testing nothing.

Note there are two implementations under the name `batched_gemm_bf16`: this is the CK one
under `csrc/`, not the Triton kernel (which is what #4075's int32 fix touched).

`csrc/ck_batched_gemm_a8w8` carries the same six expressions and the same exposure. It is
left alone here because this change is only verified for bf16; happy to extend it in this
PR if maintainers prefer one fix for both.

### Numerics statement

**Bitwise.** Not "within tolerance" — bitwise, and provable without a numerics argument:
the same kernel runs on the same inputs twice, once into a contiguous output and once into
the strided one, and the strided buffer read back through its intended layout is bitwise
identical to the contiguous result. It is identical arithmetic in identical order, differing
only in store addresses.

Oracle, re-run against **this branch's** header on MI355X (gfx950), one case per process:

| case | result |
|---|---|
| placement, 4 tokens — contiguous strides `[512,128,1]` vs strided `[128,16384,1]` | **bitwise identical**; the consumer's flatten is a view |
| placement, 1 token — `[128,128,1]` vs `[128,16384,1]` | **bitwise identical** |
| reject: `(batch, K, N)` orientation | `RuntimeError` naming the contraction mismatch — **not** a HIP illegal access |
| reject: non-unit innermost output stride | `RuntimeError` naming the layout — **not** a HIP illegal access |

At 1 token the strided destination reports contiguous because dim 1 is degenerate, so the
4-token case is the one that exercises a genuinely strided write. Both are reported rather
than only the stronger one.

The oracle was re-run rather than cited: this branch is a clean-room port, and a port that
quietly downgrades the oracle's tier would be a finding, not a footnote. The module was
rebuilt from this branch's header inside the container to make sure the measured binary is
the one being proposed.

### How the two arms were built, so the comparison can be checked

Both arms run the same digest-pinned container on the same GPU, one case per process. The
**patched** arm bind-mounts this branch's header over the image's copy and a writable AITER
JIT cache from which `module_batched_gemm_bf16` was removed, so that module is recompiled
from the branch's source; the **stock** arm mounts neither the header nor the branch test,
so it runs the image's own source, with a JIT cache whose `module_batched_gemm_bf16` is the
stock build (verified by checksum: stock `414d0c89`, patched `ae031409`).

One honest wrinkle in the stock arm: its JIT cache is a copy of a tree that also carries a
patched *unrelated* module (a KV-cache kernel from other work). This benchmark never calls
it — the test exercises only the CK batched GEMM, the Triton batched GEMM and
`torch.einsum` — so it cannot affect these numbers, but the tree is not a pristine one and
saying so is cheaper than implying it is.

### Test plan and result

`op_tests/test_batched_gemm_bf16.py`, the repo's own harness, on MI355X (gfx950).

`op_tests/test_batched_gemm_bf16.py`, the repo's own harness, on MI355X (gfx950).
24 processes, one case per process, run in randomized order; the first process of each arm
discarded; the figure is the median of the remaining three, and the spread is the full
range across them. `err` is the harness's own `checkAllclose` result.

**The contiguous path is unchanged.** This is the claim that matters for a correctness fix:
reading the strides costs nothing where the old code was already right.

| shape (b, m, n, k) | layout | patched `ck` µs | stock `ck` µs | delta | within-arm spread |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 128, 4, 128, 512 | contiguous | 4.0912 | 4.0740 | **+0.0172 (+0.42%)** | up to 0.0256 |
| 16, 32, 1024, 4096 | contiguous | 27.4383 | 27.4339 | **+0.0044 (+0.02%)** | up to 0.0623 |

At both shapes the patched-versus-stock difference is **smaller than the run-to-run spread
within a single arm**, so this measurement does not resolve a difference — which is the
expected result, since the same kernel runs with the same strides on this path.

**The strided path now runs.** There is deliberately no stock column: upstream's own test
skips CK for this layout because it returns wrong results there, and a timing for a wrong
result is not a baseline.

| shape (b, m, n, k) | layout | patched `ck` µs | patched `ck_out` µs | err |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 128, 4, 128, 512 | strided (transposed mbk) | 4.0884 | 3.8791 | 0 |
| 16, 32, 1024, 4096 | strided (transposed mbk) | 26.8948 | 26.9781 | 0 |

Every case, both arms, all 24 processes: `checkAllclose` passed with `err = 0`, and no
process exited non-zero.

`ck` is `batched_gemm_bf16_CK`, which allocates its own contiguous output; `ck_out` is the
op called directly with a preallocated output, which is the entry the second commit adds and
the only one that exercises placement. At the small shape `ck_out` is consistently the
faster of the two (3.86 against 4.09 µs) because the caller's buffer is reused rather than
allocated per call — an incidental observation, not a claim this PR makes.

title: [FlyDSL] Bind comm-fused GEMM2 to the sorted-inter layout used by stage2
body: ## Summary - Comm-fused GEMM2 always remapped packed sort IDs to route-major `token * topk + slot`. That is wrong when ordinary stage2 is a `flydsl_moe2_layout_*` kernel: `fused_moe` then sets `skip_inter_quant` and stage1 writes sorted-row intermediates, so GEMM2 was reading the wrong A rows. - Host now sets `sorted_input` from the ordinary stage2 kernel name (`"_moe2_layout_" in kernelName`, same predicate as `skip_inter_quant`). The producer drops the row resolver in that case, and the dispatcher allows a composed GEMM2 without a resolver so it uses natural sorted rows. - Tests and the tuner build matching stage2 inputs so DSV4-Pro TP8 buckets that mix layouts (M=1/4/8 sorted, M=2/16 route-major) stay consistent. ## Test plan - [ ] `black --check` and `ruff check` on the six changed files - [ ] Layout predicate vs `get_2stage_cfgs(...).skip_inter_quant` for M=1,2,4,8,16 on DSV4-Pro TP8 (`7168/384/384/6`) — M=1/4/8 sorted, M=2/16 route-major - [ ] 8-GPU `op_tests/multigpu_tests/test_comm_fused_moe.py` per token bucket (1, 2, 4, 8, 16), uniform + skew, eager + graph, plus the M=3→4 `fused_moe` padding path - [ ] On base, M=4 ordinary stage2 still fails (`finite=False`, `max_abs=nan`); on this branch it passes ## Note Same-process multi-bucket runs can still HSA-abort (`0x1016`). That is pre-existing (v2-layout ordinary stage2 vs a second comm-fused runner) and is out of scope here. Run those tests one token bucket per process. ## Result main vs cguo/fix_dsv4 at M=1/2/4/8 — **_same speed._** comm-fused Stage2 latency (µs, max over 8 ranks) — 100 warm-up + 500 timed iterations per run, 3–5 runs per cell. Two data groups per configuration: group 1 = eager, group 2 = graph, each for both routes. How to read it. M=2 is the yardstick: there both branches execute byte-identical code, and it still spans −1.9% … +6.5% (min-based). The sorted buckets M=1/4/8 span −0.6% … +6.7% — the same band. No configuration shows the branch measurably slower than main. Don't read the −15.7% / −8.7% at M=1 skew as the fix being faster: those come from main-side runs spiking high. Both sides spike occasionally (main M=8 skew eager over five runs: 27.6 / 27.6 / 68.4 / 26.8 / 27.4; branch M=1 uniform eager: 27.5 / 40.1 / 27.8), with the ordinary path normal in those same runs — a straggler-rank artifact of max over 8 ranks, independent of branch. Hence the min column is the more robust one.

title: [ASM] [HIP] [OPUS] Add a gfx950 bf16 opus MLA decode path and consolidate the opus decode modules
body:
Adds `opus_mla_decode_fwd`, a bf16 MLA decode path for gfx950, backed by four prebuilt code objects under `hsa/gfx950/mla_opus/`. It consumes aiter's existing persistent metadata (`work_indptr` / `work_info_set`) and leaves the split-KV merge to `mla_reduce_v1`, so it drops into the current decode pipeline unchanged. The path is opt-in behind `AITER_MLA_USE_OPUS=1` and gated on gfx950 with `page_size == 1`, so nothing changes by default.

The kernels are checked in as code objects rather than sources because they need a toolchain aiter does not ship. Selection is by head count:

| heads | code object | heads per workgroup |
|---:|---|---:|
| `H <= 32` | `opus_mla_decode_a16w16_32mx1_16nx4.co` | 32 |
| `H % 128 == 0` | `opus_mla_decode_a16w16_32mx4_32nx1.co` | 128 |
| `H % 96 == 0` | `opus_mla_decode_a16w16_32mx3_32nx1.co` | 96 |
| otherwise | `opus_mla_decode_a16w16_16mx4_64nx1.co` | 64 |

The two `32mx*` variants are where most of the win comes from: putting 32 rows on each compute wave fits a 96- or 128-head block in a single workgroup, so a KV tile is read from HBM once instead of once per head block. `32mx3` spends its fourth wave staging KV rather than computing. On a 96-head shape this alone is worth up to 1.6x against splitting the heads across two workgroups.

## Performance

**All numbers below were measured on top of [PR #5582](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/5582)**, which adds a dedicated `gqa_ratio=96` asm kernel; without it the asm baseline is 15-18% slower and the gap would look correspondingly larger. MI355X, single idle GPU, bf16 Q/KV, `page_size=1`, `max_split_per_batch=32`, causal. Timings are the `decode:asm_576` column, i.e. `aiter.mla.mla_decode_fwd` end to end including the reduce. `decode:err` is 0 on both paths for all 24 configurations. TFLOPS and TB/s are derived from each configuration's `decode:flops` / `decode:bytes`, which depend only on the shape. Use `AITER_MLA_USE_OPUS=0` for the asm baseline in either command.

### Long context, `nhead=96`, `decode_qlen=4`

AITER_MLA_USE_OPUS=1 PYTHONPATH=. python3 op_tests/test_mla_persistent.py -d bf16 -kvd bf16 -n 96,4 -b 32 64 -c 4096 8192 16384 32768 65536 131072

| 4096 | 64 | 285.58 | 248.16 | 1.151x | 767 | 883 | 1.245 | 1.432 |

## Housekeeping

Landing the bf16 entry point needed a home for it, so the opus decode kernels are also collapsed from two JIT modules into one. `module_ds32_mla` (pybind, 3-buffer mxfp8) and `module_opus_mla` (ctypes, merged-buffer fp8) become a single torch-free ctypes module `module_mla_decode_opus`, built from one translation unit `csrc/kernels/mla/opus_mla_decode_fwd.cu` that now holds all three entry points:

| entry point | Q / KV layout |
|---|---|
| `opus_mla_decode_fwd` | bf16, merged `d=576` buffer |
| `opus_mla_decode_mxfp8_fwd` | fp8 NoPE + per-block E8M0 scales + bf16 RoPE, three tensors each |
| `opus_mla_decode_fp8_fwd` | fp8 NoPE and RoPE merged into one `d=576` buffer, per-tensor scalar descales |

That removes `csrc/kernels/mla/ds32_decode_fwd.cu`, `csrc/kernels/mla/mla_decode_fwd_opus.cu`, `csrc/include/mla_opus.h`, `csrc/pybind/mla_ds32_pybind.cu`, the `MLA_DS32_PYBIND` block in `rocm_ops.hpp`, and `csrc/kernels/mla/opus/defs.h`. The remaining headers move onto one naming scheme (`mla_decode_fp8_16mx8_32nx1.hpp`, `mla_decode_mxfp8_16mx8_32nx1.hpp`, `mla_decode_traits.h`) with the kernel argument structs split into `mla_decode_kargs.h`. The mxfp8 and fp8 entry points are renamed accordingly on the Python side; behaviour is unchanged.

title: [ASM] [HIP] Increase the MLA PS mode BF16 nhead96 perf
body:
## Motivation

`gqa_ratio = 96` had no kernel of its own on gfx950 bf16. It was dispatched onto the shared
`gqaratio32` build, which packs the 96 valid Q rows into that build's 128-row tile — so the 4th
wave of every workgroup owns no valid Q row at all, yet still issues its share of the K/V
`ds_read` traffic and competes for LDS bandwidth. Its Q reads came back as buffer-OOB zeros and
its stores were clipped away, i.e. a quarter of the LDS bandwidth was spent producing nothing.

Independently, the metadata packer left performance on the table for this shape. With
`gqa_ratio = 96` and `decode_qlen = 4` a sequence is cut into 4 qo tiles that all read the **same**
KV bytes, and the hardware hands workgroup `i` to XCD `i % num_xcd`. Because `work_indptr` is a
monotone prefix array, work-slot order is workgroup order, so consecutive slots land on *different*
XCDs — the 4 tiles ended up on 4 separate 4 MB L2s and the KV footprint was fetched once per XCD.

## Technical Details

Two independent mechanisms, behind two different gates.

**1. `gqaratio96` assembly kernels** (`hsa/gfx950/mla/`, `mla_asm.csv`, `asm_mla.cu`)

Same SP3 source as `gqaratio32` built with `IDLE_WAVE_SKIP = 1`: the wave whose packed-row band
starts at or past `gqa_ratio * total_qlen` runs the loop body with `exec = 0`. Its `ds_read` /
`buffer_load` / `buffer_store` generate no LDS and no HBM traffic but still issue and still tick
`lgkmcnt`/`vmcnt`, so every `s_waitcnt` budget and `s_barrier` stays exact without hand-editing the
interleaved loop. The cooperative KV DMA still runs on all 64 lanes, so the four DMA helpers
bracket themselves with `exec_all` / `exec_set`.

Eight variants are registered: `{causal, msk0} x {lse, no-lse} x {cprr, no-cprr}`. Dispatch is

```cpp
arch_id == "gfx950" && q_type == "bf16" && kv_type == "bf16" && persistent && gqa_ratio == 96
```

with `config_max_seqlen_q` pinned to 4, so every `max_seqlen_q` maps onto the same `qseqlen4`
build and there is no upper bound to carry. `gqa_ratio == 96` is exact, so nhead 80 and 128 are
untouched.

**2. XCD-affinity metadata planner** (`kn_get_mla_metadata_v1_2_xcd` in `v1_2_device.cuh`,
`num_xcd` / `xcd_lane_works` in `v1_comm.cuh`)

View the workgroups as a `num_xcd`-column grid, `wg = num_xcd*k + r`: same column means same XCD
and a shared L2. The planner makes the unit of assignment the fragment group `(batch, kv range)` —
whose tiles read identical KV — and deals group `g` to lane `g % num_xcd`, so a group's tiles sit
in different rows of one column and share an L2 by construction, independent of fragment count,
kv length and batch count.

The placement is closed form, which is what keeps the planner cheap: group `g` is lane
`r = g % num_xcd`'s `m = g / num_xcd`-th group, so its tile `t` is that lane's local work
`j = m*T + t`; row `k` of lane `r` starts at `j0(r,k) = ceil(k*w_r/rows)`, and inverting gives
`k = j*rows / w_r` directly. So the kernel builds small LDS tables warp-parallel and emits one lane
per group instead of walking the batches serially.

The gate is

```cpp
natively_supported && (num_heads*2 > kPackedQoLenPerWg) && (max_seqlen_qo > 1)
    && (topk < 0) && (num_xcd > 1) && ((num_cu / num_xcd) % max_seqlen_qo == 0)
```

`natively_supported` is read before the `num_heads` fold: a non-native shape becomes
`num_heads = 16, qk_batch_ratio > 1` where a "batch" is one q head group rather than one sequence,
so its tiles do not share KV and there is nothing to win.

The divisibility term is the non-obvious one. A lane hands its `w = q * qo_tiles` works to
`rows = num_cu / num_xcd` workgroups in whole units, so when `rows` does not divide `w` the busiest
workgroup carries `ceil(w / rows)` works against an average of `w / rows` — at `qo_tiles = 3`,
`w = 36` over 32 rows puts 2 works on 4 workgroups and 1 on the other 28, a 1.78x tail. The
batch-major packer never carries that quantum because it cuts fragments to fill each CU's payload
budget exactly. Measured, that tail cost up to 19% against the batch-major packer *despite* perfect
XCD affinity. Cutting KV finer flattens it, but each extra fragment is another reduce partial and
that came out +0.08 percentage points over simply declining those shapes — inside the measurement
resolution. So shapes whose tile count does not divide the rows keep the original packer, and
`qo_tiles` 2, 4 and 8 (on a 256-CU, 8-XCD part) take the planner.

## Test Plan

gfx950 / MI355X, ROCm 7.1. `decode:asm_576` times the whole `mla_decode_fwd` op — decode kernel
plus reduce. Per cell the fastest of 3 reps, the two trees alternating on the same GPU. Baseline is
this PR's merge-base, `eec768a47`.

Correctness, on the tiny-context grid that exercises the fragment math, for every affected
`(nhead, qlen)` and for the msk0 / lse variants:

```bash
# causal, planner-active and planner-declined tile counts
python3 op_tests/test_mla_persistent.py -d bf16 -kvd bf16 \
    -n 48,2 48,3 48,4 80,2 80,3 80,4 96,1 96,2 96,3 96,4 128,2 128,3 128,4 \
    -b 1 2 3 4 5 7 8 16 17 32 64 128 256 \
    -c 4 5 16 17 20 21 32 33 48 49 64 65 127 128 1200 8192

# qlen 5..8 (ctx must be >= qlen; ctx < qlen aborts on the baseline too)
python3 op_tests/test_mla_persistent.py -d bf16 -kvd bf16 -n 96,5 96,6 96,7 96,8 \
    -b 1 2 3 4 5 7 8 16 17 32 64 128 256 \
    -c 8 16 17 20 21 32 33 48 49 64 65 127 128 1200 8192

# the msk0 kernels
python3 op_tests/test_mla_persistent.py -d bf16 -kvd bf16 -n 96,2 96,3 96,4 96,6 96,8 \
    --no-causal -b 1 2 3 4 5 7 8 16 17 32 64 128 256 \
    -c 8 16 17 20 21 32 33 48 49 64 65 127 128 1200 8192

# the lse kernels (checks the LSE values, not just the output)
python3 op_tests/test_mla_persistent.py -d bf16 -kvd bf16 -n 96,2 96,4 96,8 \
    -lse -b 1 2 3 4 5 7 8 16 17 32 64 128 256 \
    -c 8 16 17 20 21 32 33 48 49 64 65 127 128 1200 8192

# fp8, which the planner also reaches (nhead 96 up to qlen 6, nhead 128 any qlen)
python3 op_tests/test_mla_persistent.py -d fp8 -kvd fp8 -n 96,2 96,3 96,4 128,2 128,4 128,8
```

Performance, the test's own default `-b`/`-c` grid over all 26 affected and control shapes, plus
the shape this PR targets and an extra-long case:

```bash
python3 op_tests/test_mla_persistent.py -d bf16 -kvd bf16 -n 96,4 \
    -b 32 64 -c 4096 8192 16384 32768 65536 131072
python3 op_tests/test_mla_persistent.py -d bf16 -kvd bf16 -n 96,4 -b 64 -c 131072
```

The metadata kernel is a single warp and draws no power, so on an idle card it never triggers a
clock boost (`sclk` read 94 MHz at rest) and every scheme collapses to the same number. It was
profiled inside a real decode run instead, so the decode loop holds the clocks up:

```bash
rocprofv3 --kernel-trace --output-format csv -d prof -o meta -- \
    python3 op_tests/test_mla_persistent.py -d bf16 -kvd bf16 -n 96,4 \
        -b 1 3 5 16 32 64 128 256 -c 512 4096
```

## Test Result

**Correctness — no regression, and 0 hard failures anywhere.**

| coverage | kernel exercised | result |
|---|---|---|
| bf16, 19 shapes, default `-b`/`-c` grid (64 cells each) | causal `gqaratio96` + planner | 64/64 passed each, 0 failed |
| bf16 48/80/96/128, tiny-context grid | causal | 208/208 passed, 0 failed |
| bf16 96, qlen 5–8, tiny-context grid | causal | 195/195 passed, 0 failed |
| bf16 96, qlen 2/3/4/6/8, `--no-causal` | `gqaratio96_msk0_ps` | 195/195 passed, 0 failed |
| bf16 96, qlen 2/4/8, `-lse` | `gqaratio96_lse_ps` | output 195/195, **LSE values 195/195** |
