title: [FlyDSL] Add flydsl radix topk one block kernel
body:
## Motivation

This PR adds a FlyDSL one-block radix per-row TopK kernel and wires it into the default dispatch on gfx950, and gfx1250, replacing the HIP one-block path in those cases.

Goals:

- Prefill (variable-length rows described by `row_starts` / `row_ends`) and decode (`seq_lens` / `next_n`) share the same kernel.
- Support any positive integer `k`, optional values output, and deterministic stable mode.
- Keep short-row semantics: when a row has fewer than `k` live elements, pad indices with `-1` and values with `-inf`.
- Replace only the HIP one-block coverage. Existing multi-block paths and other fallbacks stay unchanged, which limits the risk of turning this on by default.

## Implementation

### One-block radix TopK

New file: `aiter/ops/flydsl/kernels/topk/radix_topk_one_block.py`.

- One workgroup per row.
- Short rows (physical width `<= 4096`) cache sorted keys in LDS. Long rows use a radix histogram plus candidate compaction, and fall back to a global-memory rescan if candidates overflow LDS.
- If `row_len <= k`, skip radix selection and copy/pad the output directly.
- gfx1250 uses wave32; gfx950 use wave64.
- Block size depends on short-row width and row count: 256 threads for short rows with `rows <= 256`, otherwise 1024.
- Stable output is sorted by index ascending (smaller index wins ties). Values always stay aligned with the corresponding indices.

### Dispatch

- Prefill: on the non-multi-block branch, try FlyDSL one-block first; fall back to HIP if `_is_flydsl_radix_topk_one_block_supported` returns false.
- Decode: insert the same FlyDSL one-block attempt before the existing path.
- Supported arches are `_FLYDSL_TOPK_ONE_BLOCK_ARCHES = ("gfx950", "gfx1250")`.
- Dispatch reads only physical `logits.shape[1]` and the row count, not device-side row bounds, so it is CUDAGraph-safe.
- This PR does not change the existing `topk_use_mulblocks` multi-block path or per-arch HIP fallbacks.
- New prefill kill-switch; decode reuses the existing one:

```bash
AITER_DISABLE_FLYDSL_TOPK_PREFILL=1   # added in this PR
AITER_DISABLE_FLYDSL_TOPK_DECODE=1    # existing
```

### Layout cleanup

TopK files are grouped into their own subpackages. In this PR these moves are renames only:

- `aiter/ops/flydsl/kernels/topk/` — six kernel modules.
- `aiter/ops/flydsl/topk/` — three launch wrappers.

### Optimizations for concentrated value distributions

Real logits often span a narrow range, so radix bins on float bits collapse onto a few buckets. That causes atomic contention on the first-pass histogram, and more first-pass survivors than the LDS candidate buffer can hold. This PR addresses both:

- **Wider first radix digit.** A finer first pass cuts both surviving candidates and the number of lanes hitting the same bin. At the same LDS cost, this is cheaper than replicating a coarser first pass. Later digits keep the same bin counts, so the candidate buffer is unaffected.
- **Grow the candidate buffer from leftover LDS.** If candidates overflow the buffer, pass 3 and the final emit rescan the full row in global memory (2 global passes become 4). More concentrated distributions hit this more often. The candidate buffer now takes the remaining LDS budget instead of a fixed 4096 entries.
- **Scatter pass-1 atomics by lane.** Histogram replicas are chosen by lane, not by wave: when one bin owns most of a row, a whole wave no longer serializes onto one address. Wave-index replicas only split waves that were already concurrent, which does not help.
- **In-wave reduction for same-bin vectors.** If the four keys from one vector load share the same first-pass digit, ballot-merge the counts in the wave and issue a single atomic add. More concentrated data means neighboring elements share a bin more often.

These changes affect performance only; output semantics are unchanged.

## Correctness

`op_tests/test_topk_per_row.py` now calls the one-block kernel directly (bypassing dispatch). On supported arches, each prefill shape also runs the four stable × write_values combinations, so dispatch changes cannot hide a kernel regression.

Coverage:

- Prefill and decode.
- Full rows, padded rows, and non-zero row starts.
- `next_n=1` and MTP decode.
- Stable and unstable.
- Indices-only and indices+values.
- Random inputs and several degrees of value ties.
- Workspace reuse and CUDAGraph replay.

## How to test

```bash
python -m op_tests.test_topk_per_row
python -m op_tests.test_topk_per_row_stable
```

## Performance

### Method

- Latency after CUDAGraph capture: 3 warmups, 5 alternating HIP / FlyDSL rounds, median. Both HIP and FlyDSL use one-block.
- Full rows, padding, and uneven logits (narrow, single-peak, few discrete values).
- M (rows): 1, 2, 16, 32, 52, 64, 128, 512, 1024, 4096, 16384.
- N (width): 128, 4096, 4097, 16384, 32768, 65536, 98304, 131072, 164401, 200000.
- K: 128, 512, 2048, 4096.

### GFX1250

**Conclusion: default FlyDSL one-block is faster overall, with no systematic regression.**  
775 cases, geomean **1.41×**; 731 faster, 44 slower.

| Scenario | n | Geomean speedup | Faster |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| All | 775 | **1.41×** | 731/775 |
| Prefill | 377 | **1.40×** | 355/377 |
| Decode | 398 | **1.42×** | 376/398 |
| Uneven distribution | 214 | **1.36×** | 210/214 |

Representative points (k=2048, stable+values, full rows):

| rows × width | Prefill | Decode |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 × 4096 | 1.78× | 1.82× |
| 16 × 65536 | 1.51× | 1.37× |
| 64 × 65536 | 1.51× | 1.48× |
| 128 × 131072 | 1.40× | 1.38× |
| 16384 × 4096 | 2.51× | 2.78× |
| 16384 × 200000 | 1.18× | 1.29× |

Of the 44 slower cases, 42 differ by at most 5 µs; the median relative regression is 3.3%. The remaining 2 cases regress by 6.6%–6.9%.

### GFX950

**Conclusion: default FlyDSL one-block is faster overall, with no systematic regression.**  
775 cases, geomean **1.44×**; 741 faster, 34 slower (worst about 0.88×, ~5.5 µs slower).

| Scenario | n | Geomean speedup | Faster |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| All | 775 | **1.44×** | 741/775 |
| Prefill | 377 | **1.44×** | 360/377 |
| Decode | 398 | **1.44×** | 381/398 |
| Uneven distribution | 214 | **1.40×** | 195/214 |

Representative points (k=2048, stable+values, full rows):

| rows × width | Prefill | Decode |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 × 4096 | 1.65× | 1.75× |
| 16 × 65536 | 1.68× | 1.49× |
| 64 × 65536 | 1.67× | 1.69× |
| 128 × 131072 | 1.68× | 1.73× |
| 16384 × 4096 | 2.30× | 2.35× |
| 16384 × 200000 | 1.52× | 1.53× |

Slower cases are mostly large batches that also write values; most are only a few percent slower, typically about 5 µs.

## Checklist

- [x] I have read the contributing guide https://github.com/ROCm/ROCm/blob/develop/CONTRIBUTING.md#pull-requests

title: [CK] [FlyDSL] Add FlyDSL FP8 MoE kernels (decode weight-decompression + prefill) for MI308 — Qwen3.5-35B/397B, Hunyuan3
body:
## Motivation

FP8 MoE on MI308X (gfx942) has overhead from `moe_sorting` and inter-stage
quantization. This PR adds FlyDSL JIT kernels that dequantize FP8 weights
on-the-fly to BF16 for the GEMM, covering both the decode (small-batch,
weight-decompression) and prefill (large-batch) paths. Based on the approach
from #3309, reimplemented as FlyDSL JIT kernels instead of pre-compiled AOT
binaries.

## What's included

- FlyDSL JIT kernels (`aiter/ops/flydsl/kernels/moe_gemm_2stage_gfx942.py`) with
  on-the-fly FP8→BF16 weight decompression for the decode and prefill MoE GEMM.
- End-to-end dispatch: `aiter/fused_moe_gfx942.py` + `aiter/fused_moe.py`
  (`MOEMetadata.stage0` routing of `fused_moe_gfx942` configs).
- Tuner support in `csrc/ck_gemm_moe_2stages_codegen/gemm_moe_tune.py`
  (`--e2e_tune`), plus an `AITER_FMOE_TUNE_EXCLUDE_KERNELS` knob (comma-separated
  kernel-name substrings) to keep a known-bad kernel out of a model's tuned
  config.
- Tuned configs (batch 1…131072) for:
  - Qwen3.5-35B  (dim 2048/128, E=257, topk=9, per_Token fp8)
  - Qwen3.5-397B (dim 4096/128, E=513, topk=11, per_Token fp8)
  - Hunyuan3     (dim 4096/192, E=192, topk=8, per_Tensor fp8)

## Performance (MI308X, gfx942)

Baseline = pre-PR aiter default dispatch; FlyDSL = best tuned config per shape.

† For a few batch sizes (35B: 256/512; 397B: 256/512/1024; Hunyuan3: 256) the
FlyDSL kernel is slower than baseline; the tuner auto-selects the faster CK/asm
kernel there, so end-to-end dispatch never regresses below baseline.

**Correctness:** all tuned shapes pass `op_tests/test_moe_2stage.py`
(cosine-similarity accuracy gate); the FlyDSL kernels are the selected dispatch
for the tuned shapes. For Qwen3.5-397B, one ASM stage1 kernel
(`fmoe_stage1_bf16_pertokenFp8_g1u1_16x64_5tg_pf3`) passes per-stage tuning but
emits NaN **end-to-end** at E=513 — it leaves the padded sorted-token rows
unwritten, which a CK stage2 then reads. It is kept out of the candidate set via
`AITER_FMOE_TUNE_EXCLUDE_KERNELS` so the tuner falls back to an accurate CK
2-stage combo (scoped to the 397B tune; other models are unaffected).

## Tune & Test

Run from the repository root on an idle MI308X/gfx942 GPU 2.
Results are written directly to the corresponding model tuned CSVs.

Explicitly select staged FlyDSL v2, CK, and FlyDSL candidates. ASM is excluded
because large-token stage1 launches may exceed the `grid.y` limit of 65535.

```bash
set -e

export HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=2
export TUNE_ONLY=flydslv2,cktile,flydsl

TUNER=csrc/ck_gemm_moe_2stages_codegen/gemm_moe_tune.py
DIR=aiter/configs/model_configs

for model in \
  qwen3_5_35b_fp8_ptpc \
  qwen3_5_397b_fp8_ptpc \
  hunyuan3_fp8_per_tensor \
  minimax_m3_fp8_ptpc
do
  input="${DIR}/${model}_untuned_fmoe.csv"
  output="${DIR}/${model}_tuned_fmoe.csv"

  export AITER_FMOE_TUNE_EXCLUDE_KERNELS=""
  if [[ "${model}" == "qwen3_5_397b_fp8_ptpc" ]]; then
    export AITER_FMOE_TUNE_EXCLUDE_KERNELS=fmoe_stage1_bf16_pertokenFp8_g1u1_16x64_5tg_pf3
  fi

  # 1. Tune staged baseline.
  python3 "${TUNER}" -i "${input}" -o "${output}" \
    --all --mp 1 --timeout 300

  # 2. Tune whole-graph FlyDSL candidates.
  python3 "${TUNER}" -i "${input}" -o "${output}" \
    --all --e2e_tune --mp 1 --timeout 300

  # 3. Show production dispatch and validate every tuned shape.
  python3 "${TUNER}" --run_config "${output}" --warmup 2 --iters 5
done
```

### Verification

- Inspect `[fused_moe] using ... for (...)` to confirm the selected kernels.
  `impl__flydsl_gfx942__...` identifies a whole-graph FlyDSL configuration;
  `kernelName1`/`kernelName2` identify staged kernels.
- Every expected shape must report `OK`, with no `ERROR`, `MISMATCH`, or `SKIP`.
  A zero exit code alone does not guarantee correctness.

The Qwen3.5-397B exclusion records its known NaN-producing ASM kernel.
It only affects searches that enable ASM; it does not filter whole-graph
e2e candidates.

## Limitations

- MI308X (gfx942) only.

Co-authors: Tingqian.Li@amd.com

title: [HIP] Fix a missing block_reduce barrier and rewrite indexer_qk_rope_quant_and_cache around the wave
body:
Two commits against one file, `csrc/kernels/cache_kernels.cu` (+376 / −151).

## `#1` Fix a missing barrier between `block_reduce` rounds

`block_reduce` stages its cross-wave partials through one block-scoped
`__shared__` buffer and its only barrier sits *after* that write, so two calls of
the same instantiation have to be separated by the caller. Three call sites did
not do that:

- `reshape_and_cache_with_block_quant_kernel`, K amax then V amax
- `reshape_and_cache_with_block_quant_kernel_for_asmpa`, same pair
- `indexer_qk_rope_quant_and_cache_kernel`, the K layernorm mean then variance

In the indexer this silently corrupts `kv_cache`: a raced variance gives a wrong
`inv_std`, so the stored K row does not match its input. Nothing asserts, and it
is occupancy-dependent — it does not reproduce at small launches, which is why
the existing tests never caught it.

One `__syncthreads()` per site, 9 lines total. Cost is within noise (every point
moves less than 0.3%). This commit can be cherry-picked on its own.

## `#2` Rewrite `indexer_qk_rope_quant_and_cache` around the wave

The old kernel launched one 128-thread block per (token, head) and moved 2 bytes
per lane, with a shared-memory round trip and four `__syncthreads()` per block.

- **One wave per block**, `HEAD_DIM / THREADS` dims per lane, so every reduction
  is wave-level and the reduction staging buffer and its barriers are gone.
- **Vectorized q loads**: a lane reads 16 bytes of a q row in one `dwordx4`,
  16 lanes cover a head row, a wave covers 4. FP4 packing loses its lane shuffle
  as a side effect, because both nibbles of an output byte now live in one lane.
- **RoPE pairs exchange in-wave** on the wide instantiation. The narrow one keeps
  the shared-memory exchange, because lane shuffles are the more expensive of the
  two when the launch is small.
- The lane width is a template parameter chosen at launch from `num_tokens` —
  one code path, two instantiations, nothing inspected at run time.

Four invariants that were previously only prose are now `static_assert`s:
`THREADS == ROPE_DIM`, `ROPE_DIM % VEC == 0`,
`!SHARED_ROPE || HEADS_PER_BLOCK == 1`, and
`LANES_PER_HEAD % LANES_PER_GROUP == 0`. Each one guards a silent failure that
would follow from changing a constant.

### Prefill, medians of 3 independent processes

`n_heads=32`

| tokens | fp8 before | after | speedup | fp4 before | after | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2048 | 33.51 us | 23.88 | 1.40x | 36.31 | 27.66 | 1.31x |
| 2560 | 41.92 | 24.12 | 1.74x | 44.63 | 27.68 | 1.61x |
| 3072 | 52.02 | 24.09 | 2.16x | 53.89 | 27.67 | 1.95x |
| 4096 | 69.99 | 28.70 | 2.44x | 74.54 | 27.78 | 2.68x |
| 5120 | 86.58 | 34.68 | 2.50x | 92.38 | 30.69 | 3.01x |
| 6144 | 102.96 | 40.27 | 2.56x | 110.03 | 35.91 | 3.06x |
| 8192 | 136.48 | 51.84 | 2.63x | 145.53 | 46.98 | 3.10x |
| 10240 | 169.68 | 64.84 | 2.62x | 181.71 | 56.49 | 3.22x |
| 12288 | 203.48 | 77.58 | 2.62x | 217.81 | 67.75 | 3.22x |
| 16384 | 273.39 | 99.97 | **2.73x** | 291.93 | 89.08 | **3.28x** |

`n_heads=64`

| tokens | fp8 before | after | speedup | fp4 before | after | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2048 | 69.16 us | 28.36 | 2.44x | 71.75 | 27.76 | 2.58x |
| 4096 | 134.20 | 51.63 | 2.60x | 140.21 | 44.78 | 3.13x |
| 8192 | 265.50 | 97.82 | 2.71x | 277.99 | 84.80 | 3.28x |
| 12288 | 462.22 | 158.38 | 2.92x | 417.50 | 126.41 | 3.30x |
| 16384 | 628.86 | 213.00 | **2.95x** | 650.69 | 191.51 | **3.40x** |

Below about 4096 tokens at `n_heads=32` the per-launch cost has not amortized and
the kernel is not memory-bound, which is why 2048 shows 1.40x and 16384 shows
2.73x. Baselines were measured in the same batch, on the same node, with the same
protocol as the after column.

### Decode, 1-64 tokens

No regression: all 24 configurations (both modes x Q-only and KV-append x
1/8/32/64 tokens) land between **1.01x and 1.16x**, measured under graph replay.

### Where the width switch changes over

Both instantiations forced, fp8, medians of 3 processes:

| tokens | narrow | wide | wide/narrow | selected |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 64 | 3.595 us | 4.023 | 1.119x | narrow |
| 128 | 3.716 | 4.372 | 1.177x | narrow |
| 256 | 4.462 | 4.755 | 1.066x | narrow |
| 512 | 6.477 | 5.837 | 0.901x | wide |
| 1024 | 10.087 | 8.822 | 0.875x | wide |
| 2048 | 24.530 | 24.082 | 0.982x | wide |

Narrow wins at every size at or below 256 and wide at every size above it, so the
threshold is 256. Re-measured after the decode fix, since that made the narrow
instantiation faster and could have moved the crossover.

## Output equivalence

384 output tensors compared byte for byte over the full ABI surface, three
repeats, covering both instantiations, with a control confirming the reference is
deterministic.

- `q_out`, `q_scale_out`, `weights_out`: **0 differences**.
- **All FP4 output byte-identical**, including `kv_cache` and `kv_cache_scale`.
- fp8 `kv_cache`: one byte in 4 of 384 tensors, only at 16384 x 64, `14 -> 15` in
  e4m3 = 1 ULP. One K element in 2.1 M, on dim 100, which never rotates.

Four candidate causes for that byte were each tested by building and counting
bytes, and each is excluded: sum association in both directions, and FMA
contraction in the layernorm, in the K RoPE line and in the store multiply.

It changes nothing the indexer selects. Both `kv_cache` versions were
dequantized, the MQA logits formed, and the selected index sets compared:
**0 of 512 queries differ** at k = 64, 256, 512, 1024 and 2048, across all four
affected configurations.

## Testing

`op_tests/test_indexer_qk_rope_quant_and_cache.py --mode fp8 fp4 e2e` passes on
gfx950 for both instantiations. No test files are modified by this PR.

title: [Bugfix] Prevent resource leaks on repeated hipBLASLt extension initialization
body:
## Summary

Make hipBLASLt extension initialization idempotent on its owning device and
allow safe destruction followed by re-initialization. Repeated initialization
currently overwrites live global resources and leaks device memory.

## Motivation

`hipb_create_extension()` creates a hipBLASLt handle, allocates a 256 MiB device
workspace, and creates a matmul preference on every call. The previous pointers
are overwritten without being released, so a later `hipb_destroy_extension()`
can free only the most recent resource set.

A downstream tuning loop exposed this by initializing once per shape. The
problem also reproduces independently of that tuner on upstream AITER: four
additional initialization calls consumed 1,130 MiB on MI250. A separate minimal
probe of the installed build measured exactly 282 MiB per additional call,
including the explicit 256 MiB workspace and 26 MiB not separately attributed.

AITER's GEMM tuner and tuned GEMM runtime already guard their initialization
calls independently. Making the native resource owner handle repeated calls
prevents accidental resource loss without requiring every caller to maintain
its own initialization flag.

## Technical Details

### Changes

- Track the device owning the module's existing resource set, with `-1`
  representing the uninitialized state.
- Return without allocating on repeated initialization for that device.
- Raise `RuntimeError` if initialization is requested on another device while
  the existing resources are still live. The original resources remain usable.
- Make destruction a no-op when uninitialized, including after a prior destroy.
- Destroy resources on their owning device and restore the caller's current
  device with `HipDeviceGuard`.
- Clear resource pointers and reset the device state after successful teardown.
- Document lifecycle expectations in the Python API and add a standalone
  regression test in `op_tests/test_hipblaslt_lifecycle.py`.

The module continues to hold one resource set at a time. Lifecycle entry points
retain the Python GIL. Callers must synchronize outstanding GEMMs before
teardown. Existing fatal HIP/hipBLASLt allocation-error handling is unchanged;
this patch does not introduce recoverable allocation failures or a per-device
resource pool. GEMM kernel computation and solution selection are unchanged.

### The sibling entry point was checked and is not affected

`gradlib/csrc/rocsolgemm.cu` exposes the same shape of entry point,
`rocb_create_extension()`. It is not affected and is left unchanged: its body is
entirely commented out, so it creates no handle, allocates no workspace and owns
no state that a repeated call could overwrite. No other `*_create_extension`
entry point in `gradlib/csrc/` holds resources.

### Two implementation choices worth calling out

**`aiter_detail::g_aiter_can_throw` is set in `hipb_create_extension()`.** The
cross-device rejection is reported through `AITER_CHECK`, which reaches
`aiter_check_fatal`. That flag is `inline thread_local bool ... = false`, so
without setting it the rejection would abort the process instead of raising
`RuntimeError`, and the documented recovery path — destroy, switch device,
initialize again — would not be reachable from Python. The bare set matches the
existing usage in `csrc/opus_gemm/opus_gemm.cu`. It is deliberate, and it is a
side effect on the calling thread: after the first initialization on that thread,
subsequent AITER fatal checks raise rather than abort. If maintainers prefer the
save-and-restore discipline used by `aiter_safe_call()` in
`csrc/include/aiter_ctypes_error.h`, that would need a scope guard so the value
is restored on the throwing path as well; say the word and it will be changed.

**`HIP_CALL` is used for the new `hipGetDevice()` call** while the surrounding
pre-existing lines keep `CHECK_HIP_ERROR`. `HIP_CALL` routes into
`aiter_check_fatal`, the same error path as the `AITER_CHECK` immediately below
it, so the two new failure modes report consistently. `CHECK_HIP_ERROR` is
gradlib's local macro and is left untouched on every line that already used it.

## Test Plan

Run on an idle ROCm GPU in fresh processes, with separate JIT caches for the
baseline and patched builds. The test defaults to four repeated calls so that
running it on an unfixed build consumes about 1.1 GiB rather than exhausting VRAM.

```bash
# Regression and lifecycle tests, including FP16/BF16 and bias/no-bias.
python op_tests/test_hipblaslt_lifecycle.py

# Longer repeated-init check on the patched build.
python op_tests/test_hipblaslt_lifecycle.py --iterations 300

# Opt-in two-device coverage; indices refer to visible devices.
python op_tests/test_hipblaslt_lifecycle.py --device 0 --other-device 1

# Run the new test through AITER's CI test driver.
AITER_TEST=op_tests/test_hipblaslt_lifecycle.py bash .github/scripts/aiter_test.sh
```

Numerical checks build the reference in FP32 and cast it to the output dtype
before comparing, with `rtol=0, atol=0`. That is safe here rather than a
precision trap: inputs are integers in `[-2, 2]`, so every partial product and
every partial sum is exact in FP32, and both the reference and the hipBLASLt
result are therefore rounded exactly once from the same exact FP32 value when
they are written out in FP16/BF16. The comparison is not calibrated against a
higher-precision baseline; it compares two values that must be bit-identical.
The checks cover both heuristic selection (`solution_index=-1`) and an explicit
solution returned by `hipb_findallsols()`, before and after lifecycle
transitions.

## Test Result

Base: `ed5fc689b6a0872372d7010d0776e721e9ea9e56`. `gradlib/csrc/hipbsolgemm.cu`
and `aiter/ops/gradlib.py` are byte-identical at that commit and at
`9b410476af86cdd35328ba054b29827a64933b4b`, so these results still describe the
patch as it applies to current `main`.
Hardware: MI250 (`gfx90a`). Environment: ROCm 7.2.3 container,
PyTorch `2.11.0+gitd0c8b1f`, `torch.version.hip=7.2.53211`, Python 3.12.
Baseline and patched hipBLASLt modules were built from source with separate,
initially empty JIT caches and `GPU_ARCHS=gfx90a`.

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Upstream baseline, four additional init calls | Expected regression failure: 1,184,890,880 bytes (1,130 MiB) lost |
| Patched, four additional init calls via CI driver | PASS: 2 MiB difference, below the 16 MiB tolerance |
| Patched, 300 additional init calls | PASS: the same 2 MiB difference, without growth proportional to call count |
| FP16/BF16 GEMM, bias/no bias, heuristic/explicit solution | PASS with exact numerical comparison |
| Three destroy/re-init cycles and repeated destruction | PASS; workspace released and allocated again each cycle |
| Rejected cross-device init preserves original GEMM resources | PASS |
| Destruction from another current device preserves that current device | PASS |
| Initialization and GEMM on the second device after teardown | PASS |
| Repository pre-commit hook, Black, Ruff, whitespace check | PASS for the patch |

Representative regression output:

```text
# Upstream baseline (expected failure)
Repeated init: before=67926753280, after=66741862400, loss=1184890880
AssertionError: Repeated init leaked device memory

# Patched, --iterations 300
Repeated init: before=67926753280, after=67924656128, loss=2097152
Destroy/re-init cycle 1: PASS
Destroy/re-init cycle 2: PASS
Destroy/re-init cycle 3: PASS
hipBLASLt lifecycle: PASS

# Patched, two-device check
Device rejection, owner-device destruction, and device migration: PASS
hipBLASLt lifecycle: PASS

# Repository CI driver, AITER_TEST=op_tests/test_hipblaslt_lifecycle.py
All tests passed in shard 0.
```

The original 398-shape downstream tuning workload was not re-run. These tests
establish the isolated repeated-init leak and validate the native fix, without
claiming that the leak was the sole cause of the historical tuning OOM.

No gfx942 or gfx950 hardware was available locally, so no results on those
architectures are claimed here. `op_tests/test_hipblaslt_lifecycle.py` is placed
at the top level of `op_tests/`, which is where `.github/scripts/aiter_test.sh`
collects files with `find op_tests -maxdepth 1 -type f -name "*.py"`, so the
standard per-PR op-test job should exercise it on gfx942 and gfx950 without an
opt-in label. The test is single-GPU by default; the two-device path only runs
when `--other-device` is passed explicitly.

One property of the test is worth a reviewer's judgement: its memory assertions
read absolute free memory with `torch.cuda.mem_get_info()` and allow 16 MiB of
slack. `mem_get_info` is already used by `test_batch_prefill.py`,
`test_gated_delta_rule.py` and `test_moe_2stage.py`, but this test additionally
*asserts* on the delta, so it assumes the GPU is not shared with another process
for its duration. If CI runners can be shared, the tolerance should be raised or
the assertion scoped to the workspace-sized step rather than an absolute delta.

The existing `test_gemm_a16w16.py` also hit gfx90a limitations on both the
baseline and patched builds: shape `(16, 256, 256)` could not select an ASM
kernel, and `(16, 96, 256)` selected a skinny path whose `module_custom` build
uses an FP8 instruction unavailable on gfx90a. Shape `(33, 96, 256)` avoided
those paths but failed because the Triton GEMM default config for gfx90a is
absent. These failures are not counted as passing tests; these paths are not
modified by this patch. Full-suite success is not claimed.

### Testing checklist

- [x] Regression test added under `op_tests/`.
- [x] Patched hipBLASLt module built successfully from source.
- [x] Correctness, memory, lifecycle, and two-device tests passed on MI250.
- [x] Before/after performance measurements completed.
- [ ] Upstream CI on gfx942/gfx950 completed.

## Performance

BF16 GEMM on MI250, using the same shapes and inputs in separate baseline and
patched processes. Six processes were run in A/B/B/A/A/B order. Each process
reported the median of seven HIP-event samples, each timing ten replays of a
64-GEMM graph. The table reports the median of three process medians per variant.
Negative latency change means faster. These small differences do not establish
a speedup or a material GEMM regression.

| M, N, K | Baseline (µs) | Patched (µs) | Latency change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 16, 256, 256 | 4.369 | 4.352 | -0.40% |
| 128, 1024, 1024 | 9.455 | 9.466 | +0.12% |
| 1024, 1024, 1024 | 26.538 | 26.512 | -0.10% |

A complete create/destroy pair measured 220.62 µs before and 214.34 µs after
(median of three process medians, ten cycles per process). These host timings
are noisy and no lifecycle speedup is claimed. The intended improvement is
bounded memory consumption on repeated initialization. Kernel bandwidth and
roofline analysis are not applicable to this resource-lifecycle change.

## Documentation

- [x] Updated create/destroy API docstrings, including synchronization and
  device-change expectations.
- User and performance guides: no changes needed for this lifecycle fix.

## Dependencies

- [x] No new third-party dependencies added.

## Breaking Changes

No Python function signatures change. Direct re-initialization on a different
device while the previous resource set is live now raises `RuntimeError`
instead of replacing and leaking those resources. To move to another device,
synchronize outstanding work, destroy the extension, select the new device,
and initialize again. Same-device repeated initialization and repeated
destruction are now no-ops.

## Submission Checklist

- [x] Look over the contributing guidelines at https://github.com/ROCm/ROCm/blob/develop/CONTRIBUTING.md#pull-requests.
- [x] Follow AITER's `CONTRIBUTE.md` and prepare the change against `main`.
- [x] Pass applicable local pre-commit, formatting, and lint checks.
- [x] Include regression tests, test results, and applicable benchmarks.
- [x] Document the final lifecycle behavior and compatibility impact.
- [x] Author commits carry the DCO `Signed-off-by` line (`git commit -s`).
- [ ] Required upstream CI checks pass.

title: [CK] Add GLM-5.2 (TP4) a8w8 blockscale GEMM tunings for gfx942 (MI300X/MI325)
body:
## Summary

Model: zai-org/GLM-5.2-FP8

- Add tuned FP8 blockscale GEMM configs (155 shapes) for GLM-5.2 at TP4 on MI300X/MI325 (gfx942)
- Shapes are N=6144 with K in {3072, 4096, 6144}, M from 1 to 16384 — the row-parallel
projections whose K doubles relative to TP8. The existing glm5_1 config only covers the
TP8 K values, so these shapes currently fall back to the default CK kernel on a TP4
deployment.
- Sorted GEMM configs
- Expand the gfx942 CK-Tile candidate list from 2 to 20 tile configurations so CK-Tile can
actually compete with CK legacy on this arch (thanks @ThomasNing — [CK Tile] Expand gfx942 blockscale GEMM instances jin-amd/aiter#1)
- Build the CK-Tile name registry from every arch list rather than only the one `get_gfx()`
selects, so a multi-arch wheel can resolve tuned rows for all of its targets
- Add CPU-only tests pinning the gfx942 tile matrix and the BlockPerCu expansion

Tuned with `csrc/ck_gemm_a8w8_blockscale/gemm_a8w8_blockscale_tune.py --libtype both`.
All shapes tuned with errRatio 0.0. CK legacy wins all but one; CK-Tile wins
(M=1, N=6144, K=6144) at 19.59us versus 21.73us for the best CK legacy kernel — a win that
only became reachable once the gfx942 CK-Tile tile list was expanded.

## Overlap with the GLM-5.3-Flash configs

The sweep originally covered 174 shapes. `a8w8_blockscale_tuned_gemm_glm5_3_flash.csv`
subsequently landed in main via #5343 and tunes the same
gfx942 / cu_num=304 / N=6144 / K=4096 shapes, so 19 of those rows duplicated it on the
runtime merge key `(M, N, K, cu_num, gfx)`.

That is a hard failure rather than a silent preference: `AITER_CONFIGS.get_config_file()`
merges every matching model CSV, and `update_config_files()` rewrites the source files and
raises on a duplicate shape. Those 19 rows are dropped here and the GLM-5.3-Flash table is
left untouched, leaving 155 shapes. 17 of the 19 had already selected the identical kernel
in both tuning runs, and the two that differ disagree by under 2% across separate runs, so
no measurable coverage is lost.

## Multi-arch build fix

Expanding the gfx942 CK-Tile list exposed a latent bug in
`gemm_a8w8_blockscale_cktile_instance.py`. In a multi-arch build
(`GPU_ARCHS="gfx942;gfx950"`), `build_tune_dict` keeps tuned rows for every target because
it filters on `get_build_targets()`, but the candidate registry was built from the single
list that `get_gfx()` selects — and `get_gfx()` resolves a multi-arch `GPU_ARCHS` to its
last entry. Rows tuned for the other arch therefore had no registry entry, and the build
aborted rather than emit a `.so` that would `TORCH_CHECK(false, ...)` at runtime.

This stayed latent because the only pre-existing gfx942 CK-Tile tuned row in the repo names
a tile that happens to exist in both arch lists. The winner above (`16x64x512`) exists only
in `kernels_list_942`.

`candidate_kernels_by_name` is now built from every arch list. The arch-specific
`candidate_kernels_cktile_dict` used for tuning is unchanged, so kernel IDs and sweep
behavior are identical.

## Tested

- Cross-file dedup across all `*a8w8_blockscale_tuned_gemm*.csv` — 0 duplicates
(12 files, 40,122 merged rows, dedup key `(M,N,K,cu_num,gfx)`)
- Verified no overlap with any existing a8w8_blockscale GEMM config on any arch,
including gfx950 — all 155 shapes are new to the family, none are re-tunes
- Replayed the runtime merge (`get_config_file` globbing plus the untuned-derived dedup
key) for every tuned config family that has `model_configs/` entries; all GEMM families
are collision-free
- Under `GPU_ARCHS="gfx942;gfx950"`, `build_tune_dict` resolves all CK-Tile tuned rows
in the merged config set, and `gen_instances_cktile.py` runs to completion and emits
`gemm_a8w8_blockscale_cktile_lookup.h`
- The newly reachable `16x64x512` instance compiles cleanly for both targets
(`--offload-arch=gfx942 --offload-arch=gfx950`), alongside a gfx950-list control instance
- Isolated GEMM benchmark vs the default kernels, measured over the original 174-shape
sweep (19 of which are now covered by the GLM-5.3-Flash table instead):
  - decode sizes (M <= 256, 105 shapes) median 1.62x
  - prefill sizes (M > 256, 69 shapes) median 3.22x
  - all 174 shapes median 1.79x
- End-to-end vLLM serving A/B on 4x MI325X, 131072 in / 1024 out, images identical
apart from this config: +7.9% total token throughput, -5.8% median TPOT,
-7.4% median TTFT at concurrency 2/4/6

title: [Config] [GEMM] Tune GLM-5.2 native-MTP M=4 projections for gfx950
body:
## Motivation

GLM-5.2's native-MTP target verification pass uses `M=4` at the
single-request serving point. A production TP8 graph showed five BF16
projection shapes that were absent from the model's tuning input. Current
AITER `main`, including ROCm/AITER#5328, already has exact tuned rows for two
of them, but the other three still fall back to the generic Torch path.

This change records all five production shapes in the GLM-5.2 tuning input,
adds the three missing gfx950 winners, and updates one existing row only after
it clears the tuner's 3% current-main comparison gate. The newer upstream
`(4, 6144, 1536)` row is retained because its fresh candidate was only 0.5%
faster.

No model-specific dispatch logic is added; this is tuning data consumed by
AITER's existing GEMM selector.

## Technical details

The multi-backend tuner evaluated 4,704 correctness-filtered candidates on an
MI355X against AITER `0923a53ea6c4609fa85a165ccc8b3236b43d0d4e`. The accepted
rows all resolve to FlyDSL.

| M, N, K | Current-main state | Runtime before | Runtime after | Change | Result |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 4, 512, 6144 | Torch fallback | 10.17 us | 5.87 us | -42.30% | add |
| 4, 2048, 2048 | tuned Triton | 6.34 us | 6.01 us | -5.29% | replace |
| 4, 3072, 6144 | Torch fallback | 11.62 us | 10.38 us | -10.70% | add |
| 4, 6144, 256 | Torch fallback | 5.37 us | 3.91 us | -27.15% | add |
| 4, 6144, 1536 | tuned FlyDSL | 6.47 us | 6.43 us | -0.51% | keep current |

These are the tuner's end-to-end runtime measurements through
`gemm_a16w16`, not the kernel-only `us` field stored in the CSV. Pre- and

title: [Triton/Gluon] Tune gfx950 FP8 MQA prefill dispatch
body:
## Summary

Tune gfx950 FP8 MQA prefill dispatch for `M=4096, H=32, D=128` using eight sweep-selected configurations. The selected configurations reduced latency by 8.03%–31.19% in the measurements below.

## Motivation

For these prefill shapes, the current gfx950 heuristic processes one query row per workgroup and uses the same KV tile and occupancy hint across all measured N values. The sweep found faster configurations using two query rows per workgroup, larger KV tiles for long sequences, and reduction-chain counts selected by N and `clean_logits`.

## Changes

- Modify only the gfx950 dispatch in `aiter/ops/triton/attention/fp8_mqa_logits.py` for `M=4096, H=32, D=128`, `N={4096,16384,65664,131072}`, and both `clean_logits=True/False`.
- Select `BLOCK_M=2` for all four measured KV lengths, `BLOCK_KV=128` for N=65664/131072, and `waves_per_eu` and `NUM_CHAINS` by N and `clean_logits`.
- Apply the measured buckets to contiguous FP8 E4M3FN Q/KV, FP32 scales/weights, and INT32 window bounds, on Triton 3.7 with distributed-layout async copy and folded reduction support.
- Retain the old heuristic for uncovered shapes, layouts, dtypes, compiler versions, and feature combinations, including the existing Triton 3.8 register-spill workaround.

## Performance

The results below are local configuration-selection measurements on Triton 3.7 / gfx950, not CI results.

### Measurement environment and source

- Environment: gfx950 / Triton 3.7, with clocks unlocked.
- Source: ROCm/aiter PR [#5434](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/5434), `op_tests/test_mqa_logits.py`. The local sweep reused its input construction and `aiter.test_common.run_perftest`; the script, sweep driver, and CSV files are not included in this PR.
- Timing: 2 warmups and 101 calls per measurement; results are medians from three independent processes. The default `(BM,BKV,W,C)` is `(1,64,3,1)`.

### Shapes and timing

Fixed `M=4096, H=32, D=128`, with Q shaped `[M,H,D]`, KV `[N,D]`, and row i's valid window `[0,N-M+i+1)`. Seed 0 inputs use BF16 normal Q cast to FP8 E4M3FN, per-token quantized FP8 KV with FP32 scales, and FP32 weights. Output rows are padded to a multiple of 256 columns.

Each measurement uses 2 warmups and 101 calls through `run_perftest`, summing GPU profiler kernel durations per invocation, discarding the first iteration and IQR outliers. Calls reuse the same inputs. Input generation, quantization, and reference computation are outside timing. `clean_logits=True` includes output clearing; False omits clearing and does not include downstream masking. These are GPU kernel times, not host wall-clock latency.

The sweep evaluated `BM={1,2}`, `BKV={32,64,128}`, `W={2,3,4}`, `C={1,2,4}`: 54 configurations per N and clean mode. For each combination, the lowest measured latency among configurations passing accuracy checks determined the selection. Default and selected configurations were then remeasured in three independent processes; the table reports their medians. These are the selection measurements, not a new performance run of this commit.

BM/BKV/W/C denote `BLOCK_M/BLOCK_KV/waves_per_eu/NUM_CHAINS`. The default is `(1,64,3,1)` in every row; `num_warps=2`, `NUM_BUFFERS=2`, and `UNROLL=2` throughout.

| N | clean_logits | Selected (BM,BKV,W,C) | Default (μs) | Selected (μs) | Latency reduction | Selected TFLOPS | Selected TB/s |
| ---: | :---: | :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 4096 | True | (2,64,2,1) | 71.669 | 65.912 | 8.03% | 1042.852 | 1.288859 |
| 4096 | False | (2,64,3,2) | 61.420 | 54.440 | 11.36% | 1262.599 | 0.944242 |
| 16384 | True | (2,64,2,1) | 399.883 | 335.493 | 16.10% | 1433.868 | 0.858138 |
| 16384 | False | (2,64,2,2) | 346.291 | 301.284 | 13.00% | 1596.678 | 0.844232 |
| 65664 | True | (2,128,2,2) | 1857.917 | 1440.587 | 22.46% | 1481.768 | 0.766289 |
| 65664 | False | (2,128,2,4) | 1569.104 | 1221.959 | 22.12% | 1746.880 | 0.874221 |
| 131072 | True | (2,128,2,2) | 3888.200 | 2886.358 | 25.77% | 1499.933 | 0.756000 |
| 131072 | False | (2,128,2,4) | 3575.558 | 2460.491 | 31.19% | 1759.544 | 0.873216 |

For valid query–KV pair count V and latency t in μs, TFLOPS is `2×H×D×V/(t×10^6)`. TB/s estimates Q/KV/scales/weights bytes plus output bytes, divided by `t×10^6`; output bytes are `4×M×N_padded` for True and `4×V` for False. This is an effective byte estimate, not a hardware bandwidth counter. Performance outside the measured shapes and causal windows has not been characterized.

## Testing

Run the existing test module from the patched repository root in the environment above:

```bash
export ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1
export AITER_TRITON_ONLY=1
export PYTHONPATH="$PWD"
python -m pytest -q op_tests/triton_tests/attention/test_fp8_mqa_logits.py
```

The existing test module's shape list does not exercise the eight new M=4096 dispatch buckets. MI250X and MI300X were not tested.

## Documentation

- [ ] Docstrings updated — not needed; the public interface and output semantics are unchanged.
- [ ] User guide updated — not needed; no new user-facing configuration is introduced.
- [ ] Performance guide updated — no repository guide changes; measurement environment, methodology, and results are documented in this PR description.

## Dependencies

- [x] No new third-party dependencies added.

PR #5434's test script was used as the measurement source described above; this change does not require that PR to be merged or add its script as a runtime dependency.

## Breaking Changes

None. The public API, kernel arithmetic, output allocation, and `clean_logits` semantics are unchanged. No migration is required.

title: [Triton/Gluon] [Bugfix][MLA] Mask the >2GB global_load path in mla_gluon decode (fixes gfx950 IMA)
body:
## Problem
On gfx950, serving **Kimi-K2.6** (8 heads/rank @ TP8, `kv_lora_rank=512`, bf16 KV) with vLLM crashes at decode warmup with a GPU **illegal memory access** inside the Gluon MLA decode kernel (`mla_gluon`). Its paged KV cache is far larger than 2 GB, so the wrapper sets `within_2gb=False` and KV is loaded via `global_load_to_shared` (64-bit offsets) instead of `buffer_load_to_shared`.

## Root cause
The `>2GB` `global_load_to_shared` calls (the `else` of each `if WITHIN_2GB:`) dropped the bounds `mask` that their `buffer_load_to_shared` siblings carry. The last partial split block then dereferences out-of-bounds KV rows -> IMA. Additionally, `buffer_load` returns `0` for masked lanes while `global_load` leaves them undefined, so a mask alone yields **NaNs** on partial blocks -- `other=0.0` is required to match `buffer_load` semantics.

Introduced by #4474 (which added the int64 `>2GB` global_load path) -- bisected: that commit is the first to fault, its parent passes. The missing mask has persisted through `v0.1.22.post1`.

## Fix
Add `mask=<same predicate as the buffer_load sibling>, other=0.0` to all 8 `global_load_to_shared` calls in `_mla_gluon`.

## Test
Adds `test_mla_gluon_decode_over_2gb` to `op_tests/triton_tests/attention/test_mla.py`. It drives a >2 GB cache through the `global_load` path and asserts finiteness + bit-parity against the `<2GB` `buffer_load` reference on identical KV, across full and partial-block configs.

```
pytest op_tests/triton_tests/attention/test_mla.py -k test_mla_gluon_decode_over_2gb
# 10 passed  (batch,ctx) in {(4,1024),(1,1300),(8,777),(2,4096),(16,513)} x nhead {8,16}
```

Validated on MI350 (gfx950): output matches the buffer_load reference (`max_abs_diff=0.0`); the standalone repro goes from memory-access-fault -> clean, and **Kimi-K2.6 `-tp 8` now serves** on upstream vLLM.

AI assistance was used; changes were human-reviewed.

title: [Triton/Gluon] [Config] gfx942: fix unified-attention prefill config for head_size >= 512 (Gemma-4 full-attention layers)
body:
## Summary

Adds one gfx942 `attn_2d` entry so that prefill on layers with `head_size >= 512` (Gemma-4's ten full-attention layers: head_dim 512, 32 q / 4 kv heads) stops running on configs that were never right for that shape:

```json
"D_GEQ_512.Q_GEQ_256": {"BLOCK_M": 64, "num_warps": 4, "num_stages": 2, "waves_per_eu": 2, "TILE_SIZE_MIN": 16, "TILE_SIZE_MAX": 16}
```

Measured on MI325X (gfx942), fp8 q + fp8 paged KV, block 64, one causal sequence, cache flushed before every call, median of 7, same kernel body for every row (config is the only variable):

| tokens | pre-#4044 default (M128 / T64) | current table (M16 / T32) | this entry (M64 / T16) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4096 | 7.80 ms | 2.95 ms (2.64x) | 2.09 ms (3.74x) |
| 16384 | 115.8 ms | 44.7 ms (2.59x) | 26.0 ms (4.45x) |

End to end in vLLM (`ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN`, gemma-4-31B FP8-block, 16k-token cold prefill): the ten layers go from 107 to 24.7 ms each, prefill wall time -32%, prefill throughput +47% in a same-GPU A/B. Output relative error vs. the current config 6e-3 (bf16 output noise); lm_eval IFEval / GSM8K unchanged within noise.

## What is wrong today, version by version

| version | config selected for Gemma-4 fp8 prefill on gfx942 | 16k tokens, per layer | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| before #4044 (<= v0.1.19) | head-256 defaults, BLOCK_M 128 / TILE 64 | 115.8 ms | no head-512 branch. At head 512 the K and V tiles are 32 KB each, so one workgroup owns the CU's whole 64 KB LDS, one workgroup per CU, ~6% MFU |
| #4044 (v0.1.19.post1+) | head >= 512 branch: TILE 16 / stages 2 / warps 4, but BLOCK_M 16, and placed before the fp8 clamp `TILE_SIZE = max(32, TILE_SIZE)` -> fp8 gets TILE 32 | 44.7 ms | (1) the clamp belongs to the pre-shuffled A8W8 KV branch (`block_size >= 32` assert there); applied to plain fp8 at head 512 it pushes LDS back to 32 KB per stage. (2) BLOCK_M 16 = 2 query positions per program at nqpkv 8: each K/V tile is re-read 8x and the QK^T M-dimension starves the MFMA units |
| #5088 (v0.1.21+, JSON tables) | fp8: `D_GEQ_512.DT_fp8_fp8` = BLOCK_M 16 / TILE_SIZE_MIN 32; bf16: `D_GEQ_512` = BLOCK_M 16 / TILE 16 | fp8 44.7 ms; bf16 entry 198 ms | the clamp survived as `TILE_SIZE_MIN 32` on the fp8 keys; the lookup resolves the D axis before Q, so `Q_GEQ_256` (BLOCK_M 128) is unreachable for head >= 256 (#5063 reports the same). The bf16 entry M16/T16 is 0.58x of the pre-#4044 default |

## Why these values, and why the entry is conditional

The head-512 slowdown is an LDS occupancy cliff, not an MFMA-shape problem. LDS per workgroup scales with TILE x head_size x bytes x (K + V) x stages; the default fills the 64 KB per CU exactly at head 512. TILE 16 brings it to 16 KB per stage so several workgroups co-reside and loads overlap compute. BLOCK_M has to stay large enough for K/V reuse and the QK^T M-dimension, while the fp32 accumulator (BLOCK_M x 512) grows with it; M64 / T16 / stages 2 / warps 4 was the measured optimum.

The same tile on other head sizes goes the other way, hence the `D_GEQ_512` condition instead of touching any default:

| shape (fp8, 16k) | default | TILE 16 | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| head 512 | 115.6 ms | 26.0 ms | 4.44x |
| head 256 | 12.10 ms | 11.61 ms | 1.04x |
| head 128 | 3.45 ms | 7.88 ms | 0.44x |

The key is deliberately dtype-agnostic: at head 512 the small tile is needed regardless of dtype, and `TILE_SIZE_MIN 32` on the `DT_fp8_fp8` keys is exactly what blocks it for fp8 today. `Q_GEQ_256` restricts it to prefill; the `Q_LEQ_1` decode entries are untouched.

## Relation to #5063

#5063 adds the same key with BLOCK_M 128 for the same reason (the D-axis shadowing). M128/T16 and M64/T16 have not been compared side by side on gfx942; happy to run that on MI325X and converge on one entry. Only gfx942 is changed here (measured); the gfx950 table has the same structure and may deserve the same look.

## Testing

- Kernel bake-off and vLLM end-to-end numbers above; raw logs available on request.
- The key uses the same axes and form as the existing `D_GEQ_512.Q_LEQ_1*` entries, so it is matched by the same lookup path (`explain("attn_2d", ...)` prints the selected entry; with this change a (D=512, Q>=256) prefill should report `D_GEQ_512.Q_GEQ_256`).

## Side notes (not changed here)

- `TILE_SIZE_MIN 32` on `D_GEQ_512.DT_fp8_fp8` comes from the pre-shuffled-KV assert; whether the plain fp8 decode path still needs it is worth a look.
- Resolving the D axis before Q means any `Q_GEQ_*` entry is unreachable for head sizes that have a D key; composite keys work around it, the ordering is the root cause.

title: [Triton/Gluon] Fix BLOCK_M for large prefill with head_size >= 256
body:
## Summary

Fix `BLOCK_M` for large prefill (max_seqlen_q >= 256) when `head_size >= 256`. Models like **Gemma-4** (full-attn head_dim=512, sliding head_dim=256) previously ran large prefills at `BLOCK_M=16` — 16 query rows per program instead of 128 — causing severe underutilization.

Measured on gfx942 (MI325X) with Gemma-4-31B FP8-block, 32k in / 1k out:
- **5.9% e2e latency improvement** (17.13s → 16.12s warm avg)
- **7.8% mean ITL improvement** (16.8ms → 15.5ms/tok)

## What changed

Upstream #5088 refactored unified attention from Python `select_2d_config` heuristics to per-arch JSON config tables (`aiter/ops/triton/configs/<arch>/triton/attention/unified_attention/DEFAULT.json`). This PR is rewritten against that architecture — **config-only change** (1 JSON file, gfx942, +16 lines), no Python/kernel code touched.

The bug survives the refactor: the D-axis `D_GEQ_512`/`D_GEQ_256` entries match Gemma-4's head sizes *before* the `Q_GEQ_256` entry (BLOCK_M=128) is ever consulted — the lookup's candidate ordering (GEQ sorted descending, then `any`) tries `(D_GEQ_512, any)` before `(any, Q_GEQ_256)`, so large-head prefill fell through to `D_GEQ_512`/`D_GEQ_256` at BLOCK_M=16. Both gfx942 and gfx950 tables are affected.

New composite keys (matching the head-size-specific warps/stages/TILE from #4044):

| Key | BLOCK_M | num_warps | num_stages | TILE_SIZE |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `D_GEQ_512.Q_GEQ_256` | 128 | 4 | 2 | 16 |
| `D_GEQ_256.Q_GEQ_256` | 128 | 2 | 2 | 32 |

The `_unified_attention_2d_triton` wrapper already raises `BLOCK_M` to `next_power_of_2(num_queries_per_kv)` after the lookup, so these entries remain safe for any GQA ratio (the earlier review note about BLOCK_M clobbering the nqpkv floor is handled there).

The keys are intentionally dtype-agnostic (no `DT_*` component → matches any dtype), faithfully preserving the dtype-agnostic behavior of the original #4044/#5063 Python fix: bf16 large-head prefill also ran at BLOCK_M=128 there. Decode (Q=1), small-head prefill (D≤128), and everything below the composite gates are unchanged — verified by table-lookup simulation for D∈{128,256,512} × Q∈{1,16384} × fp8/bf16 (gfx942 table; the gfx950 table was verified the same way before its entries were dropped — see the gfx950 note below).


### Scope

gfx942 (CDNA) only — where the fix matches pre-refactor behavior and is benchmark-verified end-to-end. The same D-before-Q key shadowing exists in the gfx1250 table, but RDNA large-prefill used different parameters pre-refactor (BLOCK_M=64, head-size tiers skipped for `is_rdna`), the gfx1250 table is independently tuned, and RDNA large-head LDS overflow has in-flight guard work (#4868, #4385) — so gfx1250 needs its own tuning pass with RDNA4 hardware, not a port of these keys.

## Related PRs

- **#4044** (merged): the original Python-tier fix for Gemma-4 unified attention; this PR ports its intent into the new JSON-table architecture.
- **#5027** (merged): fused QK-norm + RoPE + KV-cache with head_dim 512 and weightless V-norm — the complementary Gemma-4 serving path (same model motivated both; this PR tunes attention, #5027 fuses the norm/rope/cache ops).

## Test plan

- Table-lookup simulation (gfx942 + gfx950): Gemma-4 full (D=512, Q≥256) and sliding (D=256, Q≥256) now select the new keys with BLOCK_M=128; decode (Q=1) and small-head paths unchanged.
- `black`/`ruff` clean (no Python changes).
- End-to-end Gemma-4-31B FP8-block on MI325X: numbers above.

AI assistance was used; a human reviewed every line.

title: [HIP] fix(sampling): drop unused out_idx workspace in topk_renorm_from_probs
body:
## Motivation

`top_k_renorm_probs` writes out of bounds on any sampler batch that mixes a request setting `top_k` with one that does not. This crashes vLLM serving Kimi-K3 on MI355X with `Memory access fault by GPU node-N`, one fault per TP rank. No unusual flags are needed - two ordinary concurrent requests are enough.

At a production vocab the same write usually does *not* fault: the overrun is ~640 KB, which typically lands inside the allocator's 2 MB rounding slack and corrupts silently instead. The write happens on **every** mixed-`top_k` batch; only the crash is probabilistic. An absence of reported crashes is therefore not evidence that the bug is absent.

## Technical Details

The op takes `(probs, maybe_top_k_arr, top_k_val)`. Per the convention this repo's own tests use (`_to_tensor_scalar_tuple` in `op_tests/test_sampling.py`), passing a per-row tensor sends `top_k_val = 0`, so the host wrapper falls back to a hardcoded `max_k`:

```cpp
int max_k = top_k_val;                                            // sampling.cuh:1414
if (max_k <= 0) max_k = 50;                                       // :1415
size_t out_idx_bytes = (size_t)batch_size * max_k * sizeof(int);  // :1426
```

`radix_topk_one_block_kernel` then takes its stride from that host scalar but its bound from the per-row array:

```cpp
const IdxT k_actual = (top_k_arr != nullptr) ? top_k_arr[batch_id] : k;  // :458
if (out_idx) out_idx += batch_id * k;                                   // :474  stride = max_k = 50
...
out_idx[i] = i < row_len ? i + rowStart : -1;   // bounded by k_actual  // :480
```

Any row with `k > 50` overruns its 50-int slot. vLLM encodes "top_k disabled" as `k = vocab_size`, so such a row takes the `row_len <= k_actual` branch at `:477` and writes `vocab_size` ints - 163840 for Kimi-K3, ~640 KB - into a 200-byte slot, running off the ee
nd of the workspace.

The fix is to stop allocating and passing that buffer. `out_idx` has no consumer on this path: the only downstream reader is `TopKRenormWriteOnlyKernel(probs, pivot_buf, norm_buf, renormed_probs, vocab_size)` at `:1450`, which takes no indices. Every `out_idx` store is already null-guarded, and `WRITE_TOPK_VALUES` is `false` here, so the value store nested inside the `if (out_idx)` guard at `:481` is compiled out regardless - no writes are lost. `max_k` still drives `k_actual` correctly on the scalar path, which is unaffected.

Present since #3217.

## Test Plan

Two tests added to `op_tests/test_sampling.py`:

- `test_top_k_renorm_probs_per_row_k` - per-row tensor path, mixing `k=10`, `k=100` and `k=vocab_size`. The existing `test_top_k_renorm_probs` only ever passes a Python `int`, taking the scalar path where `max_k == k_actual` and the indexing is exactly in bounds. Thh
e tensor overload had no coverage at all, which is why CI never caught this.
- `test_top_k_renorm_probs_mixed_batch_does_not_fault` - regression guard for `k = [50, vocab_size]`. Runs in a child process, because the workspace is a per-process `static` allocated on first call, so a process that has already called the op is a spent trial. Usess
 a 1M vocab to put the overrun ~4 MB past the end, clearing the 2 MB slack so it faults deterministically rather than flaking.

Reproduction note: `not_built()` (`csrc/cpp_itfs/utils.py:297`) keys the JIT cache on `lib.so` existing, and the folder name is the md5 of the kwargs - empty for this op - so editing `sampling.cuh` silently reuses a stale binary. Use a fresh `AITER_ROOT_DIR` whee
n comparing before and after.

## Test Result

MI355X (gfx950), ROCm 7.2, torch 2.10:

- Regression guard, unpatched: **5/5** fresh processes abort with `Memory access fault by GPU node-N` at a 2 MB-aligned address. Patched: **6/6** pass.
- At vocab 163840 the unpatched build survived, confirming the silent-corruption case described above.
- Full `op_tests/test_sampling.py` on the patched build: **358 passed, 4 skipped**.

title: [HIP] [OPUS] [JIT] [Bugfix] Stop an unbaked tuned kernel id from killing the rank, and key the lookup on CU count
body:
Stops a tuned row naming a kernel id this build does not contain from killing the rank. The id dispatcher now raises a distinct type, `tuned_gemm` catches it and falls back to torch, and the shape is remembered so a serving loop pays for the miss once. That is a prerequisite for loading a 128-CU CSV in serving at all (ROCm/aiter#4735 bug 2). Keys the opus a16w16 GEMM lookup on CU count, and starts dispatching gfx1250's tuned split-K kernels, which the build already contained but nothing ever selected.

Stacked on #5340, which introduces `AITER_GPU_TARGETS`: build targets written as `gfx:cu_num` pairs, as in `AITER_GPU_TARGETS="gfx950:128;gfx950:256"`, and the build and runtime target resolution behind them. The opus codegen here resolves its rows and its compile set through those targets, which is what lets one build carry a tuned winner per SKU.

## Motivation

**The lookup key had no CU count.** Tuned rows are keyed `(gfx, cu_num, ...)`, but the generated C++ tables were keyed `(M, N, K)` per arch. A shape tuned on two SKUs of one arch kept whichever row was read last, and the other SKU silently fell back to its heuristic. One build could never hold both. No checked-in CSV carries two CU counts for one arch today, so this is a fix ahead of the need.

**gfx1250's split-K winners were unreachable.** `opus_gemm.cu` resolved every gfx1250 shape through `opus_dispatch_a16w16_gfx1250<fp32_t>`, and rows bucket into tables by output dtype. Every checked-in gfx1250 opus row is bf16-output, so the fp32 table it consulted was empty and the 150 baked split-K winners never dispatched through it. The 147 `.co` winners did dispatch, through the separate `.co` lookup ahead of it.

**A tuned row naming a kernel id the build lacks killed the rank.** The CSV ships every target's winners; a build bakes only its own, so the two disagree whenever a package is used on a target it was not built for.

## Changes

One shared key type and search (`csrc/opus_gemm/include/opus_gemm_lookup_entry.cuh`) replaces three per-arch comparator copies. The ladder is exact CU, then a legacy `cu_num=0` row, then a miss so the caller reaches its heuristic, which is what the Python lookup already does when no row matches the live count. `allow_fallback` gating keeps a count-less `.co` row from shadowing an exact-CU split-K winner, which is the rule `opus_gemm.cu` depends on.

Codegen filters the emitted rows and the compile set through one target resolution, so the kid set and the lookup tables cannot disagree about which arch the build serves. The generated `OPUS_GFX1250_WS_PARTIAL_BYTES` is static-asserted against the bf16 workspace the host allocates, so a baked kid storing a wider partial fails the build rather than overrunning the buffer.

## Scope

1. **gfx1250 split-K shapes move from heuristic to tuned, and the `.co` shapes become CU-conditional.** No CI job exercises gfx1250 (`GPU_ARCH_LIST` in `aiter-test.yaml` is `gfx942;gfx950`). The A/B is cheap for the split-K half, since the old path is today's heuristic. The `.co` half is the exposure: that lookup was shape-only and always hit, it now goes through the CU-aware search, and every `.co` row is stamped 256, so on silicon reporting any other count those 147 shapes fall to the heuristic instead.
2. **`aiter/tuned_gemm.py` is the one non-opus file here, and it is the live serving route.** `tuned_gemm.opus_gemm` called the id dispatcher unguarded, so an unbaked id escaped and killed the rank. The dispatcher now raises `unbaked_kernel_error`, registered through pybind as `UnbakedKernelError`; `try_opus_gemm_a16w16_tune` catches it by type, returns False, and `tuned_gemm` falls back to `torch_gemm`, which is what the same function already does when opus is unavailable. A split-K workspace OOM is a `RuntimeError` too but not that type, so it still propagates. The `(id, splitK)` is remembered, because the dispatcher writes to stderr before it raises and a serving loop pays for that once.

## Testing

`op_tests/test_gemm_codegen.py`, `op_tests/test_opus_serving_fallback.py` and `op_tests/opus/test_opus_basic` all pass, the last building and running on a host with no GPU. One new codegen case, `test_opus_bakes_both_skus`, covers per-SKU baking, both SKUs keeping their own winner, and mixed-schema CSVs with a NaN `cu_num`. The C++ cases cover exact-CU selection and the fallback ladder, including the miss that ends it, and `test_opus_serving_fallback.py` covers each serving-degradation path. `ruff` and `black` are clean.

title: [CI] [JIT] [Build] [Bugfix] Build pybind modules against torch's bundled pybind11; drop pip pybind11 dep
body:
## Problem

aiter's JIT builder (`aiter/jit/utils/cpp_extension.py`) appends the **pip-installed** pybind11's include path via `pybind11.get_include()`, emitted as a `-I` **ahead of** torch's bundled headers (`-isystem <torch>/include`). So every compiled pybind module resolves `#include <pybind11/...>` to whatever pybind11 pip has.

pybind11 **3.1.0** (2026-08-06) bumped `PYBIND11_INTERNALS_VERSION` **11 → 12**. Modules built at different pip epochs then disagree on the internals version, and pybind11 does not share registered types across internals versions. The prebuilt `module_aiter_core` (which registers `aiter_tensor_t`) and a JIT module built later end up incompatible:

```
TypeError: fmha_fwd_bf16_opus_fwd(): incompatible function arguments.
  Invoked with: <aiter.jit.module_aiter_core.aiter_tensor_t object at ...>
```

Fixes #4770.

## Root cause detail

`module_aiter_core` is a **torch-free** (`torch_exclude:True`) pybind module — it registers `aiter_tensor_t` and is loaded via `ctypes`. It has no torch headers on its include path, so it previously took its pybind headers **only from pip**. Torch-backed consumer modules (e.g. `fmha`) also took pip's. Because they were compiled at different times, a drifting pip pybind11 desynchronized producer and consumers.

## Fix

torch already bundles pybind11 at `torch/include` (3.0.1 / internals **v11** in torch 2.10), which satisfied aiter's former `pybind11>=3.0.1`. This PR builds **every** python module — torch-backed **and** torch-free — against torch's bundled pybind headers:

- Drop the pip `get_include()` append entirely.
- For `torch_exclude` builds (which otherwise omit `torch/include`), add `torch/include` back **only for header resolution** — pybind is header-only, so the torch-free `.so` gains **no runtime libtorch dependency**.

Now producer (`module_aiter_core`) and all consumers compile against the *same* pybind (torch's), so `aiter_tensor_t` stays ABI-compatible regardless of any pip pybind11. (Vendoring pybind instead would re-break this: torch-backed modules must use torch's pybind to interop with torch types, so everything has to converge on torch's copy.)

With the ABI sourced from torch, **aiter no longer needs a pip pybind11 dependency at all**. Removed from:
- `requirements.txt`, `pyproject.toml` (`build-system.requires`), `setup.py` (`install_requires`)
- the `pip install --upgrade pybind11` steps in CI workflows (`aiter-test`, `atom-test`, `kimi-downstream`, `kimi-perf-downstream`, `vllm_benchmark`) and `.github/requirements/triton-test.txt`

## Test

`rocm/pytorch:latest` (torch 2.10.0+rocm, bundled pybind **v11**), **with no pip pybind11 installed**, building trivial pybind modules through aiter's `load()`:

| Module | `is_python_module` | `torch_exclude` | `.so` internals | links libtorch? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| torch-backed | True | False | `__pybind11_internals_v11__` ✅ | yes (expected) |
| torch-free (like `module_aiter_core`) | True | True | `__pybind11_internals_v11__` ✅ | **no** ✅ |

Both compile with **zero pip pybind11 present**. For contrast, with `pip install pybind11==3.1.0`, the pre-change code produced `__pybind11_internals_v12__` (the mismatch); this change yields `v11` regardless.

title: [Bugfix] Include headers necessary for ROCm 10.0.0
body:
## Motivation

vLLM CI fails on the [ROCm 10.0.0rc2 release](https://rocm.prereleases.amd.com/whl-multi-arch/rocm/), partly due to missing includes in Aiter. ROCm 10.0.0rc2 uses `hipcub` 5.0.0 that does not transitively include the attributes listed below.

Fixes #4769 

## Technical Details

`hipcub::Min` and `hipcub::Max` are in [thread_operators.hpp](https://github.com/ROCm/rocm-libraries/blob/a66ba22a4ce40f703f1168d10ead0a36f9258cea/projects/hipcub/hipcub/include/hipcub/backend/rocprim/thread/thread_operators.hpp#L112-L133). `hipcub::Traits` is in [util_type.hpp](https://github.com/ROCm/rocm-libraries/blob/1eae5f68a435f7de4e42ad63b9bab924d2382a29/projects/hipcub/hipcub/include/hipcub/backend/rocprim/util_type.hpp#L838-L840).

## Test Plan

Reproducer for compiler fail and, with changes, compiler success:
```bash
WORKDIR="$(mktemp -d)"
trap 'rm -rf "$WORKDIR"' EXIT
cd "$WORKDIR"

echo "== Installing ROCm SDK 10.0.0rc2 into a throwaway uv venv =="
uv venv --python 3.12 .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install --index-url https://rocm.prereleases.amd.com/whl-multi-arch "rocm[libraries,devel]==10.0.0rc2"
rocm-sdk init

echo "== Fetching upstream AITER's sampling.cuh from source (main) =="
AITER_RAW="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ROCm/aiter/main/csrc/cpp_itfs/sampling"
mkdir -p sampling
curl -sL -o sampling/sampling.cuh "$AITER_RAW/sampling.cuh"
curl -sL -o sampling/vec_dtypes.cuh "$AITER_RAW/vec_dtypes.cuh"

SAMPLING_CUH="sampling/sampling.cuh"

ROCM_DEVEL="$(python3 -c 'import _rocm_sdk_devel, os; print(os.path.dirname(_rocm_sdk_devel.__file__))')"
CLANGXX="$ROCM_DEVEL/lib/llvm/bin/clang++"
echo "== Compiler under test: $("$CLANGXX" --version | head -1) =="

for variant in unpatched patched; do
    if [[ "$variant" == "patched" ]]; then
        sed -i '/#include <hipcub\/block\/block_store.hpp>/a\
#include <hipcub/util_type.hpp>\
#include <hipcub/thread/thread_operators.hpp>' "$SAMPLING_CUH"
    fi

    echo "== [$variant] Compiling sampling.cuh =="
    if "$CLANGXX" -w -x hip -c "$SAMPLING_CUH" -o sampling.o --offload-arch=gfx942 -I"$ROCM_DEVEL/include"; then
        echo "== [$variant] OK: sampling.cuh compiled successfully =="
    else
        echo "== [$variant] FAILED: sampling.cuh did not compile =="
    fi
done
```

## Test Result

The test succeeds when the needed headers are included.

## Submission Checklist

- [X] Look over the contributing guidelines at https://github.com/ROCm/ROCm/blob/develop/CONTRIBUTING.md#pull-requests.

I didn't run the pre-commit hooks in order not to pollute this minimal change.
